lessons.title: Charge, current and static
lessons.teach: Charge comes in two signs: like charges repel and opposite charges attract. A neutral object is not empty; its positive and negative charge simply balance. The force between two charges falls with the square of distance, so doubling the gap quarters the force. Current is the rate charge passes a point: current equals charge divided by time, current in amps, charge in coulombs, time in seconds. Conventional current points the way positive charge would move, so electrons in a wire drift the opposite way. Electrostatic discharge, a quick jump of charge between objects at different potentials, can damage a chip even when you feel and see nothing. That is why you wear a grounded wrist strap before handling integrated circuits.

lessons.title: Voltage compares two points
lessons.teach: A voltage always compares two points. V A B means the potential at A minus the potential at B; reverse the order and the sign flips. Ground is simply the node we choose to call zero volts. It is a reference, and the negative battery terminal is not automatically ground. Moving the reference changes the number given to each node, but every difference between two nodes stays the same. A voltmeter follows the same rule: its reading equals the red-probe potential minus the black-probe potential. Red on 7 volts and black on 2 volts reads plus 5 volts.

lessons.title: Series drops and node voltage
lessons.teach: In a series circuit the same current flows through every resistor, and Kirchhoff's voltage law says the drops add up to the supply. Combine that with Ohm's law, voltage equals current times resistance, voltage in volts, current in amps, resistance in ohms, and the current is the supply voltage divided by the total resistance. Example: 12 volts across 2 kilohms on top and 4 kilohms at the bottom, in series. Total resistance is 6 kilohms, so the current is 2 milliamps. The drops are 4 volts and 8 volts, which add to 12. With the bottom of the 4 kilohm resistor grounded, the junction sits at 8 volts.

lessons.title: Prefixes and four-step calculations
lessons.teach: Engineering notation uses powers of ten in steps of three, written as prefixes, with the number kept between 1 and 999. Kilo is ten to the three, milli ten to the minus three, micro ten to the minus six. Moving to a smaller prefix makes the number a thousand times bigger: 0.025 millivolts is 25 microvolts. Letter case matters: small m is milli, capital M is mega. Every calculation uses four steps: name the quantity, write the formula, substitute values with units, give the answer with units. For example, Ohm's law, current equals voltage over resistance, amps, volts, ohms: 4.7 volts over 4.7 kilohms is 1 milliamp. A result off by exactly a thousand points to a prefix slip.

lessons.title: Drawing IC pins and designators
lessons.teach: On a circuit drawing, each IC pin's number goes outside the body and its function goes inside. A horizontal pin has its number sitting just above the wire; a vertical pin has it beside the wire, so wires never run through the numbers. Every IC gets a designator, U1, U2, U3, with the part number, such as 74LS47, written below it. To find pin 1 on the real chip, hold it with the notch at the top; pin 1 is top left, and numbering runs down that side and back up the other. A bar over a pin name means the function is active low.

lessons.title: Gates drawn where they work
lessons.teach: A circuit drawing draws each gate where it does its job, not grouped inside a picture of the chip. The link to hardware is kept by labels. U1 names the package. A suffix letter, as in U1A or U1B, names which gate inside it. The part number sits below, and pin numbers go on the leads. A quad package has one supply pin and one ground pin, so its power connections are shown on exactly one of its gates, together with a decoupling capacitor from V C C to ground. Unused gates are still drawn, in a column at the edge, with inputs tied to plus 5 volts and outputs marked N C.

lessons.title: Binary place values and fractions
lessons.teach: Binary uses only 0 and 1, and each place is worth twice the place to its right. From the right the weights are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. To convert to decimal, add the weights of the places holding a 1: one zero one one is 8 plus 2 plus 1, which is 11. Places to the right of the binary point keep halving: one half, one quarter, one eighth. So one zero one point zero one one is 4 plus 1 plus a quarter plus an eighth, which is 5.375. Never read binary fraction digits as if they were decimal.

lessons.title: Decimal to binary
lessons.teach: To convert decimal to binary, subtract the largest weight that fits and mark a 1 there, then carry on with what is left. For 43: 32 fits, leaving 11; 16 does not fit, so 0; 8 fits, leaving 3; 4 does not, so 0; 2 fits, leaving 1; and 1 fits. That gives one zero one zero one one. The other method is repeated division by two: write each remainder, then read them in reverse, last remainder first, because the first remainder is the ones bit. Always check by adding the weights back up.

lessons.title: Octal and hex groupings
lessons.teach: Octal is base eight, digits 0 to 7, place weights 1, 8, 64. Each octal digit is exactly three bits, so group binary in threes from the right: one one one, zero one one is 7 and 3, octal 73. Hexadecimal is base sixteen, using 0 to 9 then A to F for ten to fifteen. Each hex digit is four bits, a nibble, so group binary in fours: zero one one zero, one zero one one is 6 and B, hex 6B. For hex to decimal, the left digit counts sixteens: hex 2F is 2 times 16 plus 15, which is 47. For decimal to hex, count the sixteens, then write the remainder as one digit.

lessons.title: BCD: four bits per digit
lessons.teach: Binary coded decimal, or B C D, codes each decimal digit separately in four bits. So 59 in B C D is zero one zero one for the 5, then one zero zero one for the 9. That differs from pure binary, where 59 is one number, one one one zero one one. Only the groups zero zero zero zero to one zero zero one, 0 to 9, are valid; the six patterns for ten to fifteen are invalid in B C D. A three-digit display needs twelve B C D bits, four per digit.

lessons.title: ASCII character codes
lessons.teach: A S C I I, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, gives each letter, digit, symbol and control character a seven-bit code, 128 codes in all, usually stored in a byte with a leading zero. Capital A is hex 41, and the capitals count up from there, so B is hex 42. Lowercase a is hex 61. The digit characters start at hex 30, so the character 5 is hex 35. That means the character 5 is not the number five: the code names a symbol to display, not a value to calculate with.

lessons.title: Bits, states and status flags
lessons.teach: With n bits you get two to the n different patterns. As unsigned numbers they run from 0 up to two to the n, minus 1. Four bits give 16 patterns, 0 to 15. Six bits give 64 patterns, 0 to 63. To encode a number of states, pick the smallest n whose two to the n reaches it: 40 states need 6 bits, because 5 bits only give 32. Bits can also be status flags, where each bit position reports one condition. Then the pattern is a set of yes or no answers, read position by position, not a single number.

lessons.title: Gray code: one bit at a time
lessons.source: Assigned problems guide, Gray code handout
lessons.teach: In Gray code, neighbouring values differ in exactly one bit, unlike binary, where 3 to 4 flips three bits. To convert binary to Gray, copy the first bit; then each next Gray bit is the exclusive OR of that binary bit and the binary bit to its left, where same gives 0 and different gives 1. So binary one one zero zero becomes one zero one zero. To convert Gray back to binary, copy the first bit; then each Gray 1 flips the binary bit you just found, and each Gray 0 keeps it.

lessons.title: Analog versus digital
lessons.teach: An analog quantity varies smoothly and continuously, like temperature, wind speed or sound pressure. A digital quantity takes distinct steps, and in binary systems just two states, 0 and 1. To bring an analog signal into a computer you use an analog-to-digital converter, an A D C, which outputs a digital code. A digital-to-analog converter, a D A C, does the reverse, turning codes back into a smooth voltage, as a music player does before the speaker. Digital signals tolerate noise better, because a slightly noisy HIGH still reads as HIGH.

lessons.title: Period and frequency
lessons.teach: A clock waveform repeats. Its period is the time for one full cycle, measured from one rising edge to the next rising edge. Frequency is the number of cycles per second. They are reciprocals: frequency equals one over period, frequency in hertz, period in seconds. Handy pairs: 1 kilohertz goes with 1 millisecond, and 1 megahertz goes with 1 microsecond. So 2 megahertz has a period of half a microsecond, and a 100 microsecond period means 10 kilohertz. An oscilloscope shows voltage on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis.

lessons.title: Duty cycle
lessons.teach: A pulse waveform spends part of each period HIGH and the rest LOW. The period is the HIGH time plus the LOW time. Duty cycle is the fraction of the period spent HIGH: duty cycle equals HIGH time divided by period, times 100 percent, with both times in the same unit. For example, HIGH for 20 microseconds out of an 80 microsecond period is 25 percent. Duty cycle and frequency are separate ideas: you can change how long the pulse stays HIGH without changing how often it repeats.

lessons.title: Serial versus parallel data
lessons.teach: Serial transmission sends one bit per clock period down a single line; Kleitz sends the least significant bit first. Parallel transmission uses one line per bit and sends a whole group in a single clock period. The time to send equals the number of clock periods used, times the period. Example: at 1 megahertz the period is 1 microsecond. Eight bits in serial take 8 microseconds; on an eight-bit parallel bus they take 1 microsecond. Parallel is faster in this model, but it needs more wires and circuitry.

lessons.title: Poles and throws
lessons.teach: A mechanical switch is named by poles and throws. A pole is one independent path the switch controls; the instructor counts the pivot points of the moving contacts. A throw is a destination each pole can connect to. S P S T, single pole single throw, makes or breaks one path, and its open position is not a second throw. S P D T connects one common terminal to either of two destinations. A double-pole switch has two pivots moving together, shown by a dashed link, but their circuits stay separate. A stereo selector with three inputs needs D P 3 T.

lessons.title: Relays: coil and contacts
lessons.teach: A relay is a switch worked by an electromagnet. Current through its coil pulls the contacts over. Normal means the coil is de-energized. Normally open, N O, contacts are open at rest and close when the coil is energized. Normally closed, N C, contacts are closed at rest and open when energized. A closed contact is an ideal short, with zero volts across it; an open contact carries no current but can have voltage across it. So N O contacts wired across the lower resistor of a divider short it when the coil is energized, pulling the output to zero volts.

lessons.title: Pull-ups, pull-downs and floating inputs
lessons.teach: A pull-up resistor runs from the supply to the output node, and a switch connects that node to ground. Switch open: no current, so the resistor drops nothing and the output sits at the supply, HIGH, while the open switch holds the full supply across it. Switch closed: the output is grounded, LOW, and the resistor limits current; current equals voltage over resistance, amps, volts, ohms, so 5 volts over 1 kilohm is 5 milliamps. A pull-down swaps the parts, so released is LOW and pressed is HIGH. With no resistor at all, an open switch leaves the input floating, with no defined level.

lessons.title: Diode bias and series circuits
lessons.teach: A diode passes conventional current from anode to cathode only; the bar on its symbol is the cathode. It is forward biased when the anode is more positive than the cathode, so judge by anode minus cathode, not either voltage alone. In the course model a conducting silicon diode holds about 0.7 volts, and a reverse-biased diode is open. Assume a state, then check. Five volts through a forward diode and 1 kilohm: the resistor gets 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts, and Ohm's law, current equals voltage over resistance, gives 4.3 milliamps. Reverse the diode and no current flows.

lessons.title: Diode AND and OR gates
lessons.teach: Diodes can make simple gates. In a diode AND, a resistor pulls the output up toward 5 volts, and each input connects through a diode with its cathode on the input. If any input goes to 0 volts, that diode conducts and clamps the output at 0.7 volts, a LOW. Only when all inputs are HIGH does the output stay HIGH. In a diode OR, a resistor pulls the output down to ground and each input drives an anode. Any input at 5 volts conducts and lifts the output to 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts, a HIGH.

lessons.title: Transistor switch and inverter
lessons.teach: A bipolar transistor has a base, a collector and an emitter. For an N P N switch, positive base drive through a base resistor turns it on: the collector-to-emitter path acts as a short, called saturation. No base current means cutoff, an open path. In the common-emitter inverter the input drives the base, the emitter is grounded, and a collector resistor pulls the collector up; the output is the collector. Input HIGH, transistor on, output LOW. Input LOW, transistor off, output HIGH. Base current equals input voltage minus 0.7, divided by base resistance, amps, volts, ohms.

lessons.title: Loading the inverter output
lessons.teach: When the inverter's transistor is off, the output is not guaranteed to be the full supply. A load from the output to ground forms a divider with the collector resistor: output voltage equals supply times load resistance, over collector resistance plus load resistance, all in volts and ohms. With 5 volts, a 1 kilohm collector resistor and a 10 kilohm load, the output is about 4.55 volts; add more loads and it sags further. A small collector resistor helps the HIGH, but passes a large current when the transistor turns on. T T L's totem-pole output fixes this with an active pull-up transistor.

lessons.title: TTL and the hex inverter
lessons.teach: T T L stands for transistor-transistor logic: gates built from bipolar transistors, diodes and resistors on one chip, running from a 5 volt supply. The simplest T T L function is the inverter, drawn as a triangle with a small bubble on its output. The 7404 is a hex inverter, and hex here means six, so the package holds six inverters. Inside each one are four transistors, two diodes and four resistors, ending in a totem-pole output stage. The symbol is the abstraction; the transistor circuit is what is really on the chip.

lessons.title: Inside a TTL input
lessons.teach: The T T L input transistor has its base pulled toward 5 volts by a resistor. With the input LOW, current flows out through the base-emitter junction into the input pin, so the next stage stays off. With the input HIGH, that path is blocked, and the resistor's current flows instead through the base-collector junction into the next stage, turning it on. A protection diode sits on the input, anode at ground and cathode at the pin. At 0 or 5 volts it does not conduct. If ringing pulls the pin below about minus 0.7 volts, it conducts and clamps the pin there.

lessons.title: Unused inputs: tie them high
lessons.teach: An input left unconnected is floating. It picks up noise and its level is effectively random, causing failures that come and go and are hard to find. Every input must be driven or tied. For T T L, tie unused inputs HIGH, straight to plus 5 volts in this lab. Tying them LOW also works logically, but a LOW T T L input has to push current out of the input stage, up to about 0.4 milliamps each for the L S family, so the chip draws more supply current. A HIGH input draws very little. Unused outputs are different: leave them unconnected and mark them N C.

lessons.title: AND and OR gate ICs
lessons.teach: Gates come packaged in integrated circuits, usually 14-pin dual in-line packages. The 7408 holds four two-input AND gates, the 7432 four two-input OR gates, the 7411 three three-input AND gates, and the 7421 two four-input AND gates. On these 14-pin T T L parts, pin 14 is V C C, plus 5 volts, and pin 7 is ground. On the 7408, the first gate takes inputs on pins 1 and 2 and outputs on pin 3. Always check the exact datasheet before wiring, because not every chip uses the same arrangement.

lessons.title: NAND, NOR and inverter ICs
lessons.teach: The same 14-pin family includes the 7400, four two-input NAND gates; the 7402, four two-input NOR gates; and the 7404, six inverters. The 7410 holds three three-input NAND gates. C M O S versions exist too, such as the 4001 NOR. Power is still pin 14 and pin 7 on these T T L parts, but the gate pins are not all the same. On the 7402 NOR, the first gate's output is pin 1 and its inputs are pins 2 and 3, the reverse of the 7408. Always wire from the exact part's top-view pinout.

lessons.title: Input levels and CMOS
lessons.source: Quiz study pack, TTL input limits; Kleitz §2–11
lessons.teach: A logic input reads a voltage range, not an exact value. For the 74 L S 00 example in your notes, any input up to 0.8 volts is guaranteed LOW, and anything from 2.0 volts up is guaranteed HIGH. Between 0.8 and 2.0 volts nothing is guaranteed. These are input limits; outputs have their own separate guarantees. C M O S is the other main family, built from complementary M O S transistors, and it draws very little power while it is not switching. Floating C M O S inputs are especially troublesome, so they must be tied too.

lessons.title: AND and OR gates
lessons.teach: An AND gate outputs HIGH only when every input is HIGH; any LOW forces LOW. Its equation is X equals A and B, and it acts like switches in series. An OR gate outputs HIGH when at least one input is HIGH, and LOW only when all are LOW. Its equation uses a plus sign, but read it as or: in Boolean algebra, 1 or 1 is 1. It acts like switches in parallel. A truth table lists every input combination, and n inputs give two to the n rows. In an AND table only the all-ones row is 1; in an OR table only the all-zeros row is 0.

lessons.title: Reading timing charts
lessons.teach: A timing chart plots several signals against one shared time axis, the way a logic analyzer displays them. To find a gate's output, slice the chart vertically. Mark a boundary wherever any input changes, and in each interval read every input's level and apply the gate's rule. Example: A is HIGH from 0 to 4 microseconds, and B is HIGH from 2 to 6 microseconds. An AND output is HIGH only where both overlap, from 2 to 4 microseconds. An OR output is HIGH wherever either one is HIGH, from 0 to 6 microseconds.

lessons.title: Enable and disable
lessons.teach: A gate can let a signal through or block it. With an AND gate, hold the control input HIGH and the output copies the data signal: the gate is enabled. Hold the control LOW and the output is stuck LOW: disabled. That is how a clock is started and stopped: run equals enable and clock. An OR gate works the other way round: control LOW passes the signal, control HIGH forces the output HIGH. The value that takes over the output, 0 for AND and 1 for OR, is called the controlling value.

lessons.title: Inverter, NAND and NOR
lessons.teach: An inverter complements its single input: 1 becomes 0, and 0 becomes 1. The small bubble on a symbol means inversion. A NAND gate is an AND with its output inverted, so its output is LOW only when every input is HIGH, and HIGH otherwise. A NOR gate is an OR with its output inverted, so its output is HIGH only when every input is LOW. Their equations put one bar over the whole AND or OR result: X equals A and B, all complemented. The bar covers the whole expression, not each variable separately.

lessons.title: Name the gate from its behaviour
lessons.teach: Each basic gate has a one-line rule. AND: HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH. OR: LOW only when all inputs are LOW. NAND: LOW only when all inputs are HIGH. NOR: HIGH only when all inputs are LOW. Inverter: the output is the opposite of its single input. Listen for two clues: which input row is the special one, and is the output there HIGH or LOW? Also, a NAND with one input held HIGH acts as an inverter for the other input, and so does a NOR with one input held LOW.

lessons.title: Probe and pulser troubleshooting
lessons.teach: A logic probe touches a point and shows its level: HIGH, LOW, or pulsing. A logic pulser injects short pulses into a point so you can watch what the circuit does with them. To test one input of a gate with a pulser, hold the other input at the value that lets the signal through. For AND and NAND that means HIGH, since a LOW would lock the output. For OR and NOR that means LOW, since a HIGH would lock it. Then check that the output pulses. Before blaming the chip, check its supply, its actual input pins and its load.

lessons.title: Making a waveform window
lessons.teach: Gates can carve a window out of timed waveforms, such as the outputs of a Johnson counter, which the chapter uses as a repeating waveform generator. Say A is HIGH from 1 to 6 microseconds, and B is HIGH from 3 to 8. You want an output HIGH only from 1 to 3. In that interval A is HIGH and B is LOW, so the output is A and B bar: invert B, then AND. To pass clock pulses only inside the window, AND the clock in as a third input.

lessons.title: Combinational logic and equations
lessons.teach: In combinational logic, signals flow one way, from inputs to output, and nothing is fed back, so the output depends only on the present inputs. Feed an output back and it becomes sequential logic. To read a circuit into algebra, give each gate's output its own letter, write one small equation per gate, and substitute at the end. For example, D equals A and B; F equals D bar; E equals A or C; and Z equals E and F. To count gates, count the AND, OR and inverter operations the expression needs.

lessons.title: Laws of Boolean algebra
lessons.teach: Three laws let you rearrange expressions. Commutative: order does not matter, so A and B equals B and A, and the same for OR. Associative: grouping does not matter, so A or the group B or C equals the group A or B, or C. That is why a four-input AND can be built from two-input ANDs. Distributive: A and the group B or C equals A and B, or A and C, like multiplying out brackets. Read the plus sign as OR and the dot as AND, never as plus and times.

lessons.title: Rules with 0, 1 and complements
lessons.teach: Kleitz lists simple rules. A and 0 is 0; A and 1 is A. A or 0 is A; A or 1 is 1. Notice the pair that trips people: 1 leaves A unchanged under AND but forces 1 under OR. A and A is A, not A squared, and A or A is A, not 2A. A and A bar is 0, since one of them is always 0, while A or A bar is 1. A double bar cancels: A double-bar is A. You can prove any of these by checking the two cases, A equals 0 and A equals 1.

lessons.title: Absorption and Rule 10
lessons.teach: Two look-alike rules make expressions shorter. Absorption: A or the group A and B equals A. If A is 1, the whole thing is 1; if A is 0, A and B is 0 too, so the result is 0. Either way it equals A. Kleitz's Rule 10 is different: A or the group A bar and B equals A or B. If A is 1, both sides are 1; if A is 0, the left side is B and so is the right. Changing A to A bar inside the second term changes the answer completely.

lessons.title: DeMorgan's theorem
lessons.teach: DeMorgan's theorem gets a bar off a group. The complement of A and B equals A bar or B bar. The complement of A or B equals A bar and B bar. The rule of thumb: break the bar, and change the operator. The bar lands on each variable, inverting it, and on the operator, flipping AND to OR or OR to AND. The common trap is inverting the variables but keeping the operator. Test it with A equals 1 and B equals 0: the complement of 1 and 0 is 1, but 0 and 1 is 0, so the operator must flip.

lessons.title: Simplify to sum of products
lessons.teach: To simplify, distribute, factor, then apply the rules. Kleitz's example: X equals B and the group A or C, then or C. Distribute to get A and B, or B and C, or C. Factor C out of the last two: C and the group B or 1. B or 1 is 1, and C and 1 is C, so X equals A and B, or C. The goal is sum of products: product terms such as A and B, ORed together, with no brackets and bars only on single variables. That form drops straight into a truth table. After DeMorgan, check whether a group is ANDed or ORed before distributing anything.

lessons.title: Resistor, capacitor and inductor models
lessons.teach: Lecture one introduced three ideal element models, each linking the voltage across an element to the current through it. A resistor: voltage equals current times resistance, voltage in volts, current in amps, resistance in ohms. A capacitor, measured in farads: its current equals capacitance times the rate of change of its voltage. An inductor, measured in henries: its voltage equals inductance times the rate of change of its current. The key idea is rate of change. If a capacitor's voltage holds steady, its ideal current is zero, even though the voltage itself is not zero. If an inductor's current holds steady, its ideal voltage is zero.

lessons.title: Ohm's law and the resistor graph
lessons.teach: Ohm's law: the voltage across a resistor equals the current through it times its resistance, voltage in volts, current in amps, resistance in ohms. Rearranged, current equals voltage over resistance, and resistance equals voltage over current. The voltage and the current must belong to the same resistor. A handy pairing: volts divided by kilohms gives milliamps, so 6 volts across 2 kilohms is 3 milliamps. On a graph with voltage up the side and current along the bottom, a fixed resistor is a straight line through the origin, and its slope is the resistance. A bigger resistance gives a steeper line.

lessons.title: Current direction and open paths
lessons.teach: Conventional current points the way positive charge would move. In a metal wire the moving charges are electrons, which are negative, so they drift opposite to the conventional current arrow. A resistor does not use up current: in a steady single loop, the same current enters and leaves every part, and what the resistor converts is energy, into heat. A closed path is complete; an open path is broken. An open switch carries no current, but it can still have a voltage across it. In a 6 volt loop with the switch open, the resistor drops nothing, so all 6 volts appears across the switch gap.

lessons.title: Precision, accuracy and resolution
lessons.teach: Three words describe measurement quality. Precision is how closely repeated readings agree with each other. Accuracy is how close a reading is to the accepted true value. Resolution is the smallest change the instrument can display. They are independent. A meter can give tightly clustered readings that all sit off the true value: precise but not accurate, the sign of a systematic offset. Extra digits on a display improve resolution, but they do not make the reading more accurate. When comparing two values, put them in the same unit first: 1 millivolt is one millionth of 1 kilovolt, small but not zero.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's current law at a node
lessons.teach: Kirchhoff's current law comes from conservation of charge. In a steady circuit, charge cannot pile up at a node, so the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it. As a signed sum: count entering currents as positive and leaving currents as negative, and the sum is zero. For example, 5 amps entering, with 4 amps and 1 amp leaving, balances: 5 minus 4 minus 1 is zero. When real meter readings leave a small leftover, the law has not failed; check meter uncertainty, the connections, and whether a branch was missed.

lessons.title: Counting significant figures
lessons.teach: Significant figures are the digits that carry meaning in a reported number. Nonzero digits count. Zeros between nonzero digits count. Leading zeros only locate the decimal point, so they never count. A trailing zero after the decimal point does count, because someone chose to record it. So 0.00470 has three significant figures: four, seven, and the final zero. A whole number like 1400 is ambiguous; write 1.40 times ten to the three to show three figures. The course reports calculated answers to three significant figures, rounding once, at the end.

lessons.title: Prefixes and powers of ten
lessons.teach: SI prefixes stand for powers of ten. Kilo, lowercase k, is ten to the three. Mega, capital M, is ten to the six. Milli, lowercase m, is ten to the minus three. Micro is ten to the minus six, nano ten to the minus nine, and pico ten to the minus twelve. Case matters: capital M and lowercase m differ by a factor of a billion. Engineering notation uses exponents that are multiples of three, so the number lines up with a prefix, with a coefficient from 1 up to just under 1000. When multiplying powers of ten, add the exponents. Converting to a smaller unit makes the number bigger.

lessons.title: Charge, atoms and Coulomb's law
lessons.teach: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. Remove electrons and it becomes a positive ion; add electrons and it becomes negative. Copper has 29 electrons, and its single outermost electron is loosely held, which is why copper conducts so well. The force between two point charges follows Coulomb's law: force equals a constant times the product of the charges, divided by the distance squared; force in newtons, charge in coulombs, distance in metres. Double the distance and the force drops to one quarter. An electric field is force per unit charge, and a negative charge is pushed opposite to the field.

lessons.title: Current is charge per time
lessons.teach: Current is the rate at which charge passes a point. Average current equals charge divided by time: current in amps, charge in coulombs, time in seconds. One amp is one coulomb per second, so amps already contain the per second. Rearranged, charge equals current times time, and time equals charge divided by current. Keep prefixes together: millicoulombs divided by milliamps gives plain seconds, because the prefixes cancel. Convert minutes to seconds before you divide.

lessons.title: Voltage is energy per charge
lessons.teach: Voltage is the difference in electric potential between two points: the energy transferred per unit of charge moved between them. Voltage equals energy divided by charge, volts being joules per coulomb. So 12 volts means 12 joules for every coulomb. A voltage always compares two points; one point alone has no voltage. Along a uniform resistor with a steady current, the voltage falls evenly with distance, so the midpoint sits at half the total voltage, as long as nothing else draws current there.

lessons.title: Voltmeters and ammeters
lessons.teach: A voltmeter measures a difference between two points, so it connects across the element, in parallel with it. An ammeter measures the current through a path, so you open the path and insert the meter in series, making the current flow through it. The ideal voltmeter draws no current, which means infinite input resistance. The ideal ammeter has zero resistance and drops no voltage. Never connect an ammeter directly across a supply: its low resistance can short the source. An oscilloscope shows how a voltage changes with time; a function generator produces a test signal.

lessons.title: Colour code and tolerance
lessons.teach: On a four-band resistor, the first two bands are digits, the third is the multiplier, and the fourth is tolerance. The digits run black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9. The multiplier band gives the number of zeros: orange means times a thousand. Gold tolerance is plus or minus 5 percent, silver 10 percent, and no band 20 percent. The allowed spread is the tolerance times the nominal value, so a 10 kilohm, 5 percent part may sit anywhere from 9.5 to 10.5 kilohms. Percent deviation equals the difference from nominal divided by nominal, times 100.

lessons.title: Potentiometer segments
lessons.teach: A potentiometer has a resistive track with two fixed ends and a movable contact called the wiper. The resistance between the two ends stays fixed. Moving the wiper splits the track into two segments, and the two segments always add up to the end-to-end total. As one segment grows, the other shrinks. Over the full travel, each segment can range from about zero ohms up to the whole track resistance. So for a 10 kilohm pot, if one end to the wiper reads 3 kilohms, the other end to the wiper reads 7 kilohms.

lessons.title: Measuring resistance with a DMM
lessons.teach: To measure resistance, the part must be unpowered and, ideally, isolated from other paths. The ohmmeter supplies its own small test current and applies Ohm's law, so any outside voltage upsets the reading and can damage the meter. Use the two-wire resistance function with the volts-and-ohms input and its low terminal. If the display shows OVLD or OL, the range may be too small, a lead may not be touching metal, or the path may be open. Holding both metal leads with your fingers puts your body in parallel and makes the reading low.

lessons.title: Capacitor markings and polarity
lessons.teach: The lab met the three basic passive parts: the resistor, which dissipates energy, and the capacitor and inductor, which store it. An electrolytic capacitor marked 47 microfarads, 50 volts carries two separate facts: its capacitance, and its voltage rating, the most it should ever see. The 50 volts is a limit, not the voltage it holds; its actual voltage depends on the circuit. Electrolytics are polarized. In the course symbol the curved plate is the negative side, and the part must be installed the right way round. A resistor has no polarity at all.

lessons.title: Node voltages in a three-node circuit
lessons.teach: A node is every point joined by ideal wire, so one node has one voltage. Name nodes with lowercase letters. The voltage at A with respect to B, spoken as V sub A B, equals the voltage at A minus the voltage at B. The first letter is where the red probe goes and the second is where the black probe goes. In the lab example, node A was 10 volts, node B 5 volts, and node C the zero volt reference. So V sub A B is 5 volts, and reversing the probes gives V sub B A, minus 5 volts. The circuit did not change; only the order of comparison did.

lessons.title: Diodes and solar cells
lessons.source: Lecture 03, light, diodes and solar cells; Boylestad §2.5
lessons.teach: A diode favours one direction of conventional current: forward current flows from the anode to the cathode, and the cathode is the bar on the symbol. A solar cell turns light into electrical energy. With its terminals open, it can show a voltage but delivers no current, so it delivers no power. Shorted, current flows but the voltage is zero, so again no power. Useful power, voltage times current, comes at an operating point between those extremes. A good cell has a large internal shunt resistance, so little current leaks inside, and a small internal series resistance, so little voltage is lost.

lessons.title: What sets a wire's resistance
lessons.source: Lecture 03, real wires and temperature; Boylestad §3.2 to §3.4
lessons.teach: A uniform conductor's resistance equals resistivity times length divided by cross-sectional area: resistance in ohms, resistivity in ohm-metres, length in metres, area in square metres. Double the length and resistance doubles. Double the area and it halves. Area goes with the square of diameter, so double the diameter and resistance drops to a quarter. Wire gauge numbers run backwards: a smaller gauge number is a thicker wire, so 12 gauge is thicker than 14. Copper's resistance rises as it warms; it has a positive temperature coefficient.

lessons.title: Ohm's law, power and meter placement
lessons.source: Lecture 03, resistance, meters and resistor ratings; Boylestad §4.4, §3.5, §5.3
lessons.teach: Power absorbed by a resistor equals the voltage across it times the current through it: watts from volts times amps. With Ohm's law you can also write power as current squared times resistance, or voltage squared over resistance. A resistor's ohms value says nothing about how much heat it can handle; that is its power rating, a separate specification. Choose a rating above the power it will dissipate. In a single loop, the current is the same everywhere, so an ideal ammeter reads the same before or after a resistor.

lessons.title: The potentiometer as a voltage divider
lessons.teach: Connect a potentiometer's two ends across a supply and the wiper picks off a fraction of the voltage. For an unloaded wiper, the output relative to the bottom end equals the supply voltage times the bottom segment's resistance divided by the whole track resistance. If the bottom segment is 75 percent of the track, the output is 75 percent of the supply. That simple fraction assumes nothing draws current from the wiper. Connect a load and it sits in parallel with the bottom segment, making that part's effective resistance smaller, so the output voltage falls.

lessons.title: Series current and KVL
lessons.teach: Elements are in series when they share one path with no branches between them; that is about connections, not how the drawing looks. Series resistances add: total resistance is the sum. One current flows through every series element, found by Ohm's law: current equals supply voltage over total resistance. Each resistor then drops current times its own resistance, so bigger resistors drop more. Kirchhoff's voltage law checks the loop: the drops add up to the supply. Raising the total resistance lowers the current through every part.

lessons.title: Meter loading
lessons.teach: Real meters become part of the circuit. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance, but a real one adds a little series resistance, so the current drops slightly when you insert it. An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance, but a real one forms a parallel branch that draws a little current. Across a small resistor, a 20 megohm meter changes almost nothing. Across resistors in the megohm range, it can change the reading a lot, because the meter's resistance combines in parallel with the one being measured. The meter then shows the voltage of the modified circuit.

lessons.title: How current splits between branches
lessons.teach: Lecture four previewed parallel branches. Two resistors connected across the same pair of nodes share the same voltage, and each carries its own current by Ohm's law: current equals the shared voltage over that branch's resistance. So current does not only take the path of least resistance. It takes every available path, and the smaller resistance simply takes more. With 1 ohm and 2 ohms in parallel, the 1 ohm branch carries twice the current of the 2 ohm branch. The branch currents add up to the total.

lessons.title: Voltage order and negative answers
lessons.teach: A voltage is an ordered comparison: V sub A B equals the voltage at A minus the voltage at B, and V sub B A is its negative. For a resistor, put the plus sign where your chosen current arrow enters; then voltage equals current times resistance. If you pick the arrow backwards, the arithmetic simply returns a negative current. A negative answer does not mean negative resistance or a mistake; it means the actual current flows opposite to your arrow. A 1.5 volt cell reads plus 1.5 with red on its positive terminal and minus 1.5 with the probes swapped.

lessons.title: Breadboard nodes
lessons.teach: On a breadboard, holes joined by the same metal strip form one node. Physical closeness means nothing: two holes side by side are separate nodes if a cut or gap separates their strips. To build a schematic, name each node, find a board group for it, and place every component between the two nodes it belongs to. The classic mistake is plugging both leads of a resistor into the same connected group. Then both ends sit at one voltage, the resistor has zero volts across it, carries no current, and is bypassed.

lessons.title: Reporting three significant figures
lessons.teach: The lab asks for measurements reported to three significant figures, while you keep the original readings in your raw record. Round once, at the end, and keep a meaningful final zero: 12.96 volts becomes 13.0 volts, three figures, not 13. For multiplication and division, the answer keeps the fewest significant figures among the inputs. A five-and-a-half digit meter has five full digits plus a leading digit that can only be 0 or 1; that describes the display, not accuracy. Write every calculation in four parts: the quantity, the formula, the substitution with units, and the result with its unit.

lessons.title: Rule set: EIC, EIS and EIP
lessons.teach: The course justifies every step with a named rule. EIC, elements in container: for elements on one unbranched path, three truths hold. One, the same current flows through every element. Two, the element voltages add up to the container's terminal voltage. Three, elements may be reordered, provided each keeps its own orientation; reordering is allowed, reversing is not. EIS, elements in series: series elements carry the same current. EIP, elements in parallel: elements across the same two nodes have the same voltage. Name the rule beside each line of working.

lessons.title: Rule set: OL, RIS and KVL
lessons.teach: Three more named rules. OL, Ohm's law: resistance equals the voltage across that resistor divided by the current through that resistor, rearranged as needed; the subscripts tie both quantities to one element. RIS, resistors in series: total resistance is the sum of the series resistors. RIS is for resistors only; capacitors in series do not add that way. KVL, Kirchhoff's voltage law: the directed voltages around a closed path sum to zero. When you write a step, name the rule that licenses it. That habit makes you check you really have a voltage across and a current through the same element.

lessons.title: Three faces of power
lessons.teach: Power is the rate of energy transfer, in watts, where one watt is one joule per second. For a resistor, power equals voltage times current. Substitute Ohm's law and you get two more faces: power equals current squared times resistance, and power equals voltage squared over resistance. Pick the face that uses the two quantities you already have. Voltage against current is a straight line, but power against voltage is a square law: double the voltage across a fixed resistor and the power becomes four times as large. Resistors dissipate energy as heat; ideal capacitors and inductors store it and give it back.

lessons.title: Energy, and the signs of power
lessons.teach: Energy equals power times time: joules from watts times seconds, or kilowatt-hours from kilowatts times hours. A watt is a rate; a kilowatt-hour is an amount of energy. The course sign conventions: a current referenced into a source's positive terminal comes out negative, and power delivered into the circuit is negative while power leaving it is positive, so all the powers in a closed circuit add to zero. That zero sum is conservation of energy. A real battery is modelled as an ideal source in series with a small internal resistance, and that resistance is the part that warms up.

lessons.title: Working back, and the proportional divider
lessons.teach: Solve a circuit by gathering what you know, naming the target, and using the one rule that connects them. Sometimes you work backwards: given the total resistance and two resistors, the third is the total minus the others, by resistors in series. In a series pair, one current flows through both, so the voltages are proportional to the resistances: with 1 ohm and 2 ohms, the 2 ohm resistor drops twice as much. Together with Kirchhoff's voltage law, that fixes both voltages. Carry full precision and round only at the end. The source's power equals the sum of the resistor powers.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's voltage law, and reduction
lessons.teach: Kirchhoff's voltage law has two statements of the same law. First: the sum of the directed voltages around a closed path is zero. Second: the sum of the voltage rises equals the sum of the voltage drops. The word directed matters: the sign comes from which terminal you enter as you walk the loop. Entering at plus, add the voltage; entering at minus, subtract it. Walking the other way flips every sign and still gives zero. To solve a series chain, reduce it to one equivalent resistance, find the current, then return to the original drawing for each resistor's voltage.

lessons.title: Double-subscript notation
lessons.teach: A node is a region of one voltage: everything joined by ideal wire. Name nodes with lowercase letters. V sub A B is the voltage at A with respect to B: red probe on A, black probe on B. It equals the voltage at A minus the voltage at B, so V sub B A is the negative of V sub A B. Along a series chain, add the drops between the two nodes. With a 10 volt source and drops of 7, 2 and 1 volts along nodes A, B, C and D, V sub A B is 7 volts, V sub A C is 9 volts, and V sub A D is the full 10 volts.

lessons.title: Reference nodes and single subscripts
lessons.teach: A single subscript, V sub B, names only the red probe's node. The black probe is understood to sit on a reference node, and that node must be marked, or the notation means nothing. The downward triangle marks a local zero volt common; the three-bar symbol means earth, a different idea. The reference is your choice. Moving it shifts every single-subscript voltage by the same amount, but every difference between two nodes stays the same. Choose it once, before measuring. When measuring around a loop, keep the probe orientation consistent, or account for any swap.

lessons.title: Sources and their ratings
lessons.teach: An ideal voltage source holds its terminal voltage regardless of the current drawn; an ideal current source holds its current regardless of the voltage. A supply's label carries two numbers, and one is often misread. The current on the label is the maximum that may be drawn, a boundary, not a delivery. The load decides how much current flows. With nothing connected, the load is an infinite resistance, so by Ohm's law the current is zero, whatever the label says. Nominal voltage is a representative label, not a guaranteed exact value; a fresh 1.5 volt cell can read a little above 1.5 volts unloaded.

lessons.title: Cells, batteries and capacity
lessons.teach: A cell is one electrochemical unit; a battery, in the traditional sense, is a group of cells. Cells connected in series-aiding add their voltages, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, and each carries the same current, by elements in series. Four 1.5 volt cells in series give 6 volts. A battery's capacity in ampere-hours is a charge rating. The ideal run time equals capacity divided by the load current: hours from ampere-hours over amps. Real run time depends on discharge rate, temperature, age and cutoff voltage.

lessons.title: Internal resistance and terminal voltage
lessons.teach: A real source is modelled as an ideal source in series with an internal resistance. The node between them is inside the source, so you can only measure the terminal voltage. Draw current and the internal resistance drops current times internal resistance, so the terminal voltage sags below the ideal value. With the terminals open, no current flows, the internal resistor drops nothing, and the full source voltage appears: no current is not the same as no voltage. To find the internal resistance, read the open-circuit voltage, then read again with a known load. The lost voltage divided by the load current is the internal resistance.

lessons.title: Kilo, kelvin and prefix arithmetic
lessons.teach: Lowercase k means kilo, the multiplier one thousand. Uppercase K means kelvin, a unit of temperature. Write them so they cannot be confused. Kelvin and Celsius have the same step size: a change of one degree Celsius is a change of one kelvin; the scales differ only by an offset of about 273. Prefix arithmetic makes circuit numbers easy. Kilo times milli is one, so kilohms times milliamps gives volts, and volts divided by kilohms gives milliamps. For example, 3 milliamps through 4 kilohms drops 12 volts.

lessons.title: Parallel: shared voltage, own currents
lessons.teach: Two elements are in parallel when both their ends connect to the same pair of nodes; how they are drawn does not matter. Parallel elements have the same voltage and, in general, different currents; series elements have the same current and different voltages. Each branch current comes from Ohm's law: current equals the shared voltage over that branch's resistance. So double a branch's resistance and its current halves. The branch currents add up to the total current. With 10 volts across 1 kilohm and 2 kilohms, the branches carry 10 and 5 milliamps, 15 milliamps in all.

lessons.title: Total resistance in parallel
lessons.teach: For parallel resistors, the reciprocal of the total equals the sum of the reciprocals: one over R total equals one over R one plus one over R two, and so on. The left side is a reciprocal too; forgetting to flip at the end is the commonest slip. For exactly two resistors, the shortcut is product over sum: R one times R two, divided by R one plus R two. It is for two resistors only. For equal resistors, divide one value by how many there are. Your error check: the parallel total must be less than the smallest resistor. 1 kilohm in parallel with 2 kilohms is about 667 ohms.

lessons.title: Conductance in siemens
lessons.teach: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance: G equals one over R. Its unit is the siemens, capital S, named after a person, so it is siemens in both singular and plural. Resistance describes opposition to current; conductance describes readiness to allow it. The reciprocal of a kilohm is a millisiemens, so 2 kilohms is 0.5 millisiemens. In parallel, conductances simply add, just as resistances add in series. For 1 kilohm and 2 kilohms, 1 millisiemens plus 0.5 millisiemens is 1.5 millisiemens, and the total resistance is one over that, about 667 ohms.

lessons.title: Efficiency and protection devices
lessons.teach: Efficiency compares useful output power with input power: efficiency equals output over input, as a decimal or times 100 for percent. The difference is loss, energy turned into unwanted forms such as heat, not destroyed. When stages are in cascade, each feeding the next, the total efficiency is the product of the stage efficiencies as decimals. Fuses and circuit breakers respond to excessive current: a fuse element melts open, a breaker trips and can be reset. A ground fault circuit interrupter responds to a different condition: an imbalance between the outgoing and returning current.

lessons.title: Special resistors and markings
lessons.teach: Some resistive devices are designed to change. A thermistor's resistance depends strongly on temperature: an NTC thermistor's resistance falls as it warms, a PTC's rises. A photoconductive cell's resistance usually falls as the light on it increases. Surface-mount resistors often carry a three-digit code: the first two digits are significant and the third is the power of ten. So 472 means 47 times ten to the two, 4700 ohms, which is 4.7 kilohms, while 470 means just 47 ohms.

lessons.title: Roots: one value, and no splitting over sums
lessons.teach: A root reverses a power: 2 squared is 4, so the square root of 4 is 2. The radical symbol names one value, the principal root, never negative, so the square root of 49 is 7, full stop. Solving x squared equals 49 is a different task and has two answers, 7 and negative 7. Even roots of negatives have no real value; odd roots keep the sign, so the cube root of negative 8 is negative 2. A root splits over a product: root 72 is root 36 times root 2, which is 6 root 2, and squaring back gives 36 times 2, which is 72. It never splits over a sum. The root of 36 plus 64 is one root of 100, which is 10, while root 36 plus root 64 is 6 plus 8, which is 14.

lessons.title: Undo operations to rearrange a formula
lessons.teach: To isolate a variable, undo the operations around it in reverse order, doing the same thing to both sides. Addition is undone by subtraction, multiplication by division, and so on. Nothing changes sign just by crossing the equals sign; a term moves because you subtracted it from both sides. In E equals m c squared, m is multiplied by the whole factor c squared, so divide both sides by c squared: m equals E over c squared, with c not zero. Dividing by only c would leave m c, not m. In v equals v nought plus a t, t is multiplied by a and then v nought is added, so reverse that: subtract v nought first, then divide by a. Every division carries the restriction that the divisor is not zero, and that restriction is part of the answer.

lessons.title: Number sets nest inside each other
lessons.teach: Classify a number by its value, not its appearance, so simplify first. The natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on. Add zero and you have the whole numbers. Add the negatives and you have the integers. The rationals are every ratio of integers with a nonzero denominator, which includes every integer and every decimal that terminates or repeats. The irrationals are the real numbers that are not ratios: root 2, pi, e. Rationals and irrationals together make the real numbers. The sets nest: natural inside whole inside integer inside rational inside real. So the square root of 49 is 7, a natural number, and therefore also whole, an integer, rational and real. The smallest set it belongs to is natural; it belongs to every larger one too.

lessons.title: Fractions and reciprocals
lessons.teach: The class calls it finding ones: multiplying by a fraction equal to 1 changes the form of a number without changing its value. That is how you build a common denominator to add fractions, and how you cancel a common factor to reduce one. To add or subtract, the denominators must match; then combine the numerators. To multiply, multiply tops and bottoms. To divide, multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor, the second fraction, keeping the first fraction as it is. So five sixths divided by ten ninths is five sixths times nine tenths, which reduces to three quarters. The reciprocal of a nonzero number r is 1 over r, and their product is 1. The reciprocal of negative three fifths is negative five thirds; the sign stays. Zero has no reciprocal, since nothing times zero gives 1.

lessons.title: Signs and the order of operations
lessons.teach: Subtracting a number is adding its opposite, so 3 minus negative 8 is 3 plus 8, which is 11. For multiplication and division, same signs give a positive result and different signs give a negative one. Then the order of operations: first grouping symbols, including a fraction bar and a radical bar, then powers and roots, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. Multiplication does not beat division; they share a level. The trap that catches everyone is the sign in front of a power. An exponent applies only to the base right in front of it. Minus 3 squared, with no brackets, means the negative of 3 squared, which is negative 9. Brackets around negative 3, then squared, gives positive 9.

lessons.title: Cancel factors, never terms
lessons.teach: An algebraic fraction reduces when top and bottom share a factor, because that factor over itself is a form of 1. Factor everything first. Take x squared minus 9, all over x squared plus 5 x plus 6. The top is a difference of squares, x plus 3 times x minus 3. The bottom factors as x plus 2 times x plus 3, since 2 and 3 multiply to 6 and add to 5. Before cancelling, record the original denominator's excluded inputs: x cannot be negative 2 or negative 3. Then x plus 3 cancels, leaving x minus 3 over x plus 2, and the restriction at negative 3 stays although the factor is gone. Never cancel pieces of a sum: in the quantity x plus 3 over the quantity x plus 2, the x terms are terms, not factors.

lessons.title: Expanding and the special products
lessons.teach: Expanding turns a product into a sum by the distributive law: multiply every term inside the bracket by the multiplier, sign attached. For two brackets, every term multiplies every term, four products for two binomials. Three patterns are worth knowing on sight. A sum squared: a plus b, all squared, is a squared plus 2 a b plus b squared. A difference squared: a minus b, all squared, is a squared minus 2 a b plus b squared, and the last term is positive. Conjugates: a plus b times a minus b is a squared minus b squared, because the middle terms cancel. The warning: a power does not distribute over addition. The square of a plus b is not a squared plus b squared; the cross term 2 a b must be there.

lessons.title: Factor in a sensible order
lessons.teach: Factoring reverses expanding, and the class works it in a fixed order. Step one, always: remove any common factor. Eighteen x squared minus 32 becomes 2 times 9 x squared minus 16. Step two: look for a difference of squares, a squared minus b squared, which factors as a minus b times a plus b; 9 x squared minus 16 is 3 x minus 4 times 3 x plus 4. A sum of squares does not factor. Step three, for a trinomial: the AC method. Find two numbers whose product is a times c and whose sum is b, split the middle term, and group. For x squared plus 9 x plus 20, the numbers 4 and 5 multiply to 20 and add to 9, giving x plus 4 times x plus 5. Check by expanding back.

lessons.title: The zero-product rule
lessons.teach: The zero-product rule says: if A times B equals zero, then A equals zero or B equals zero. There is no third possibility, because two nonzero real numbers cannot multiply to zero. It only works against zero, so first put the equation in zero form: everything on one side, zero on the other. Then factor, set each factor to zero, and solve. For x squared plus 3 x equals 10, move the 10 across to get x squared plus 3 x minus 10 equals zero, which factors as x plus 5 times x minus 2, so x is negative 5 or 2. One trap: in x times x minus 4 equals zero, do not divide by x. That assumes x is not zero and throws away the solution x equals zero. Never cancel a factor that could be zero.

lessons.title: The quadratic formula and the discriminant
lessons.teach: When a quadratic will not factor, put it in standard form, a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero with a not zero, and use the formula: x equals negative b, plus or minus the square root of b squared minus 4 a c, all over 2 a. The whole numerator is divided by 2 a, and every coefficient keeps its sign. The quantity under the root is the discriminant, and it predicts the outcome. Positive means two different real solutions. Zero means one repeated real solution. Negative means no real solutions, because you would need the root of a negative number. For 2 x squared plus 4 x minus 3, a is 2, b is 4 and c is negative 3, so the discriminant is 16 plus 24, which is 40: two real roots.

lessons.title: The exponent laws
lessons.teach: The exponent laws are bookkeeping for repeated multiplication. Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents, because you are counting factors; dividing subtracts them. A power of a power multiplies them. Any nonzero base to the zero is 1. The rules cover only multiplication and division: x cubed plus x squared has no shortcut. So 2 cubed times 2 squared is 2 to the fifth, which is 32. A negative exponent moves a factor across a fraction bar and never makes anything negative: 2 to the minus 3 is 1 over 8. A fractional exponent uses its denominator as a root index and its numerator as a power, for a positive base. Eight over 27 to the two thirds is the cube root, two thirds, then squared, four ninths. Take the root first; it keeps the numbers small.

lessons.title: A logarithm asks for an exponent
lessons.teach: The definition of a logarithm: log base b of x equals y means b to the power y equals x. The base b is positive and not 1, the argument x is positive, and the answer y is the exponent needed. So log base 2 of 8 asks, two to what power gives eight? Two cubed is 8, so the answer is 3. A positive argument can still give a negative answer: log base 2 of one half is negative 1, because 2 to the minus 1 is one half. Log with no base written means base 10, the common log, so log of 1000 is 3. The natural log, l n, has base e, about 2.718, so l n of e is 1. In every base, log of 1 is zero, because anything to the zero is 1.

lessons.title: The three log rules
lessons.teach: The log rules mirror the exponent laws; each changes an operation inside the log into a different operation outside. Product rule: log of u times v equals log u plus log v. Multiply inside, add outside. Quotient rule: log of u over v equals log u minus log v. Divide inside, subtract outside. Power rule: log of u to the r equals r times log u. Exponent inside becomes a multiplier outside. All within one base, and with u and v positive. So log 6 plus log 3 condenses to log 18, and 3 log 5 condenses to log 125. Two traps. There is no rule for a sum inside: log of u plus v cannot be split. And 3 log 5 means three times a log; it is not log base 3 of 5 and not log 15.

lessons.title: Inverses, change of base and matching powers
lessons.teach: Exponentials and logarithms undo each other. Log base a of a to the x is x for every real x, and a to the log base a of x is x for positive x. So 10 to the log 5 is 5 and l n of e cubed is 3. When a calculator has only log and l n, change of base handles any base: log base b of x equals l n x over l n b, argument on top, base underneath, same logarithm in both. Matching powers can shortcut this. For log base 81 of 2401, notice 81 is 3 to the fourth and 2401 is 7 to the fourth; the power rule pulls a 4 out of top and bottom, they cancel, and the value is log base 3 of 7.

lessons.title: Domain and shifts of a log graph
lessons.teach: The graph of y equals log base a of x exists only for x greater than zero, has a vertical asymptote at x equals zero, and passes through the point 1 comma 0. Its inverse, y equals a to the x, is defined for every real x, stays positive, and passes through 0 comma 1. Shifts work the same for every function family: x minus h inside moves the graph right by h, x plus h moves it left, and adding k outside moves it up. For y equals log base 2 of the quantity x minus 2, plus 1, the domain comes from the argument: x minus 2 greater than zero, so x greater than 2; the asymptote is x equals 2, and the anchor point 1 comma 0 moves to 3 comma 1.

lessons.title: Read the shape, choose the method
lessons.teach: The class gave four methods, and the shape of the equation tells you which to reach for. Method one, change the form: when one logarithm stands alone equal to a number, use the definition, log base b of M equals k means b to the k equals M. Method two, common base: when both sides can be written as powers of the same base, equate the exponents, since b to the u equals b to the v means u equals v. Method three, condense: when several logs of one base appear, combine them with the product, quotient and power rules first; this usually turns the problem into method one. Method four, log both sides: when the bases cannot be matched, take a logarithm of both sides and the power rule pulls each exponent down. Then finish with ordinary algebra.

lessons.title: Check every candidate against the domain
lessons.teach: Some methods hand you a value the algebra accepts and the original equation refuses, so every candidate goes back into the original. For log x plus log of the quantity 2 x minus 1, equals 1, the domain comes first: both arguments positive, so x greater than one half. Condensing gives log of x times the quantity 2 x minus 1, equals 1; changing the form gives x times the quantity 2 x minus 1, equals 10; and factoring gives candidates five halves and negative 2. Negative 2 fails the domain: it would ask for the log of a negative number. It is extraneous, let in because the condensed equation has a wider domain. Only five halves survives. Keep exact and approximate apart: for 2 to the x equals 7, log 7 over log 2 is exact, 2.807 is rounded.

lessons.title: Simplest radical form
lessons.teach: To simplify a square root, split the radicand into a perfect-square factor times whatever is left, using the rule that the root of a times b equals root a times root b for non-negative a and b. The root of 216 is the root of 36 times 6, which is 6 root 6. Any square factor works; take it out and repeat. Divisibility shortcuts help: even numbers divide by 2, digits summing to a multiple of 3 divide by 3. For 147, the digits sum to 12, so 147 is 3 times 49, and root 147 is 7 root 3. With letters, the root of k squared is the absolute value of k, not k. Going back to entire form, the outside factor must be non-negative: negative 3 root 2 is negative root 18, never root 18.

lessons.title: Rationalizing a denominator
lessons.teach: Rationalizing means rewriting so no radical remains below the line; the tool is a version of 1. Look only at the denominator. One term with a square root: multiply top and bottom by that root, so 1 over root 5 becomes root 5 over 5. One term with a higher root: supply just enough factors to complete a perfect n-th power; for 1 over the fourth root of 8, since 8 is 2 cubed, multiply by the fourth root of 2 over itself. Two terms: multiply by the conjugate, the same terms with the sign flipped, since a plus b times a minus b is a squared minus b squared, removing the root. So 2 plus root 3 times 2 minus root 3 is 1, and 1 over the quantity 2 minus root 3 becomes 2 plus root 3.

lessons.title: A radian comes from the circle itself
lessons.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
lessons.teach: Take the radius, bend it around the rim, and mark where it ends. The central angle you have opened is one radian: the angle whose arc length equals the radius. The circumference is 2 pi times the radius, so exactly 2 pi radii fit around, and one full turn is 2 pi radians; it falls out of the definition. The same idea gives arc length: s equals r theta, where s is the arc length, r the radius in the same length unit, and theta the angle in radians. It is a radian-only formula: theta equals 2 pi gives the circumference, but 360 gives nonsense. For converting, one relation does all the work: pi radians equals 180 degrees. Multiply by pi over 180 to go to radians, or 180 over pi to go to degrees.

lessons.title: Counting around the unit circle
lessons.topic: Radians, arc length & the unit circle
lessons.teach: The class builds the unit circle by counting, not memorising. Walk around in steps of pi over 4, which is 45 degrees: two steps is 2 pi over 4, which simplifies to pi over 2, and eight steps is a full turn. Walk again in steps of pi over 6, which is 30 degrees, twelve steps to the turn. Simplify each fraction properly: 6 pi over 4 reduces to 3 pi over 2, not pi over 2. Five steps of 30 degrees is 5 pi over 6, which is 150 degrees, in the second quadrant. Angles are measured from the positive horizontal axis, counterclockwise positive and clockwise negative. Angles that end at the same point are coterminal; they differ by whole turns of 2 pi, so negative pi over 4 and 7 pi over 4 are coterminal.

lessons.title: Coordinates and the two special triangles
lessons.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
lessons.teach: The unit circle has radius 1. Drop a vertical from any rim point and you get a right triangle with hypotenuse 1, so the ratios collapse into the coordinates: cosine of theta is the x coordinate, sine of theta is the y coordinate, and tangent is y over x. SOH CAH TOA: sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent is opposite over adjacent. Two triangles give the exact values. The 45 45 90 triangle, half a square, has both legs root 2 over 2, so sine and cosine of 45 are root 2 over 2 and tangent is 1. The 30 60 90 triangle has legs one half and root 3 over 2: sine of 30 is one half, cosine of 30 is root 3 over 2; the bigger angle faces the bigger side.

lessons.title: Signs by quadrant, and where tangent fails
lessons.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
lessons.teach: Past 90 degrees the sides of the triangle are really the coordinates x and y, and coordinates carry signs. Cosine is x, sine is y, and tangent is y over x. In quadrant one both are positive, so everything is positive. In quadrant two x is negative and y positive: sine positive, cosine and tangent negative. In quadrant three both are negative: sine and cosine negative, but tangent, a negative over a negative, is positive. In quadrant four x is positive and y negative: cosine positive, sine and tangent negative. A negative answer is not a mistake; it is the picture. So cosine of 120 degrees is negative one half: reference angle 60, second quadrant, x negative. Tangent is undefined wherever x is zero, at 90 and 270 degrees, because you cannot divide by zero.

lessons.title: Inverse trig hands back one angle
lessons.topic: Trig ratios, special triangles & reference angles
lessons.teach: The inverse keys undo a ratio, but many angles share any ratio, so each key returns one angle from a fixed band. Inverse tangent returns between negative 90 and 90 degrees, inverse sine the same band with its endpoints included, and inverse cosine between 0 and 180. Outside the band you get a different angle with the same ratio. Tangent of 298 degrees is about negative 1.88; inverse tangent of that gives negative 62. Those two are coterminal, since 298 minus 360 is negative 62. But tangent of 172 gives inverse tangent negative 8, and 172 and negative 8 differ by 180, half a turn, so they are not coterminal; tangent repeats every 180 degrees. The safe rule: decide the quadrant first; for quadrant two or three add 180 to the calculator's answer.

lessons.title: Pythagoras on the unit circle
lessons.teach: Put the unit circle's own coordinates into Pythagoras: a squared plus b squared equals c squared, where c must be the hypotenuse. On the unit circle the legs are cosine theta and sine theta and the hypotenuse is 1, so cosine squared theta plus sine squared theta equals 1. That is the first Pythagorean identity, true for every angle with no exceptions. It is usually used rearranged: sine squared equals 1 minus cosine squared, and cosine squared equals 1 minus sine squared, so any 1 minus sine squared x becomes cosine squared x on sight. Watch the notation: cosine squared theta means take the cosine, then square the result, not the cosine of theta squared. Cosine squared of 30 degrees is three quarters.

lessons.title: Six ratios, three reciprocal pairs
lessons.teach: The three new ratios are the old three turned upside down. Cosecant is 1 over sine, secant is 1 over cosine, and cotangent is 1 over tangent, which is cosine over sine. The naming rule: within each pair exactly one name carries the prefix co, so the reciprocal of cosine is secant, not cosecant. Every reciprocal inherits a restriction: secant does not exist where cosine is zero, at 90 and 270 degrees; cosecant and cotangent do not exist where sine is zero, at 0 and 180. Since cosine of 60 is one half, secant of 60 is 2. Dividing the first identity by cosine squared gives 1 plus tangent squared equals secant squared; dividing by sine squared gives cotangent squared plus 1 equals cosecant squared.

lessons.title: How to prove an identity
lessons.teach: An identity is true for every allowed angle, and proving one means transforming one side until it reads exactly like the other. Two rules. First, convert everything to sine and cosine. Second, change one side only, usually the messier side. Working on both sides assumes they are already equal, the very thing to be shown, so it proves nothing. The commonest tactic is to get sine squared and cosine squared over one denominator and added, so the first identity collapses them to 1. For tangent x sine x plus cosine x, writing tangent as sine over cosine and using a common denominator gives sine squared plus cosine squared over cosine, which is 1 over cosine, which is secant x. Conjugate denominators 1 minus sine x and 1 plus sine x multiply to 1 minus sine squared, which is cosine squared.

lessons.title: Every answer is a family
lessons.teach: A trigonometric equation is true only for particular angles; solving it means finding them. Reduce it to one trig function equals one number, then read the unit circle: reference angle from the size, quadrants from the sign. For cosine x equals negative root 3 over 2, the reference angle is pi over 6 and cosine is negative in quadrants two and three, so x is pi minus pi over 6, 5 pi over 6, or pi plus pi over 6, 7 pi over 6. The circle repeats, so each angle starts a family: add 2 n pi, n any integer; two bare angles are two answers out of infinitely many. A value between negative 1 and 1 is hit twice per turn; 1 and negative 1 once; anything beyond, never, so sine x equals 2 has no solution.

lessons.title: Four tactics for making it familiar
lessons.teach: The class calls it lazy mathematics: change an unfamiliar equation into one you have already solved. Four tactics, chosen by shape. One trig function to the first power: isolate it by algebra. A squared function alone, like 4 sine squared theta equals 3: take both square roots, plus and minus, or you lose half the answers. Every term sharing a factor, like 2 cosine theta sine theta minus cosine theta equals 0: factor out cosine theta and use the zero-product rule; never divide it away, which deletes the branch cosine theta equals 0. A squared and a first power of one function, like 2 sine squared x minus 3 sine x plus 1 equals 0: substitute y for sine x, factor, then undo the substitution. When sine and cosine are mixed, use the Pythagorean identity to reach one function first.

lessons.title: Why the practice wire is silver
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §4
lessons.teach: The practice wire looks silver, but it is copper underneath. It has been coated with a thin layer of tin. Copper oxidises, so the tin takes the oxidation instead and keeps the copper surface clean and easy to wet with solder. That is the whole point of the coating: it protects the copper and keeps it solderable. A silver surface does not certify how much current the wire can carry. Current rating depends on the conductor size, the insulation and the conditions it works in, not on the plating. One more consequence: the coating is thin, so anything sharp that bites through it, like serrated plier jaws, opens a spot where the copper can corrode.

lessons.title: Solder and what flux does
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §4
lessons.teach: The solder in the lab is a lead and tin alloy with flux in its core. Flux has one job: it removes oxide from the metal so the solder can wet it, meaning bond to the surface instead of sitting on top. On fresh, clean, tinned wire the flux in the core may be all you need, and you see that because the solder wets properly. On a surface that is already oxidised the core flux may not be enough. Then you clean the surface and use approved extra flux, or the solder will sit on top without bonding. Flux does not add strength and it does not replace heat. It only clears the way for wetting.

lessons.title: Two round wires and the heat bridge
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §5
lessons.teach: Cross two round wires and they touch at essentially a single point. Almost no heat crosses that point, so if you heat the top wire the bottom one stays cold. The fix is deliberate: put a small amount of solder right where the iron meets the work. That molten solder spreads the contact and carries heat into both wires at once. It is called a thermal bridge, and it is a technique, not sloppiness. Clean and tin the tip, place the iron on the joint, add a little solder at the iron and work contact, then leave the iron there and let the heat go in. Do not confuse this with an electrical bridge, which is unwanted solder shorting two separate pads.

lessons.title: Feeding solder from the far side
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §5
lessons.teach: Once the bridge is in place and the iron is resting on the joint, feed the solder from the side of the joint opposite the iron. This is a test as much as a technique. If solder melts when it touches the far side, the work itself is hot enough, not just the iron. If it does not melt, the joint is not ready, so keep the iron there and wait. The work tells you when; you do not count seconds. Melting solder on the iron and wiping it onto cold metal gives a blob that looks finished but never bonded. When the solder has flowed around the joint, remove the solder first, then the iron. Solder that wets one wire but not the other is a cold joint.

lessons.title: The fillet and how much solder
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §5
lessons.teach: A finished joint shows a concave, feathered curve where the solder meets each wire. That curve is the fillet. You do not shape it; surface tension pulls the solder into it once it has wetted clean, hot metal, the same property that shapes a water droplet. On a joint this small surface tension dominates and gravity matters very little. About an eighth of an inch of solder wire was the cue for the demonstrated joint, but that is a cue for that solder and that joint, not a specification. The inspection test on stranded wire: you should still see the individual strands through the solder. If the strands are hidden under a smooth blob, there is too much solder, and the blob hides exactly what an inspector wants to see.

lessons.title: Tip care and moving heat
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §3
lessons.teach: Oxide on the tip is a thermal barrier, and a freshly tinned tip goes from bright to dark in a few seconds. So you clean the tip immediately before every joint, not once an hour. Clean it by wiping and rolling the tip through the brass wool as you pull it out; that shears the oxide off. Stabbing the tip into the wool does not clean it and shortens its life. Never file a tip: it is plated, and a file goes straight through the plating. Heat moves by contact area, so put the flat face of a wedge tip against the work; the rounded edge touches at one point and transfers almost nothing. Leave fresh solder on the tip before switching off so it is protected in storage.

lessons.title: Bench layout, fumes and lead
lessons.source: EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup §2–3
lessons.teach: The benches are shared, so the layout you sit down to was set up for someone with the other dominant hand.
