Resistance value and power rating are separate specifications. A correct 1 kilohm value tells you nothing about how much heat the part can shed. Power equals voltage squared over resistance, 144 milliwatts here, so the rating must exceed that: a quarter watt.
items.concept: Resistance value and power rating are separate; choose a rating above the power dissipated.
items.hint: Convert each rating to milliwatts and compare with 144.

items.q: A 12 volt car battery drives a starter motor whose resistance is 40 milliohms. Treating the motor as a resistor, what is the starting current? Answer in amps.
items.right: Right, 300 amps. A tiny resistance draws a very large current.
items.wrong: Ohm's law: current equals voltage over resistance, amps from volts over ohms. Convert the resistance first: 40 milliohms is 0.04 ohms. Then 12 volts over 0.04 ohms is 300 amps. That huge current is why starter cables are so thick.

slips.why: You used 40 ohms instead of 40 milliohms. 40 milliohms is 0.04 ohms, so 12 over 0.04 is 300 amps.
You multiplied. Current equals voltage divided by resistance: 12 volts over 0.04 ohms is 300 amps.

items.concept: Current equals voltage over resistance; convert milliohms to ohms first.
items.hint: 40 milliohms is 0.04 ohms.

items.q: In a single loop, an ideal ammeter reads 6 amps before the resistor. You move it to after the resistor, keeping its polarity. What does it read now?
items.right: Yes. One loop has one current; the resistor converts energy, not charge.
wrong: Nothing adds current after the resistor; there is no other branch feeding in. In a single loop the current is the same at every point, because charge per second is conserved around the path. So the meter still reads 6 amps.
Zero would mean the path is open. Moving an ideal ammeter while keeping the loop closed leaves the circuit unchanged. The same current flows everywhere in one loop, so it still reads 6 amps.

The resistor does not consume current. In a single loop, charge cannot pile up anywhere, so the current entering the resistor equals the current leaving it. Current equals charge per second, and that rate is the same all around the loop. The ammeter reads 6 amps in either position.
items.concept: In a single series loop the current is the same everywhere.
items.hint: Can a resistor use up charge?

items.q: A 10 kilohm potentiometer has its ends across 10 volts. The wiper is set so the lower segment is 75 percent of the track. With nothing connected to the wiper, what is its voltage relative to the bottom end? Answer in volts.
items.right: Right, 7.5 volts: 75 percent of 10 volts.
items.wrong: For an unloaded divider, the output equals the supply voltage times the lower segment's resistance over the total track resistance, all in volts and ohms. The lower segment is 7.5 kilohms of 10 kilohms, a fraction of 0.75. So 10 volts times 0.75 is 7.5 volts. The track current is 10 volts over 10 kilohms, 1 milliamp, and 1 milliamp times 7.5 kilohms confirms 7.5 volts.

slips.why: 2.5 volts is across the upper segment. The output is measured from the bottom end, across the lower segment: 10 volts times 0.75 is 7.5 volts.

items.concept: Unloaded divider output equals supply times lower resistance over total resistance.
items.hint: What is 75 percent of 10 volts?

items.source: Lecture 03, why a load changes the answer; Boylestad §7.8
items.q: A potentiometer set to its midpoint gives 5 volts unloaded. A load resistor is then connected from the wiper to the bottom end. What happens to the wiper voltage?
options: It becomes the full supply voltage
items.right: Yes. The load parallels the lower segment, lowering its effective resistance and the output.
wrong: The full supply would appear only if the upper segment dropped nothing. With a load across the lower segment, the lower part's effective resistance shrinks, so it gets a smaller share: output equals supply times lower resistance over total. The wiper voltage falls below 5 volts.

The simple fraction assumes the wiper supplies no current. A load connected from wiper to bottom sits in parallel with the lower segment, and a parallel combination is smaller than either resistor alone. By the divider idea, output equals supply times lower resistance over total, so a smaller lower resistance gives a smaller output, below 5 volts.

A load cannot raise the output. It adds a parallel path across the lower segment, and the parallel combination is less than the segment by itself. The output equals supply times lower resistance over total resistance, so a smaller lower resistance pulls the voltage below 5 volts.
items.concept: Loading a divider's output lowers it, because the load parallels the lower resistor.
items.hint: What happens to a resistance when you put another in parallel with it?

items.q: A 20 volt source drives three resistors in series: 2 ohms, 1 ohm and 5 ohms. What is the source current? Answer in amps.
items.right: Correct, 2.5 amps: 20 volts over a total of 8 ohms.
items.wrong: First add the series resistances: total resistance equals the sum of the resistors, 2 plus 1 plus 5, which is 8 ohms. Then Ohm's law: current equals voltage over total resistance, amps from volts over ohms. 20 volts over 8 ohms is 2.5 amps, and that same current flows through all three resistors.

slips.why: You used only the 5 ohm resistor. The current is set by the whole series total, 8 ohms: 20 over 8 is 2.5 amps.
You multiplied. Current equals voltage divided by total resistance: 20 volts over 8 ohms is 2.5 amps.

items.concept: Add series resistors, then current equals supply voltage over total resistance.
items.hint: Total the resistors first.

items.q: True or false: in a series circuit with a fixed supply, raising one resistor's value lowers the current through every element in the loop.
items.right: True. The total resistance rises, so the single loop current falls everywhere.
items.wrong: Same current everywhere does not mean unchanging current. The loop current equals supply voltage over total resistance, amps from volts over ohms. Raise any resistor and the total rises, so the current falls. Because it is one path, that smaller current flows through every element, not just the changed resistor. The statement is true.
items.concept: In series, changing one resistor changes the one current that flows through all of them.
items.hint: Current equals voltage over total resistance.

items.q: Three resistors are drawn neatly side by side on a circuit board, but each one's right lead connects only to the next one's left lead, with nothing else at those joints. How are they connected?
options: It depends on how they are drawn
items.right: Right. End to end with no other branch is series, whatever the layout looks like.
wrong: They look parallel, but parallel means both ends of each element share the same two nodes. Here each joint links only two resistors end to end, forming one unbranched path. One path with the same current through each part is series.

A chain joined end to end, with nothing else connected at the joints, is exactly the definition of series: one path, so the same current through every element. Total resistance is then the sum of the three.

Series and parallel describe electrical connections, not drawing positions. Trace the path: one resistor leads into the next with no other branch at the joints, so it is a single path. That is series, however it is laid out.
items.concept: Series and parallel are about connections, never about how parts are drawn or placed.
items.hint: Trace the path from one end to the other.

items.q: A 16 volt source drives three series resistors. Two of them drop 4 volts and 9 volts. What does the third resistor drop? Answer in volts.
items.right: Right, 3 volts. The drops must add up to the 16 volt supply.
items.wrong: Kirchhoff's voltage law: around a closed loop, the voltage rises equal the voltage drops, all in volts. The only rise is the 16 volt source. The drops are 4, 9, and the unknown. So 16 equals 4 plus 9 plus the unknown, and the unknown is 16 minus 13, which is 3 volts.

slips.why: You added everything. The drops together equal the source: 16 volts minus 4 minus 9 leaves 3 volts for the third resistor.
You subtracted only one drop. Both known drops come off the source: 16 minus 4 minus 9 is 3 volts.

items.concept: Kirchhoff's voltage law: in a series loop the drops add up to the source voltage.
items.hint: Subtract both known drops from the source.

items.q: A 45 volt source drives 2 kilohms, 5 kilohms and 8 kilohms in series. What is the voltage across the 8 kilohm resistor? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, 24 volts. The 8 kilohm resistor holds 8 fifteenths of 45 volts.
items.wrong: Series drops are proportional to resistance. The voltage divider rule: the voltage across one resistor equals the total voltage times that resistor over the total resistance, in volts and ohms. The total is 2 plus 5 plus 8, which is 15 kilohms. So 45 volts times 8 over 15: 45 over 15 is 3, and 3 times 8 is 24 volts. Or find the current, 45 volts over 15 kilohms, 3 milliamps, then 3 milliamps times 8 kilohms is 24 volts.

slips.why: You split the voltage equally among three resistors. Series drops follow resistance: 3 milliamps times 8 kilohms is 24 volts.
You left the 8 kilohm resistor out of the total. The total is 15 kilohms: 45 times 8 over 15 is 24 volts.

items.concept: Series drops are proportional to resistance: V across R equals total V times R over total R.
items.hint: Find the current first: 45 volts over the total.

items.q: A 12 volt supply drives a 5 ohm resistor. You insert a real ammeter whose own resistance is 1 ohm. What does the ammeter read? Answer in amps.
items.right: Right, 2 amps. The meter's 1 ohm adds to the loop, so the current drops from 2.4 amps.
items.wrong: A real ammeter adds its resistance in series. Total resistance is 5 plus 1, which is 6 ohms. Ohm's law: current equals voltage over total resistance, amps from volts over ohms. 12 volts over 6 ohms is 2 amps. Without the meter the current would have been 12 over 5, 2.4 amps, so the meter has loaded the circuit.

slips.why: 2.4 amps is the current without the meter. Inserting a 1 ohm ammeter makes the loop 6 ohms, so it reads 12 over 6, which is 2 amps.

items.concept: A real ammeter's resistance adds to the loop and lowers the current it measures.
items.hint: Add the meter's resistance to the loop total.

items.q: A 12 volt source drives two 1 megohm resistors in series. A voltmeter whose input resistance is also 1 megohm is placed across the lower resistor. What does it read? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, 4 volts instead of the unloaded 6 volts. The meter loaded the circuit.
items.wrong: The meter's 1 megohm sits in parallel with the lower 1 megohm resistor. Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one: 0.5 megohms. Now the divider is 1 megohm on top and 0.5 megohms below, 1.5 megohms in total. The lower part gets its share: 12 volts times 0.5 over 1.5, which is one third of 12, 4 volts.

slips.why: 6 volts is the unloaded answer. The meter's 1 megohm in parallel with the lower resistor makes 0.5 megohms, so the reading is 12 times 0.5 over 1.5, which is 4 volts.

items.concept: A voltmeter across a high resistance parallels it and pulls the reading down.
items.hint: Combine the meter with the lower resistor first: two equal resistors in parallel.

items.q: A 1 kilohm and a 100 kilohm resistor are connected in parallel across a battery. Which statement is correct?
options: Both carry exactly the same current
Both conduct; the 1 kilohm carries more
items.right: Right. Current takes every path; the smaller resistance simply takes more.
wrong: Backwards. By Ohm's law, current equals the shared voltage divided by the branch resistance, so the larger resistance carries the smaller current. Both branches conduct, and the 1 kilohm branch carries a hundred times more than the 100 kilohm branch.

They share the same voltage, but not the same current. Each branch current equals the voltage over its own resistance. With resistances a hundred times apart, the currents are a hundred times apart, the 1 kilohm branch carrying more.

This is the path of least resistance myth. Both resistors have the same voltage across them, and Ohm's law gives each branch its own current: current equals voltage over that branch's resistance. The 100 kilohm branch carries a hundred times less, but not zero. Current follows every available path.
items.concept: Current follows every available path; each branch current is voltage over that branch's resistance.
items.hint: Same voltage across both. Now apply Ohm's law to each.

items.q: A total current of 6 amps enters a 1 ohm resistor and a 2 ohm resistor connected in parallel. How much current flows through the 1 ohm resistor? Answer in amps.
items.right: Correct, 4 amps. The 1 ohm branch takes twice the 2 ohm branch's 2 amps.
items.wrong: Both branches share one voltage, and each current equals that voltage over its own resistance, so the 1 ohm branch carries twice the current of the 2 ohm branch. Call the 2 ohm current x; the 1 ohm current is 2x. By Kirchhoff's current law they add to the total: 2x plus x equals 6 amps, so x is 2 amps and the 1 ohm branch carries 4 amps. Check: 4 amps times 1 ohm and 2 amps times 2 ohms are both 4 volts.

slips.why: 2 amps goes through the 2 ohm branch. The 1 ohm branch takes twice as much, 4 amps, and together they make 6 amps.
An equal split would need equal resistances. Current divides inversely with resistance: the 1 ohm branch carries 4 amps and the 2 ohm branch 2 amps.

items.concept: Parallel currents split inversely with resistance and add to the total.
items.hint: The smaller resistor takes twice as much. Split 6 into two parts, one twice the other.

items.q: You choose a current arrow from A to B through a 2 kilohm resistor. Node A is at 1 volt and node B is at 5 volts. What is the current in your chosen direction? Answer in milliamps.
items.right: Right, minus 2 milliamps. The real current is 2 milliamps flowing from B to A.
items.wrong: For current referenced from A to B, Ohm's law gives current equals the voltage at A minus the voltage at B, over the resistance: milliamps from volts over kilohms. That is 1 minus 5, which is minus 4 volts, over 2 kilohms, giving minus 2 milliamps. The negative sign says the actual conventional current flows from B to A, from higher potential to lower.

slips.why: The size is right but the sign is not. Your arrow points A to B, and A is lower than B, so current equals 1 minus 5 over 2 kilohms, which is minus 2 milliamps.
You added the node voltages. Ohm's law uses the difference: 1 minus 5 is minus 4 volts, over 2 kilohms, minus 2 milliamps.

items.concept: A negative result means the real current flows opposite to the chosen reference arrow.
items.hint: Voltage at A minus voltage at B, then divide by 2 kilohms.

items.q: Node A is at 16 volts and node B is at 20 volts, both measured from ground. What is V sub A B? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, minus 4 volts. Point B is 4 volts higher than point A.
items.wrong: V sub A B equals the voltage at A minus the voltage at B, in volts. That is 16 minus 20, which is minus 4 volts. The negative sign is information: B sits at a higher potential than A. With the red probe on A and black on B, the meter would read minus 4 volts.

slips.why: That is V sub B A. V sub A B takes A minus B: 16 minus 20 is minus 4 volts.
You added. A double-subscript voltage is a difference: 16 minus 20, which is minus 4 volts.

items.concept: V sub A B equals A minus B; a negative result means B is the higher point.
items.hint: First node minus second node.

items.q: True or false: when you reverse the meter probes on a 1.5 volt cell and the reading becomes minus 1.5 volts, the cell's voltage has changed.
items.right: Right, false. The cell is unchanged; only your reference order flipped.
items.wrong: A meter reads the red probe's potential minus the black probe's: V sub red black. With red on the positive terminal, that is plus 1.5 volts. Swap the probes and it reads the reverse order, which is minus the first reading, minus 1.5 volts. The cell did nothing; you changed which point is compared with which. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Swapping probes negates the reading without changing the circuit.
items.hint: Which changed, the cell or the comparison?

items.q: Two breadboard holes sit right next to each other, but a cut in the metal strip runs between them. With no wire added, are they the same node?
options: Yes, if they are in the same row
items.right: Right. Only a continuous conductor makes one node; closeness does not.
wrong: Adjacency is not connection. A node is a set of points joined by conductor. The cut breaks the metal strip, so the two holes belong to different groups unless you add a wire across the gap. Trace the metal, not the distance.
Rows are only connected where the metal strip is continuous. A cut or split rail divides a row into separate groups. So these holes are separate nodes until a jumper wire joins them.

Whether points are one node depends on the conductor between them, not on power. With a cut in the strip there is no conductor, so they are separate nodes, powered or not. You can check an unpowered board with a continuity or resistance test.
items.concept: One node means joined by conductor; physical closeness proves nothing.
items.hint: Is there metal connecting them?

items.q: Both leads of a resistor are pushed into holes on the same connected breadboard strip. What is the voltage across that resistor once the circuit is powered?
options: It depends on the resistor's value
Zero volts; the strip bypasses it
items.right: Right. Both ends are on one node, so there is no voltage across it and no current through it.
wrong: Its value cannot matter when both ends are on the same node. The voltage across it is the difference between its two ends, and they are the same point electrically, so zero volts. Ohm's law then gives zero current whatever the resistance.

The full supply would appear only if its two ends sat on two different nodes. Here both leads share one metal strip, one node, one voltage. A voltage is a difference between two nodes, so the difference is zero, and by Ohm's law, current equals zero volts over resistance, which is zero. The resistor is bypassed.

Half the supply would need the resistor to be one of two equal parts of a divider between different nodes. With both leads in the same strip, both ends are at one voltage. The difference is zero volts, so it carries no current: it is bypassed.
items.concept: A component with both leads on one node is shorted out: zero volts across it.
items.hint: How many nodes do its two leads touch?

items.q: A meter reads 12.96 volts. How should it be reported to three significant figures?
items.right: Correct. Rounding carries into the next place, and the final zero keeps three figures.
wrong: 12.96 has four significant figures, one more than asked. To report three, round at the third figure: the next digit is 6, so round up, giving 13.0 volts. Keep the original 12.96 in the raw record, but report 13.0.

13 has only two significant figures. Rounding 12.96 to three figures: keep 1, 2 and 9, check the next digit, 6, which rounds the 9 up, carrying to give 13.0. The final zero is what shows three figures, so keep it: 13.0 volts.
That truncates instead of rounding. Keep three figures, 1, 2 and 9, then check the next digit: 6 is 5 or more, so round up. The 9 becomes 10, carrying into the units place, giving 13.0 volts.
items.concept: Round at the third figure, carry if needed, and keep a final zero that shows precision.
items.hint: The digit after the 9 is a 6.

items.q: A bench meter is described as five and a half digits. What does the half digit mean?
options: The last digit changes by halves
The meter is accurate to half a percent
A leading digit that can only show 0 or 1
Half a significant figure of accuracy
items.right: Right. It describes display capacity, not accuracy.
wrong: The last digit steps in whole counts. The half digit is the leading position, restricted to 0 or 1. So a five and a half digit meter shows six positions, one of them limited. It is a display description.

A digit count is not an accuracy figure. Accuracy comes from the manufacturer's specification for the range and function. The half digit is simply a restricted leading position that can only show 0 or 1.

Significant figures come in whole digits, and a display count says nothing about accuracy. The half refers to the leading position, which can only show 0 or 1, while the other five positions show 0 to 9. Accuracy comes from the meter's specification, not its digit count.
items.concept: A half digit is a leading display position limited to 0 or 1; it says nothing about accuracy.
items.hint: Think about the leftmost position on the display.

items.q: In a lab calculation, a resistor R1 of 2.40 kilohms has 7.20 volts across it. What is the current through R1? Answer in milliamps.
items.right: Right, 3.00 milliamps. Volts over kilohms gives milliamps.
items.wrong: Set it out in four parts. Quantity: current through R1. Formula: current through R1 equals the voltage across R1 over R1, milliamps from volts over kilohms. Substitution: 7.20 volts over 2.40 kilohms. Result: 3.00 milliamps, three figures because both inputs have three.

slips.why: You multiplied. Ohm's law for current divides: 7.20 volts over 2.40 kilohms is 3.00 milliamps.
That is the right value in amps. Asked in milliamps: volts over kilohms gives milliamps, so 3.00.

items.concept: Current equals voltage across over resistance; volts over kilohms gives milliamps.
items.hint: Divide 7.20 by 2.40.

items.q: In the course rule set, what does E I S stand for?
items.right: Yes, elements in series: series elements carry the same current.
items.wrong: E I S stands for elements in series, and the rule it names is that every element on one series path carries the same current. Its partner is E I P, elements in parallel, which says elements across the same two nodes share the same voltage. Keep the pairing straight: series shares current, parallel shares voltage.
items.concept: EIS, elements in series: same current through every series element.
items.hint: E for elements, S for the kind of connection.

items.q: In the course rule set, what does E I P stand for?
items.right: Right, elements in parallel: they share the same voltage.
items.wrong: E I P stands for elements in parallel. The rule says elements connected across the same pair of nodes have the same voltage across them. It mirrors E I S, elements in series, where the shared quantity is current instead. Parallel shares voltage; series shares current.
items.concept: EIP, elements in parallel: same voltage across elements sharing two nodes.
items.hint: The mirror image of elements in series.

items.q: For elements in a container on one unbranched path, which statement is NOT one of the three truths?
options: Element voltages add to the terminal voltage
Elements may be reordered, keeping orientation
Elements may be reversed if kept in place
The same current flows through every element
items.right: Right. Reordering is allowed; reversing an element changes the circuit.
wrong: That is truth two, and it is genuine: the element voltages add up to the container's terminal voltage, which is Kirchhoff's voltage law in action. The false statement is the one allowing elements to be reversed. Only reordering with orientation kept is licensed.

That is truth three, and it is genuine: you may move elements along the path as long as each keeps its own orientation. What you may not do is turn one around, because reversing changes the circuit. So the reversing statement is the one that is not a truth.

That one is truth one, and it is genuine: on one unbranched path, charge has nowhere else to go, so the same current flows through every element. The statement that is not a truth is the one about reversing. Turning an element around changes the circuit.
items.concept: EIC truths: same current, voltages add, reorder but never reverse.
items.hint: Reordering and reversing are different operations.

items.q: True or false: in a series chain of a source, a capacitor, an inductor and a resistor, you may turn the capacitor around, as long as it stays in the same position.
items.right: Right, false. Reordering is allowed; reversing an element changes the circuit.
items.wrong: Truth three of the element container lets you reorder series elements, provided each keeps its own orientation. Turning an element around is a different operation: it flips its polarity in the loop and changes the circuit, and a polarized or charged capacitor must not be reversed. So you may swap the inductor and resistor, but not turn the capacitor around. The statement is false.
items.concept: Series elements may be reordered, never reversed.
items.hint: Moving and turning around are not the same thing.

items.q: In the course rule set, what does R I S stand for?
items.right: Yes, resistors in series: total resistance is the sum.
items.wrong: R I S stands for resistors in series. It states that the total resistance of series resistors equals their sum: total resistance equals R one plus R two plus and so on, all in ohms. Note the difference from E I S, elements in series, which is about sharing current. R I S is about adding resistance, and only for resistors.
items.concept: RIS, resistors in series: total resistance equals the sum of the resistors.
items.hint: R for resistors.

items.q: An ideal ammeter sits in the same unbranched path as a resistor, so you write that the ammeter current equals the resistor current. Which rule justifies that line?
options: E I S, elements in series
R I S, resistors in series
E I P, elements in parallel
items.right: Right. Elements in series carry the same current.
wrong: Ohm's law relates one element's voltage, current and resistance: resistance equals voltage across over current through. Your line relates two different elements' currents, which needs the series rule: E I S, elements in series share one current.

R I S explains why series resistances add: total resistance equals the sum. It says nothing about current being shared. The line you wrote claims equal currents on one path, and that is E I S, elements in series.

E I P is about elements across the same two nodes sharing a voltage. The ammeter and resistor are not across the same nodes; they sit one after the other on one path. Equal current on one path is E I S.
items.concept: Equal currents on one path: EIS. Equal voltages across two nodes: EIP. Adding resistors: RIS.
items.hint: Which rule is about sharing current?

items.q: In a two-resistor series circuit you write: the voltage across R two equals the source voltage minus the voltage across R one. Name the rule that justifies that step.
items.right: Yes, KVL. The element voltages around the loop must add up to the source.
items.wrong: That step is Kirchhoff's voltage law, K V L. Around the loop, the rises equal the drops: source voltage equals the voltage across R one plus the voltage across R two. Rearranged, the voltage across R two is the source minus the voltage across R one. Ohm's law would instead find it from R two's own current times its resistance.
items.concept: Subtracting one drop from the source to find another is KVL.
items.hint: Which rule is about voltages around a loop?

items.q: True or false: the R I S rule means that capacitors in series simply add their values, just like resistors.
items.right: Right, false. RIS is for resistors only; capacitors in series do not add that way.
items.wrong: The element container truths apply to any series elements: same current, voltages adding. But adding the values themselves is special to resistors: total resistance equals the sum of the resistances. Capacitors in series do not combine by simple addition. Keep the general series rule and the resistor-only rule apart, so the statement is false.
items.concept: RIS, adding values, is specific to resistors; the container truths are general.
items.hint: Is R I S named for elements or for resistors?

items.q: Name the rule: resistance equals the voltage across a resistor divided by the current through that same resistor.
items.right: Right, Ohm's law, O L in the course rule set.
items.wrong: That is Ohm's law, abbreviated O L. The course writes it with subscripts: resistance equals the voltage across R over the current through R, in ohms, volts and amps. The subscripts matter because in a circuit with several parts, the voltage and current must belong to the same element. Rearranged, it gives voltage equals current times resistance, or current equals voltage over resistance.
items.concept: OL, Ohm's law: R equals V across R over I through R.
items.hint: A two-letter abbreviation named after a German physicist.

items.q: A 10 volt source is connected across a single 5 ohm resistor. What power does the resistor dissipate? Answer in watts.
items.right: Correct, 20 watts. Current is 2 amps, and 10 volts times 2 amps is 20 watts.
items.wrong: By elements in parallel, the resistor sees the full 10 volts. Power equals voltage squared over resistance: watts from volts squared over ohms. 10 squared is 100, and 100 over 5 is 20 watts. Check another way: Ohm's law gives current as 10 over 5, 2 amps, and voltage times current is 10 times 2, also 20 watts.

slips.why: 2 is the current in amps. Power is voltage times current: 10 volts times 2 amps is 20 watts.
You multiplied voltage by resistance. Power is voltage squared over resistance: 100 over 5 is 20 watts.

items.concept: Power equals V times I, I squared times R, or V squared over R.
items.hint: Find the current first, then multiply by the voltage.

items.q: A fixed resistor dissipates 24 watts at 12 volts. The voltage across it is doubled to 24 volts. What is the new power?
items.right: Right. Power goes with voltage squared, so twice the voltage gives four times the power.
wrong: Doubling the power would be true if power were proportional to voltage. At fixed resistance, power equals voltage squared over resistance, watts from volts squared over ohms. Doubling the voltage makes voltage squared four times bigger, so 24 watts becomes 96 watts. The current doubles too, and voltage times current doubles twice.

The resistance is fixed, but the power is not. Power equals voltage squared over resistance. With twice the voltage, voltage squared is four times larger, so the power is four times 24, which is 96 watts.

192 watts would be eight times the power, as if power went with voltage cubed. It goes with voltage squared: power equals voltage squared over resistance. Doubling the voltage multiplies the power by four: 96 watts.
items.concept: Power is a square law in voltage: double the voltage, four times the power.
items.hint: Voltage appears squared in one power formula.

items.q: True or false: an ideal capacitor dissipates energy as heat, just as a resistor does.
items.right: Right, false. Ideal capacitors and inductors store energy and give it back; only resistors dissipate it.
items.wrong: Resistors dissipate: they turn electrical energy into heat, at a rate of current squared times resistance. An ideal capacitor stores energy in an electric field, and an ideal inductor stores it in a magnetic field; both can return it to the circuit and do not heat up. Real parts have small losses, but the ideal model has none. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Resistors dissipate energy; ideal capacitors and inductors store and return it.
items.hint: Which element sends energy out as heat?

items.q: A 1500 watt heater runs until it has used 12 kilowatt-hours of energy. For how many hours did it run? Answer with a plain number of hours.
items.right: Correct, 8 hours: 12 kilowatt-hours divided by 1.5 kilowatts.
items.wrong: Energy equals power times time, so time equals energy divided by power. Keep the units matched: 1500 watts is 1.5 kilowatts, and kilowatt-hours over kilowatts gives hours. 12 divided by 1.5 is 8 hours.

slips.why: You multiplied. Time equals energy divided by power: 12 kilowatt-hours over 1.5 kilowatts is 8 hours.
You divided by 1500 without converting to kilowatts. 1500 watts is 1.5 kilowatts, and 12 over 1.5 is 8 hours.

items.concept: Time equals energy over power; kilowatt-hours over kilowatts gives hours.
items.hint: Change 1500 watts into kilowatts first.

items.q: True or false: the kilowatt-hour is a unit of power.
items.right: Right, false. A kilowatt-hour is energy: power multiplied by time.
items.wrong: Power is a rate, in watts or kilowatts. Energy is power accumulated over time: energy equals power times time, so kilowatts times hours gives kilowatt-hours, an amount of energy. The electricity bill charges for energy, the kilowatt-hours used, while how fast the meter turns shows the power. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Watts measure power, a rate; kilowatt-hours measure energy, an amount.
items.hint: Kilowatts times hours gives what?

items.q: A circuit carries 2 amps. You point the source's current arrow into its positive terminal. Using the course convention, what value do you get for the source current?
items.right: Right. A current referenced into a source's positive terminal comes out negative.
wrong: Plus 2 amps would be correct if the arrow pointed out of the positive terminal, the way a supplying source actually drives current. Your arrow points in, against the real flow, so the algebra returns minus 2 amps. The physical current has not reversed; your reference did.

The circuit still carries 2 amps; drawing an arrow cannot stop the current. A reference arrow only sets the sign. Pointing into the positive terminal is opposite to the actual flow out of a supplying source, so the value is minus 2 amps.
The size of the current does not change with the arrow. Only the sign does. With the arrow pointing into the positive terminal, opposite to the actual current, the source current is minus 2 amps.
items.concept: A reference arrow sets the sign, not the physics; into a source's positive terminal gives a negative value.
items.hint: Does a supplying source push current in or out of its positive terminal?

items.q: True or false: with the course sign convention, the powers of all the elements in a closed circuit add up to zero.
items.right: True. Power delivered by the source is negative and power absorbed by the loads is positive; they cancel.
items.wrong: Energy is conserved, so every watt the source delivers is absorbed somewhere in the circuit. In the course convention, power into the circuit from the source is negative and power leaving through the resistors is positive. For example, a source delivering 20 watts counts as minus 20, and a resistor absorbing 20 watts counts as plus 20. They sum to zero, so the statement is true.
items.concept: With consistent signs, all powers in a closed circuit sum to zero: conservation of energy.
items.hint: What does conservation of energy say about supplied and absorbed power?

items.q: An ideal voltage source does not heat up, yet a real battery gets warm when it supplies current. What in the battery model explains the heating?
options: A small internal resistance in series
A capacitor stored inside the battery
items.right: Right. The internal series resistance dissipates current squared times resistance.
wrong: The ideal source has no resistance, so it dissipates nothing, whatever its voltage. The heating comes from the small internal resistance added in series. Its power is current squared times resistance, watts from amps squared times ohms, so more current means more heat.

Real batteries do warm under load, which is why the model needs something extra. An ideal source in series with a small internal resistance explains it: that resistance dissipates current squared times resistance as heat.

A capacitor stores energy and gives it back; it does not model continuous heating. The real battery is modelled as an ideal source in series with a small internal resistance. That resistor dissipates power equal to current squared times resistance, and that is the heat you feel.
items.concept: A real battery is an ideal source plus a series internal resistance, and that resistance is what heats up.
items.hint: Which part of the model has resistance?

items.q: Three resistors are in series. The total resistance is 12 kilohms, R two is 4 kilohms and R three is 6 kilohms. What is R one?
items.right: Correct, 2 kilohms: 12 minus 4 minus 6.
wrong: 10 kilohms is R two plus R three, not R one. Resistors in series: the total equals the sum of all three. 12 kilohms equals R one plus 10 kilohms, so R one is 12 minus 10, which is 2 kilohms.
4 kilohms is R two's value. By resistors in series, the total is R one plus R two plus R three: 12 equals R one plus 4 plus 6, so R one is 12 minus 10, which is 2 kilohms.

22 kilohms adds all three numbers, but the 12 kilohm total already includes R one. Resistors in series: total resistance equals R one plus R two plus R three. So 12 equals R one plus 10, and R one is 2 kilohms.
items.concept: Resistors in series: the total is the sum, so a missing resistor is the total minus the others.
items.hint: Subtract both known resistors from the total.

items.source: Boylestad §5.7, ratio rule of Example 5.15 (adapted values)
items.q: A 1 ohm and a 2 ohm resistor are in series across 9 volts. Without finding the current, what is the voltage across the 2 ohm resistor?
items.right: Right. It drops twice as much as the 1 ohm resistor, and together they make 9 volts.
wrong: The whole 9 volts is across the pair, not across one resistor. By Kirchhoff's voltage law the two drops add to 9 volts, and because one current flows through both, they divide in proportion to resistance: 3 volts and 6 volts. The 2 ohm resistor has 6 volts.

3 volts is across the 1 ohm resistor. One current flows through both, so each voltage equals current times its resistance, and the voltages are in the ratio 1 to 2. Out of 9 volts in three equal parts, the 1 ohm gets one part, 3 volts, and the 2 ohm gets two parts, 6 volts.

An even split needs equal resistors. In series the same current flows through both, and voltage equals current times resistance, so the larger resistor drops more. The ratio is 1 to 2, so the 2 ohm resistor gets two thirds of 9 volts, which is 6 volts.
items.concept: In series, voltages divide in proportion to resistance.
items.hint: Split 9 volts in the ratio 1 to 2.

items.q: Solving a 1 ohm and 2 ohm divider on 10 volts, a student writes 3.3 volts and 6.6 volts, which add to only 9.9 volts. What happened to the missing 0.1 volts?
options: Nothing is missing; he rounded too early
0.1 volts leaked out of the circuit
items.right: Right. The exact values are ten thirds and twenty thirds of a volt, which add to exactly 10.
wrong: Kirchhoff's voltage law always holds; if the numbers do not close the loop, the error is in the arithmetic. Here the exact drops, 10 over 3 and 20 over 3 volts, sum to exactly 10. Early rounding to 3.3 and 6.6 created the shortfall.

Voltage does not leak out of an ideal divider. The exact drops are 10 over 3 and 20 over 3 volts, which add to exactly 10. Rounding each one down to 3.3 and 6.6 before adding threw away a little from each, creating a false 0.1 volt gap. Round once, at the end: 3.33 and 6.67 volts.

Nothing suggests the resistors are wrong; the gap is arithmetic. The exact drops are ten thirds and twenty thirds of a volt, summing to exactly 10. Rounding each to two figures before adding produced 9.9. Carry full precision and report 3.33 and 6.67 volts.
items.concept: Carry full precision and round once at the end; early rounding creates fake discrepancies.
items.hint: What are the exact values of the two drops?

items.source: Boylestad §5.4, power distribution in a series circuit
items.q: True or false: in a series circuit, the power delivered by the source equals the sum of the powers dissipated by the resistors.
items.right: True. Energy is conserved, so the source's power is shared out among the resistors.
items.wrong: Each resistor dissipates power equal to current squared times its resistance, watts from amps squared times ohms. Energy is conserved, so the source must supply exactly the total. For example, 12 volts across 1 kilohm and 2 kilohms gives 4 milliamps: the resistors take 16 and 32 milliwatts, and the source delivers 12 volts times 4 milliamps, 48 milliwatts, the same total. So the statement is true.
items.concept: Total power delivered equals the sum of the power dissipated by each resistor.
items.hint: Where else could the energy go?

items.q: Kirchhoff's voltage law says: the sum of the blank voltages around a closed path is zero. Which single word fills the blank?
items.right: Right, directed. Without it the statement is false.
items.wrong: The missing word is directed. Kirchhoff's voltage law says the sum of the directed voltages around a closed path is zero. Directed means each voltage carries a sign set by the direction you travel through it. Signed or algebraic capture the idea, but the course wants the word directed on a test. Leave it out and you are adding plain magnitudes, which can never sum to zero.
items.concept: KVL: the directed voltages around a closed path sum to zero.
items.hint: The word tells you each voltage carries a sign.

items.q: Which of these is the second standard form of Kirchhoff's voltage law?
options: The source voltage equals the largest drop
The sum of the rises equals the sum of the drops
The sum of the currents into a node is zero
Every element in a loop has the same voltage
items.right: Yes. Rises on one side, drops on the other, and no negative terms needed.
wrong: The source voltage equals the sum of all the drops, not just the largest one. That is Kirchhoff's voltage law in its second form: the sum of the voltage rises equals the sum of the voltage drops.

That is Kirchhoff's current law, about currents at a node: current in equals current out. Kirchhoff's voltage law is about voltages around a closed loop. Its second form puts the rises on one side and the drops on the other: the sum of the rises equals the sum of the drops.

Series elements share a current, not a voltage; their voltages differ with resistance. Kirchhoff's voltage law says the voltages around a loop balance: the sum of the rises, like a source, equals the sum of the drops across the resistors.
items.concept: KVL form two: sum of rises equals sum of drops.
items.hint: Put the sources on one side and the resistors on the other.

items.q: Walking around a loop, you enter a resistor at its plus terminal and leave at its minus terminal. In the lecture's walking rule, how does its voltage enter the sum?
options: Left out, since it is not a source
items.right: Right. Enter at plus, add plus V; enter at minus, add minus V.
wrong: Every element in the loop contributes, sources and resistors alike. Kirchhoff's voltage law sums the directed voltages of all of them. The sign depends only on the terminal you enter: enter at plus, add plus V.

Each element contributes its voltage once, with a sign. Kirchhoff's voltage law adds directed voltages; entering at the plus terminal gives plus V. Any consistent convention works, provided you apply it to every element.

Minus V is what you add when you enter at the minus terminal. The lecture's rule: the sign comes from the terminal you enter first. Entering at plus, add plus V. Walking the loop this way, the source, entered at minus, contributes minus its voltage, and all the terms sum to zero.
items.concept: The sign of each term comes from which terminal you enter; stay consistent all the way round.
items.hint: Which terminal did you meet first?

items.source: Lecture 06 §1; ELTR 238 quiz study pack worked circuit
items.q: A 12 volt source drives a 1 kilohm and a 2 kilohm resistor in series. What is the voltage across the 2 kilohm resistor? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, 8 volts: 4 milliamps times 2 kilohms.
items.wrong: Reduce, then return. Resistors in series: total resistance is 1 plus 2, which is 3 kilohms. Ohm's law: current equals voltage over total resistance, 12 volts over 3 kilohms, which is 4 milliamps, and by elements in series that flows through both. Back on the original drawing, the 2 kilohm resistor drops current times resistance: 4 milliamps times 2 kilohms is 8 volts. Check by KVL: 4 plus 8 is 12.

slips.why: 4 is the current in milliamps, or the drop across the 1 kilohm resistor. The 2 kilohm resistor drops 4 milliamps times 2 kilohms, which is 8 volts.
An even split needs equal resistors. The drops follow resistance: 4 volts and 8 volts, so the 2 kilohm resistor has 8 volts.

items.concept: Reduce to find the current, then apply Ohm's law to each original resistor.
items.hint: Find the current through the 3 kilohm total first.

items.q: You replace a 1 ohm and a 2 ohm series pair with a single 3 ohm equivalent to find the current. Why can you not read the 1 ohm resistor's voltage from the reduced circuit?
options: The node between them no longer exists
items.right: Right. The equivalent only matches at the outer terminals; the inside node is gone.
wrong: The reduction keeps the current exactly the same; that is its whole purpose. Total resistance equals the sum, and current equals voltage over total. What it throws away is the internal node between the two resistors. Go back to the original drawing and use Ohm's law on the 1 ohm resistor.

The equivalent resistor carries the full loop current: current equals source voltage over the 3 ohm total. The problem is that the node between the original resistors has vanished inside it. Return to the original circuit to find each element's voltage.

Reduction does not touch the source. The equivalent reproduces the source voltage and current at the outer terminals, and that is all it promises. The node between the two original resistors no longer exists, so return to the original drawing for their separate voltages.
items.concept: An equivalent resistor matches only at its outer terminals; return to the original for internal voltages.
items.hint: What happened to the point between the two resistors?

items.q: A 10 volt source drives three series resistors dropping 7 volts, 2 volts and 1 volt. Nodes A, B, C and D run along the chain, with A at the source's positive terminal. What is V sub A C?
items.right: Right, 9 volts: the 7 volt and 2 volt drops between A and C.
wrong: 2 volts is V sub B C, the middle resistor alone. From A to C you pass both the first and second resistors, so V sub A C is the sum of their drops, 7 plus 2, which is 9 volts.
3 volts is the voltage from B to D, the last two drops. V sub A C covers the first two resistors, between A and C: 7 plus 2, which is 9 volts.
10 volts is V sub A D, across all three resistors. V sub A C, the voltage at A with respect to C, includes only the drops between A and C: 7 plus 2, which is 9 volts.
items.concept: V sub A C adds the drops between A and C only.
items.hint: Which resistors lie between A and C?

items.q: Measured from ground, node A is at plus 20 volts and node B is at minus 15 volts. What is V sub A B? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, 35 volts. Going from plus 20 down to minus 15 is a 35 volt drop.
items.wrong: V sub A B equals the voltage at A minus the voltage at B. That is 20 minus minus 15. Subtracting a negative adds, so 20 plus 15 is 35 volts. Think of a bank balance going from plus 20 to owing 15: the total change is 35.

slips.why: You subtracted 15 from 20. B is at minus 15, so A minus B is 20 minus minus 15, which is 35 volts.
That is V sub B A. V sub A B is A minus B: 20 minus minus 15, plus 35 volts.

items.concept: Subtracting a negative node voltage adds its size.
items.hint: Minus a minus becomes a plus.

items.q: A meter reads V sub A B equal to plus 4.2 volts. What is V sub B A, and has the circuit changed?
options: Minus 4.2 volts; the circuit is unchanged
Plus 4.2 volts; the circuit is unchanged
items.right: Right. Swapping the order negates the reading; the circuit itself is untouched.
wrong: The value, minus 4.2 volts, is right, but nothing in the circuit changed. V sub B A is simply B minus A, the negative of A minus B. Swapping the probes changes the comparison, not the voltages at the nodes.

V sub A B and V sub B A describe the same pair of nodes in opposite order; they are negatives of each other, not quantities that add. V sub B A equals B minus A, which is minus 4.2 volts, and the circuit is unchanged.

Order matters in double-subscript notation. V sub B A equals the voltage at B minus the voltage at A, which is the negative of V sub A B. So it is minus 4.2 volts. The circuit is unchanged; only the probe order swapped.
items.concept: V sub B A equals minus V sub A B; swapping probes changes the sign, not the circuit.
items.hint: Red on B, black on A.

items.q: True or false: if V sub A B is 5 volts and node B is at 4 volts from ground, then node A is at 9 volts from ground.
items.right: True. A minus B is 5, so A is 5 volts above B's 4 volts.
items.wrong: V sub A B equals the voltage at A minus the voltage at B. Rearranged, the voltage at A equals V sub A B plus the voltage at B. That is 5 plus 4, which is 9 volts. A sits 5 volts above B, and B is 4 volts above ground. So the statement is true.
items.concept: Voltage at A equals V sub A B plus the voltage at B.
items.hint: A is 5 volts above B.

items.q: In a chain with drops of 7, 2 and 1 volts along nodes A, B, C and D, the reference is placed at node B. What is the single-subscript voltage at node D? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, minus 3 volts. D sits 2 plus 1 volts below B.
items.wrong: With B as the reference, it is zero volts. Walking from B toward D you go down through the 2 volt drop to reach C, at minus 2 volts, then down through the 1 volt drop to reach D, at minus 3 volts. Check: A is plus 7, and A minus D is 7 minus minus 3, which is the full 10 volts.

slips.why: The size is right, but D is below the reference, so its voltage is negative: minus 3 volts.
Minus 1 volt is the drop from C to D alone. From B you also pass the 2 volt drop, so D is at minus 3 volts.

items.concept: Single-subscript voltages are measured from the chosen reference; below the reference they are negative.
items.hint: Count the drops from B down to D.

items.q: On a schematic, the downward triangle marks a local zero volt common. What does the three-bar symbol mean?
items.right: Right, earth. It is a different idea from the local common.
items.wrong: The downward triangle marks the local zero volt reference, the common point for measurements in that circuit. The three-bar symbol means an actual earth connection. People say ground loosely for both, which is why the symbol on the page matters more than the word. A circuit can have a local common without being connected to earth at all.
items.concept: Triangle: local zero volt common. Three bars: earth.
items.hint: Something you could push a rod into.

items.q: A schematic labels nodes A, B and C but marks no reference node anywhere. What can you say about V sub B?
options: It is undefined until a reference is chosen
It is measured from earth by default
It is measured from node A, the first label
items.right: Right. A single subscript needs a stated reference; otherwise use double subscripts.
wrong: A node is zero only if it is the chosen reference. With no reference marked, V sub B has no defined value at all. Name both nodes with a double subscript, or declare a reference node explicitly.

Earth is not an automatic reference. A single-subscript voltage names only the red probe's node, and the black probe must sit on a marked reference. With none marked, V sub B has no meaning. Use a double subscript such as V sub B C, or declare a reference yourself and say where it is.

There is no rule that the first label is the reference. With no reference marked, V sub B is undefined. Double subscripts always work, because they name both nodes: V sub B A is the voltage at B minus the voltage at A.
items.concept: No marked reference, no single subscripts; double subscripts always work.
items.hint: Where would the black probe go?

items.q: True or false: moving the reference node from one point to another changes the voltage between any two nodes, such as V sub A B.
items.right: Right, false. Every node voltage shifts by the same amount, so every difference stays the same.
items.wrong: Moving the reference adds the same constant to every single-subscript voltage. V sub A B equals the voltage at A minus the voltage at B, and when both shift by the same amount, the shift cancels in the subtraction. So V sub A B is unchanged. Only the single-subscript values change, which is why you pick the reference once and keep it. The statement is false.
items.concept: Moving the reference shifts all node voltages equally and leaves every difference unchanged.
items.hint: What happens to a difference when both terms shift equally?

items.q: You measure voltages around a loop with a meter, but partway round you swap which probe leads. What must you do before checking that the readings sum to zero?
options: Flip the sign of the reading you took reversed
Discard the whole loop and start again
items.right: Right. Keep the signs consistent, and one flipped reading must be negated.
wrong: The meter model does not matter. Kirchhoff's voltage law needs every reading taken in the same direction of travel. A swapped reading has the opposite sign, so negate it before adding.

Ignoring the swap leaves one term with the wrong sign, and the sum will not come out to zero. Kirchhoff's voltage law adds directed voltages, so every reading must follow the same direction of travel. Negate the reading that was taken the other way round, then sum.
A full restart is not needed. What matters is sign consistency: Kirchhoff's voltage law sums directed voltages. Negate the one reading taken with the probes reversed, and the loop will close.
items.concept: Around a loop, keep probe orientation consistent, or negate any reading taken reversed.
items.hint: A swapped probe flips the sign of that one reading.

items.q: A plug-in supply is labelled 5 volts, 2 amps. What does the 2 amps tell you?
options: The current it draws from the wall
The most current it can safely supply
items.right: Right. It is a rated maximum; the load decides the actual current.
wrong: The supply does not push out a fixed current. The load decides: by Ohm's law, current equals the supply voltage over the load resistance. A 5 kilohm load would draw only 1 milliamp. The 2 amps is the ceiling the supply can provide within its rating.
The label describes the output, not the input. The 2 amps is the maximum output current the supply is rated to deliver. What it draws from the wall is a separate specification.

With nothing connected, the load is an open circuit, an infinite resistance. By Ohm's law, current equals 5 volts over infinity, which is zero. The 2 amps is only the maximum the supply can deliver when a load asks for it.
items.concept: A supply's current rating is a maximum; the load sets the actual current.
items.hint: Who decides how much current flows, the supply or the load?

items.q: True or false: a 5 volt, 2 amp supply with nothing connected to its terminals is delivering 2 amps.
items.right: Right, false. With nothing connected, no current flows at all.
items.wrong: Nothing connected means the terminals see an open circuit, an infinite resistance. Ohm's law gives the current: current equals voltage over resistance, 5 volts over infinity, which is zero amps. The 2 amp figure is a maximum the supply can deliver, not a current it forces out. So the statement is false.
items.concept: An open circuit draws zero current, whatever the supply's rating.
items.hint: What resistance does an open circuit present?

items.q: What does an ideal current source hold constant?
options: Both its voltage and its current
Its current, whatever voltage that needs
Its terminal voltage, whatever the load
items.right: Yes. An ideal current source fixes current; its voltage adjusts to the load.
wrong: A source cannot fix both; the load would then be overdetermined. By Ohm's law, voltage equals current times load resistance, so fixing the current leaves the voltage to be set by the load. An ideal current source fixes current only.

Power equals voltage times current, and an ideal current source does not hold it constant. It fixes the current; the voltage, and therefore the power, change with the load. Voltage equals current times load resistance.

That describes an ideal voltage source, which fixes its terminal voltage regardless of current. A current source is the mirror image: it fixes the current and lets its terminal voltage be whatever the load needs, by Ohm's law, voltage equals current times load resistance.
items.concept: Ideal voltage source: fixed voltage. Ideal current source: fixed current, voltage set by the load.
items.hint: It is named for the quantity it fixes.

items.q: A battery is rated at 72 ampere-hours. For about how long could it ideally supply a steady 1.8 amps?
items.right: Correct, 40 hours: 72 ampere-hours over 1.8 amps.
wrong: That comes from multiplying capacity by current. Ideal run time equals capacity divided by current: hours from ampere-hours over amps. 72 over 1.8 is 40, because 1.8 times 40 is 72. So about 40 hours.
4 hours is off by a factor of ten. Run time equals capacity divided by current: 72 ampere-hours over 1.8 amps. 1.8 times 40 is 72, so the answer is 40 hours.
72 hours would need a 1 amp load. Run time equals capacity divided by current, so a larger current means less time: 72 over 1.8 is 40 hours.
items.concept: Run time equals ampere-hour capacity divided by load current.
items.hint: How many times does 1.8 go into 72?

items.q: Four 1.5 volt cells are connected in series, each positive terminal joined to the next cell's negative terminal. What is the total voltage?
items.right: Right. Series-aiding cells add: four times 1.5 is 6 volts.
wrong: 1.5 volts would be the result of connecting the cells in parallel. In series-aiding, each cell's rise adds to the next. By Kirchhoff's voltage law the total equals the sum of the rises: 1.5 plus 1.5 plus 1.5 plus 1.5, which is 6 volts.
3 volts is only two cells, like a two-cell flashlight. Here four cells add: by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the total is the sum of the rises, four times 1.5, which is 6 volts.
Dividing makes no physical sense here. Series-aiding cells add their voltages: the total equals the sum of the rises, by Kirchhoff's voltage law. Four times 1.5 volts is 6 volts.
items.concept: Series-aiding cells add their voltages.
items.hint: Each cell stacks on top of the last.

items.q: True or false: a cell's nominal voltage, such as 1.5 volts, is a guaranteed exact value at all times.
items.right: Right, false. Nominal is a representative label; the real terminal voltage varies.
items.wrong: Nominal voltage is a representative designation. The actual terminal voltage depends on chemistry, state of charge, temperature, load and age. A fresh 1.5 volt alkaline cell can read about 1.6 volts on a voltmeter with no load, and it falls as it discharges or supplies current. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Nominal voltage is a label for normal operation, not a guaranteed exact value.
items.hint: Does a fresh cell read exactly 1.5 volts?

items.q: A 10 volt ideal source has 10 ohms of internal resistance and drives a 10 ohm load. What is the terminal voltage across the load? Answer in volts.
items.right: Correct, 5 volts: exactly half, the signature of a load equal to the internal resistance.
items.wrong: The internal resistance and the load are in series. Resistors in series: 10 plus 10 is 20 ohms. Ohm's law: current equals 10 volts over 20 ohms, which is 0.5 amps. The load drops current times resistance: 0.5 amps times 10 ohms is 5 volts. The other 5 volts is lost inside the source.

slips.why: 10 volts is the open-circuit value. With a 10 ohm load, 0.5 amps flows and the internal resistance drops 5 volts, leaving 5 volts at the terminals.
1 amp would need 10 ohms total. The loop is 20 ohms, so the current is 0.5 amps, and the load drops 0.5 times 10, which is 5 volts.

items.concept: Terminal voltage equals source voltage minus the internal drop, current times internal resistance.
items.hint: The internal resistor and the load share the voltage.

items.q: The same source, 10 volts ideal with 10 ohms internal, now has its load removed. What does an ideal voltmeter read across its terminals?
items.right: Right. No current, so no internal drop, so the full 10 volts appears.
wrong: It is predictable. Open terminals mean zero current. The internal resistor then drops zero volts, current times resistance, and Kirchhoff's voltage law gives terminal voltage equals source voltage minus zero: 10 volts.

This is the classic beginner's mistake: open circuit does not mean zero voltage. With the load removed, the current is zero. The internal resistor drops current times resistance, zero times 10 ohms, which is zero volts. By Kirchhoff's voltage law the terminals then show the full 10 volts.

5 volts was the loaded value, when 0.5 amps flowed through the internal resistance. With the load removed the current is zero, the internal drop is current times resistance, zero, so the terminal voltage rises to the full 10 volts.
items.concept: An unloaded source shows its full voltage: zero current means zero internal drop.
items.hint: What does the internal resistor drop with no current?

items.q: A generator has 0.5 ohms of internal resistance. How much terminal voltage is lost inside it when it supplies 10 amps? Answer in volts.
items.right: Right, 5 volts lost across the internal resistance.
items.wrong: The internal resistance carries the full load current, so Ohm's law gives its drop: voltage equals current times resistance, volts from amps times ohms. 10 amps times 0.5 ohms is 5 volts. The terminal voltage is 5 volts less than the no-load value.

slips.why: You divided current by resistance. The drop is current times resistance: 10 amps times 0.5 ohms is 5 volts.

items.concept: Internal voltage loss equals load current times internal resistance.
items.hint: Current times the internal resistance.

items.source: Boylestad §5.11, method of Chapter 5 Problem 47 (adapted values)
items.q: A battery reads 12 volts with nothing connected, and 10 volts with a 5 ohm load connected. What is its internal resistance? Answer in ohms.
items.right: Correct, 1 ohm. The load current is 2 amps and the lost voltage is 2 volts.
items.wrong: The open reading, 12 volts, is the ideal source voltage. Under load, the current is the terminal voltage over the load: 10 volts over 5 ohms, 2 amps. The voltage lost inside is 12 minus 10, 2 volts. By Ohm's law, internal resistance equals lost voltage over current: 2 volts over 2 amps is 1 ohm.

slips.why: You scaled the load by the voltage ratio. Internal resistance is lost voltage over current: 2 volts over 2 amps is 1 ohm.
2 is the lost voltage, or the current. Divide one by the other: 2 volts over 2 amps is 1 ohm.

items.concept: Internal resistance equals the lost voltage divided by the load current.
items.hint: First find the load current: 10 volts over 5 ohms.

items.q: Why can you not measure a live battery's internal resistance by putting an ohmmeter across its terminals?
options: Its own voltage swamps the meter's test signal
Its internal resistance is far too large to read
Ohmmeters only work above one megohm
Internal resistance is not a real quantity
items.right: Right. An ohmmeter assumes an unpowered part; the live source breaks that assumption.
wrong: Internal resistance is usually small, often a fraction of an ohm. The real problem is the method. An ohmmeter pushes its own small test current and computes resistance as voltage over current. A live battery adds its own voltage, so the result is meaningless. Use the open-circuit and loaded readings instead.

Ohmmeters read low values too. The issue is that they supply their own test current and apply Ohm's law, resistance equals voltage over current. A live source's own voltage overwhelms that small test signal, so the reading means nothing. Infer the internal resistance from two terminal readings.

Internal resistance is real; it is why a battery's terminal voltage sags under load. It just cannot be measured directly, because the node inside is unreachable and an ohmmeter's test signal is swamped by the source voltage. Compare open-circuit and loaded readings.
items.concept: Measure internal resistance indirectly: open-circuit reading, loaded reading, then lost voltage over current.
items.hint: What does an ohmmeter assume about the part it measures?

items.q: In a written unit, what is the difference between lowercase k and uppercase K?
options: k is kilograms; K is kilo
k is kilo; K is kelvin
k is kelvin; K is kilo
items.right: Right. Lowercase k multiplies by 1000; uppercase K is the kelvin, a temperature unit.
wrong: SI symbols are case-sensitive. Lowercase k is kilo, a multiplier of 1000; uppercase K is kelvin, a temperature. Written carelessly, 20 kilograms could read as kelvin-grams, which is meaningless.
Lowercase k is only a prefix; on its own it is not a unit. It multiplies whatever unit follows by 1000, so kilograms is k plus g. Uppercase K is kelvin, a temperature unit.
That is backwards. Lowercase k is the prefix kilo, times 1000, as in kilohms. Uppercase K is the kelvin, the SI unit of temperature. So 20 kilohms, written with a lowercase k, is 20,000 ohms.
items.concept: Lowercase k: kilo, times 1000. Uppercase K: kelvin, temperature.
items.hint: One is a multiplier, the other a temperature.

items.q: Kilohms multiplied by milliamps gives which unit?
items.right: Right, volts. Kilo times milli is one.
items.wrong: Ohm's law: voltage equals current times resistance, volts from amps times ohms. Kilo is ten to the three and milli is ten to the minus three, so kilohms times milliamps multiplies by ten to the three times ten to the minus three, which is one. The prefixes cancel and you are left with plain volts. For example, 3 milliamps times 4 kilohms is 12 volts.
items.concept: Kilo times milli equals one, so kilohms times milliamps gives volts.
items.hint: Ten to the three times ten to the minus three.

items.q: Which statement defines two elements being in parallel?
options: They are the same distance apart everywhere
Both their ends share the same two nodes
They are drawn side by side
items.right: Right. Parallel is a statement about nodes, never about the picture.
wrong: Sharing a current is the series property, elements in series. Parallel elements share a voltage, because they connect across the same two nodes, and they generally carry different currents, each equal to that voltage over its own resistance.
Equal spacing is the geometry meaning of parallel, and it is the wrong one here. Electrically, parallel means both ends of each element connect to the same pair of nodes.

Side by side is a drawing position, not an electrical fact. Components placed side by side can be wired end to end, in series. Parallel means both ends of one element connect to the same pair of nodes as both ends of the other, which is why they share one voltage.
items.concept: Parallel: both ends on the same two nodes, so the same voltage.
items.hint: Think about nodes, not the drawing.

items.q: True or false: three resistors drawn side by side, evenly spaced, must be in parallel.
items.right: Right, false. The same drawing positions can be wired in series or in parallel.
items.wrong: Parallel is decided by connections: both ends of each element must land on the same two nodes. Three resistors in identical positions can be wired end to end, making one path in series, or across one pair of nodes, in parallel. Trace the nodes before deciding. So the statement is false.
items.concept: Series and parallel are electrical, never visual; trace the nodes.
items.hint: Could the same layout be wired end to end?

items.q: 10 volts is across a 1 kilohm resistor and a 2 kilohm resistor connected in parallel. What total current does the source supply? Answer in milliamps.
items.right: Correct, 15 milliamps: 10 through the 1 kilohm branch and 5 through the 2 kilohm branch.
items.wrong: Both branches see the full 10 volts, by elements in parallel. Ohm's law for each: current equals voltage over resistance, milliamps from volts over kilohms. 10 over 1 is 10 milliamps; 10 over 2 is 5 milliamps. The branch currents add to the total, 10 plus 5, which is 15 milliamps.

slips.why: You added the resistors as if in series. In parallel each branch has 10 volts: 10 plus 5 milliamps is 15 milliamps.
10 milliamps is only the 1 kilohm branch. Add the 2 kilohm branch's 5 milliamps: 15 milliamps.

items.concept: Parallel branch currents each equal V over R, and they add to the total.
items.hint: Find each branch current, then add.

items.q: In a parallel circuit, one branch's resistance is doubled while the voltage stays the same. What happens to that branch's current?
items.right: Right. Branch current equals voltage over resistance, so twice the resistance gives half the current.
wrong: Doubling resistance halves the current; it does not eliminate it. Branch current equals the shared voltage over that branch's resistance, in amps from volts over ohms. Current takes every path; a harder path carries less, not none.
Current and resistance are inversely related here. Branch current equals voltage divided by resistance, so with the voltage fixed, a resistance twice as large gives a current half as large.
The branch voltage is fixed, but its current depends on its resistance. Ohm's law gives branch current equals voltage over resistance, so doubling the resistance halves the current.
items.concept: Branch current is inversely proportional to branch resistance.
items.hint: Current equals voltage over resistance, with the voltage fixed.

items.q: A 3 ohm and a 6 ohm resistor are connected in parallel. What is their total resistance? Answer in ohms.
items.right: Correct, 2 ohms: 18 over 9, and less than the smaller resistor.
items.wrong: For two resistors, total resistance equals the product over the sum: R one times R two, over R one plus R two, in ohms. 3 times 6 is 18, and 3 plus 6 is 9, so 18 over 9 is 2 ohms. Check: 2 ohms is less than 3 ohms, the smallest resistor, as every parallel total must be.

slips.why: You added them as if in series. In parallel, use product over sum: 18 over 9 is 2 ohms.
0.5 is one over R total, in siemens. Flip it: one over 0.5 is 2 ohms.

items.concept: Two resistors in parallel: product over sum, and the result is below the smaller one.
items.hint: Multiply them, then divide by their sum.

items.q: Three 12 ohm resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
items.right: Right. Equal resistors in parallel: one value divided by how many, 12 over 3.
wrong: 36 ohms is the series total, 12 plus 12 plus 12. In parallel the total must be less than the smallest resistor. For equal resistors, total resistance equals one resistor's value divided by the number of them: 12 over 3, which is 4 ohms.

The parallel total can never equal one of the resistors; it must be smaller than the smallest. Each extra branch adds another path. For equal resistors, total equals R over N, the value over the count: 12 over 3 is 4 ohms.
6 ohms is what two 12 ohm resistors give. With three, the total is one value over the count: total resistance equals R over N, 12 over 3, which is 4 ohms.
items.concept: N equal resistors in parallel give R divided by N.
items.hint: Divide one value by how many there are.

items.q: A student adds one over 1 kilohm plus one over 2 kilohms, gets 1.5, and reports the total as 1.5 kilohms. What went wrong?
options: He did not take the reciprocal of the sum
He should have simply added 1 and 2 kilohms
He forgot to convert kilohms to ohms
items.right: Right. The sum is one over R total, so flip it: one over 1.5 millisiemens is about 667 ohms.
wrong: Adding the resistances directly is the series rule, and it would give 3 kilohms. For parallel, one over R total equals the sum of the reciprocals. The student's sum, 1.5, is one over R total, in millisiemens. Flip it once: R total is one over 1.5 millisiemens, about 667 ohms.

The kilohm units are consistent; that is not the problem. The reciprocal formula gives one over R total, not R total. The sum of 1 plus 0.5 is 1.5 per kilohm, so R total is one over 1.5 kilohms, about 667 ohms.
1.5 kilohms fails the parallel check at once: a parallel total must be less than the smallest resistor, 1 kilohm. The sum of reciprocals is one over R total, so it must be flipped: about 667 ohms.
items.concept: Sum the reciprocals, then flip once more: the formula gives one over R total.
items.hint: Is 1.5 kilohms smaller than 1 kilohm?

items.q: True or false: a meter across a genuine 1 kilohm and 2 kilohm parallel pair could correctly read 1.5 kilohms.
items.right: Right, false. A parallel total must be below the smallest resistor, 1 kilohm.
items.wrong: The bound catches this at once: a parallel combination is less than its smallest resistor. Product over sum gives 2 over 3 kilohms, about 667 ohms. A 1.5 kilohm reading means a wiring fault, perhaps the resistors are in series or something else is connected, or a meter problem. Find it before calculating further. The statement is false.
items.concept: Parallel total is always less than the smallest resistor; use that to catch errors.
items.hint: Compare 1.5 kilohms with the smaller resistor.

items.q: What is the conductance of a 2 kilohm resistor? Answer in millisiemens.
items.right: Right, 0.5 millisiemens. One over a kilohm is a millisiemens.
items.wrong: Conductance equals one over resistance: siemens from one over ohms. One over 2 kilohms: the reciprocal of kilo is milli, so this is one half of a millisiemens, 0.5 millisiemens. In plain units, one over 2000 ohms is 0.0005 siemens.

slips.why: 2 is the resistance in kilohms. Conductance is its reciprocal: one over 2 kilohms is 0.5 millisiemens.
500 is the value in microsiemens. Asked in millisiemens, one over 2 kilohms is 0.5 millisiemens, because kilo becomes milli.

items.concept: Conductance is one over resistance; one over kilohms gives millisiemens.
items.hint: One over 2, then kilo becomes milli.

items.q: What is the unit of conductance?
items.right: Yes, the siemens: one siemens is one over an ohm.
items.wrong: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, G equals one over R, and its unit is the siemens, symbol capital S. One siemens equals one per ohm. The name belongs to a person, so the unit keeps its final s in both singular and plural: one siemens, ten siemens.
items.concept: Conductance, G, is one over R, measured in siemens.
items.hint: Named after the German engineer Werner von Siemens.

items.q: True or false: for resistors in parallel, the total conductance is the sum of the individual conductances.
items.right: True. Conductances add in parallel, just as resistances add in series.
items.wrong: Each parallel branch carries current equal to the shared voltage times its conductance. Adding the branch currents gives total current equals voltage times the sum of the conductances, so total conductance is the sum: G total equals G one plus G two, in siemens. For example, a 3 ohm and a 6 ohm resistor give one third plus one sixth, one half siemens, which is 2 ohms. The statement is true.
items.concept: Resistances add in series; conductances add in parallel.
items.hint: Think of each branch as another path for current.

items.q: A motor draws 100 watts of electrical input and delivers 80 watts of mechanical output. What is its efficiency? Answer in percent.
items.right: Correct, 80 percent. The other 20 watts is lost, mostly as heat.
items.wrong: Efficiency equals useful output power over input power, times 100 for percent. The output is 80 watts and the input 100 watts, so 80 over 100 is 0.80, which is 80 percent. The 20 watt difference is the loss.

slips.why: 20 is the power lost, in watts. Efficiency is output over input: 80 over 100 is 80 percent.
You divided input by output. Efficiency is output over input, which can never exceed 100 percent: 80 percent.

items.concept: Efficiency is output over input; the difference is loss.
items.hint: Output divided by input.

items.q: An 80 percent efficient stage feeds a 90 percent efficient stage. What is the overall efficiency?
items.right: Right. Cascaded efficiencies multiply as decimals: 0.8 times 0.9 is 0.72.
wrong: Subtracting the percentages has no meaning here. For cascaded stages, total efficiency equals efficiency one times efficiency two, as decimals. 0.8 times 0.9 is 0.72, which is 72 percent.

Averaging the two gives 85 percent, but cascaded losses compound. Total efficiency equals the first efficiency times the second, as decimals. 0.8 times 0.9 is 0.72, so 72 percent. With 100 watts in, 80 watts leave the first stage and 72 watts leave the second.

Adding them gives more than 100 percent, which is impossible. For stages in cascade, total efficiency equals the product of the stage efficiencies as decimals: 0.8 times 0.9, which is 0.72, or 72 percent.
items.concept: Cascaded efficiencies multiply as decimals.
items.hint: Multiply 0.8 by 0.9.

items.q: What condition does a ground fault circuit interrupter respond to?
options: Outgoing and returning current not matching
Current rising above the breaker rating
Too much power used over a month
items.right: Right. It trips when some current returns by another path.
wrong: Excess current is what fuses and ordinary breakers respond to. A ground fault circuit interrupter watches for a different condition: the current going out on one conductor not matching the current returning on the other. That imbalance means current is leaking by another path, possibly through a person.

Voltage level is not what it senses. A ground fault circuit interrupter compares outgoing and returning current. If they differ, some current is taking another path to ground, and it disconnects the circuit.

Energy use over time is what the utility meter records. A ground fault circuit interrupter responds within moments to an imbalance between outgoing and returning current, which signals leakage by another path.
items.concept: Fuses and breakers: overcurrent. GFCI: outgoing and returning current imbalance.
items.hint: What does it compare?

items.q: An NTC thermistor warms up. What happens to its resistance?
items.right: Right. NTC means negative temperature coefficient: hotter, lower resistance.
wrong: A rising resistance with temperature is a positive temperature coefficient, like copper or a PTC thermistor. NTC stands for negative temperature coefficient, so its resistance falls as its temperature rises. That strong, deliberate change is what makes it useful as a temperature sensor.
A thermistor is built to change with temperature; that is its whole purpose. NTC means negative temperature coefficient: as it warms, its resistance falls, often steeply and not in a straight line.

Its resistance falls, but not to zero. An NTC thermistor has a negative temperature coefficient, so warming lowers its resistance smoothly over its range. Zero resistance would describe a superconductor, a different thing entirely.
items.concept: NTC thermistor: resistance falls as temperature rises.
items.hint: N stands for negative.

items.q: A surface-mount resistor is marked 4, 7, 2. What is its resistance?
