The rule of thumb: move to a smaller unit and the number gets bigger; move to a larger unit and the number gets smaller. Take 0.025 millivolts. One millivolt is 1000 microvolts, because milli is ten to the minus three and micro is ten to the minus six. So 0.025 millivolts times 1000 is 25 microvolts. That is the same voltage, now with a sensible number in front. Going the other way, 2700 ohms divided by 1000 is 2.7 kilohms. A classic mistake is to change the prefix without changing the number: writing 0.025 millivolts as 0.025 microvolts makes the value a thousand times too small. Another is reading 2.7 kilohms as 2.7 ohms. Whenever you switch prefixes, say to yourself, smaller unit, bigger number, and check that your number moved the right way by the right factor.
segments.expand: Walk through two more conversions, one to a smaller prefix and one to a larger prefix, and the check for each.

segments.title: The four-step calculation format
segments.text: Every calculation should show four things. Step one names the quantity you are finding, such as I X. Step two writes the formula in symbols, such as I X equals V two divided by R three. Step three substitutes the values with their units. Step four gives the numerical answer with its unit. The steps can sit in one connected line; they do not need four separate paragraphs. The point is that someone reading your work, including you tomorrow, can see what you were finding, which relationship you used, and exactly which numbers and prefixes went in. Here is an example. A resistor of 2.7 kilohms has 4.76 volts peak to peak across it. The current, by Ohm's law, is voltage divided by resistance, amps from volts over ohms. So I X equals 4.76 volts peak to peak over 2.7 kilohms, which is about 1.76 milliamps peak to peak. Keep the peak to peak label on the answer too.
segments.expand: Show a second four-step calculation, and explain why the unit label such as peak to peak must travel with the answer.

segments.title: A mental unit check
segments.text: A lovely shortcut falls out of the prefixes. Volts divided by kilohms gives milliamps, because dividing by ten to the three is the same as multiplying by ten to the minus three. So 4.76 volts over 2.7 kilohms comes out directly in milliamps, about 1.76. The same trick works the other way: milliamps times kilohms gives volts, because the ten to the minus three and the ten to the three cancel. Two milliamps through 4 kilohms drops 8 volts. You can also do it all in base units if you prefer: 4.76 divided by 2700 is about 0.00176 amps, which is 1.76 milliamps. Either way you get the same result. The point of the shortcut is speed and a sanity check. If your calculator says 1760 and you expected milliamps, you know immediately that a kilo went missing somewhere in step three.
segments.expand: Give more pairings like volts over kilohms equals milliamps, including microamps times kilohms, and show how to use them as sanity checks.

segments.title: Finding your own mistakes
segments.text: The four steps are not only for the reader; they let you backtrack. If you found the wrong quantity altogether, look back at step one. If the relationship itself is wrong, say you used the total voltage instead of the voltage across one resistor, the problem is in step two. If the answer is off by a clean factor such as a thousand, the problem is almost certainly step three, a prefix or unit substituted wrongly, because each engineering prefix is a factor of a thousand from its neighbour. And if the formula and substitution are right but the number is still wrong, check step four, your calculator entry and rounding. A related habit: keep enough digits during the working and round only once, at the end, to the precision asked for. Rounding early and then multiplying can drift the last digit and make a correct method look wrong.
segments.expand: Give an example of a factor-of-one-thousand error and trace it back to the exact step where it happened.

segments.title: Prefixes on a clock: period and frequency
segments.text: Here is where prefixes meet digital electronics directly. A digital clock repeats. Its period is the time for one complete cycle, from one rising edge to the next. Its frequency is how many cycles happen each second. They are reciprocals: frequency equals one over period, with frequency in hertz and period in seconds. Kleitz's first example has a period of 2 microseconds. One over 2 microseconds is 0.5 times ten to the six hertz, which is 0.5 megahertz, or 500 kilohertz. His second example goes the other way: a processor clock of 4 gigahertz has a period of one over 4 times ten to the nine seconds, which is 250 picoseconds. Two pairings are worth memorising, because they make these conversions almost instant: 1 kilohertz goes with 1 millisecond, and 1 megahertz goes with 1 microsecond. Double the frequency and the period halves.
segments.expand: Work one more frequency to period conversion in nanoseconds, and explain why rising edge to rising edge is one period.

segments.title: Choosing a sensible prefix for an answer
segments.text: Once you have a number, pick the prefix that puts it between 1 and 999. A calculator might give 0.000877 amps. Move the decimal three places at a time: 0.877 milliamps is still below 1, so move again to 877 microamps. That is the engineering form. Similarly, 0.877 volts is better said as 877 millivolts. Do not overdo it in the other direction; 0.47 milliamps is a correct value but not engineering notation, because the number is below 1, so write 470 microamps. Finally, every final answer needs its unit. A bare number such as 1.76 tells the reader nothing, because it could be amps, milliamps or volts. In spoken work, say the unit every time, the way you are hearing it in this lecture. That habit will stop more errors than any clever technique.
segments.expand: Practise converting three calculator outputs into engineering notation and explain the move of three decimal places.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Four ideas from this lecture. One: engineering notation uses exponents in steps of three, written as prefixes, with the number kept between 1 and 999, and prefix letters are case sensitive, so small m is milli and capital M is mega. Two: changing prefix never changes the quantity; smaller unit means bigger number, by a factor of a thousand per step. Three: every calculation shows the target, the formula, the values with units, and the answer with its unit, and when something goes wrong a clean factor of a thousand points straight at the substitution step. Four: frequency and period are reciprocals, and the pairs 1 kilohertz with 1 millisecond and 1 megahertz with 1 microsecond let you convert in your head. Carry these habits into every lecture from here on.
segments.expand: Give the student a quick mixed drill: one prefix conversion, one Ohm's law answer in milliamps, and one frequency to period conversion.

lectures.title: Charge, current and static discharge
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 03 - Charge, Current and ESD.md; Kleitz §9-5 (handling MOS devices, as cited)

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture connects three ideas: charge exerts force, moving charge is current, and a potential difference can drive that motion. Along the way we will see why a spark forms, why static electricity can quietly destroy an integrated circuit, how a wrist strap protects your chips, how to calculate current from charge and time, and which way current flows compared with the electrons. We will end with a short piece of history: why Volta's battery was such a big step beyond static electricity. Keep in mind the distinction we started last class: charge is an amount, current is a rate, and voltage is a difference between two points.
segments.expand: Summarise how charge, current and voltage relate, using the water tank and pipe comparison, and where the comparison breaks down.

segments.title: Attraction, repulsion and neutral objects
segments.text: Charge comes in two signs. Positive and positive repel; negative and negative repel; positive and negative attract. The labels positive and negative are a convention, but the forces are real and measurable. A neutral object has balanced positive and negative charge; it does not contain no charge. When solid objects become charged, it is usually electrons that move. Gain electrons and an object becomes more negative; lose them and it becomes more positive. Now the balloon. Rub a balloon so it picks up extra electrons, hold it near a neutral wall, and it sticks. The wall has not become positively charged. Instead the balloon's charge nudges the charges inside the wall surface, so the opposite charge sits slightly closer to the balloon than the like charge. The nearer charge wins, giving a net attraction. That is called polarization. So attraction alone does not prove the other object has the opposite charge. Repulsion is the clearer sign of like charges.
segments.expand: Explain polarization in more detail and why the nearer charges win because force depends on distance.

segments.title: Coulomb's law
segments.text: Charles Coulomb measured electrical forces in 1785 using a torsion balance, where a tiny force twists a suspended arm and the twist is calibrated. His result is Coulomb's law. The force between two point charges equals a constant k times the product of the two charges, divided by the distance between them squared. Force is in newtons, charge in coulombs, distance in metres, and k is about 8.99 times ten to the nine in newton metres squared per coulomb squared. The most useful part is the scaling. Double one charge and the force doubles. Double both and it quadruples. Because distance is squared, double the separation and the force drops to one quarter; triple it and the force drops to one ninth. Combine changes by multiplying the factors: double one charge and triple the distance, and the new force is two over nine of the old. The signs only tell you direction: like signs repel, opposite signs attract.
segments.expand: Work a combined scaling example and explain why separating size from direction makes Coulomb problems easier.

segments.title: How a spark forms
segments.text: When you shuffle across a carpet, contact and separation leave you with extra charge, and a large potential difference can build up between you and a doorknob without you noticing. Air is normally an insulator. But a strong enough electric field can rip electrons free from air molecules. Those electrons collide with more molecules and free more electrons, and very quickly a conducting channel of ionized gas, a plasma, forms. Charge rushes across it, and that brief discharge is the spark. Remember the chain: charge separation, then a potential difference, then a strong field, then air breakdown, then a brief discharge. As a rough classroom estimate, a centimetre spark suggests something like twenty thousand volts; the textbook figure for breakdown of air in a uniform field is about thirty kilovolts per centimetre. Either way, treat it as a scale estimate. Real breakdown depends on the gap shape, humidity and pressure, so a spark is not a precise voltmeter.
segments.expand: Explain avalanche ionization step by step, and why sharp points break down at lower voltages than smooth surfaces.

segments.title: Electrostatic discharge and chips
segments.text: Electrostatic discharge, or E S D, is a rapid transfer of charge between objects at different potentials. A spark is one visible form, but here is the key point for this course: a discharge that damages an integrated circuit does not have to be visible, and you do not have to feel it. The tiny structures inside a chip can be harmed by discharges far below what your fingertip can sense. So I did not feel anything is not evidence that a chip is safe. That is why E S D control is part of every bench where chips are handled. Kleitz's list of rules for handling M O S devices, the family of transistors used in C M O S chips, exists for exactly this reason. We protect the parts by making sure charge never gets the chance to build up on us or on the work surface in the first place.
segments.expand: Explain why modern integrated circuits are so sensitive to static discharge, and why damage may appear later rather than immediately.

segments.title: How a wrist strap works
segments.text: The wrist strap gives your body a controlled path to the workstation's ground point, so charge cannot accumulate on you. It works as part of a system: the band, a cord, the grounding point, and a protective work surface, all keeping you and your parts near the same potential. For it to work, the band has to sit snugly against bare skin, and its cord has to be connected to the designated grounding point. A loose band or an unplugged cord provides no reliable path at all. The cord contains a current-limiting resistor, around one megohm in Kleitz's example, and it should never be bypassed. That resistor lets static charge bleed away slowly while limiting current. One important boundary: a wrist strap is for static control, not protection from electric shock. It is not a licence to work near hazardous voltages.
segments.expand: Explain why the strap's resistor matters, both for bleeding charge gradually and for personal safety.

segments.title: Current is the rate of charge flow
segments.text: Charge and current are different quantities. Charge is an amount; current is how fast charge passes a chosen cross-section of a wire. Average current equals the change in charge divided by the change in time, with current in amps, charge in coulombs and time in seconds. So one amp is one coulomb per second. Count the charge that crosses the section during the interval, not all the charge sitting in the wire. Example: 12 millicoulombs pass in 4 milliseconds. The average current is 12 millicoulombs over 4 milliseconds. Both have the milli prefix, so they cancel, and the answer is 12 over 4, which is 3 amps. You can rearrange the same relationship. Charge equals current times time, and time equals charge divided by current. For instance, 2 milliamps flowing for 3 seconds moves 6 millicoulombs. Voltage, by contrast, is measured between two points and can exist with no current at all, as in a battery sitting on a shelf.
segments.expand: Work a problem that solves for time from charge and current, taking care with prefixes that do not cancel.

segments.title: Conventional current and electron drift
segments.text: Conventional current points in the direction positive charge would move. That definition was set before anyone knew about electrons, and it remains the standard. In a metal, the mobile charges are electrons, which are negative, so their average drift is opposite to conventional current. If electrons drift left, the conventional current is to the right. Outside a battery that is powering a resistor, conventional current flows from the positive terminal through the circuit to the negative terminal, while electrons in the wire drift from negative to positive. Current is not restricted to electrons, though. In salt water or a plasma, positive ions and negative ions both move. Positive charge moving right and negative charge moving left both count as conventional current to the right, so they add. And a negative calculated current, say minus 8 milliamps with the arrow pointing right, means 8 milliamps really flows left.
segments.expand: Explain how positive and negative carriers both contribute current in an ionic solution, with a numeric example.

segments.title: From static sparks to Volta's battery
segments.text: Static charging can produce a very high voltage, but a discharge quickly uses up the stored charge separation. It cannot supply a steady current for an experiment. That is why Alessandro Volta's voltaic pile, announced in 1800, mattered so much. It was a stack of two different metals separated by electrolyte-soaked layers, and chemical reactions kept a potential difference going, supporting a sustained current through an external circuit. Compare the two. A static discharge is brief, and its voltage collapses as it discharges. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy and keeps supplying current while its chemicals last, though its terminal voltage still depends on its condition and load. The milestones in order: Franklin in the mid seventeen hundreds, who gave us positive and negative; Coulomb in 1785 with his measured force law; and Volta in 1800 with the first practical battery.
segments.expand: Explain why a sustained current needs a continuous energy source, and compare a static discharge with a battery in a closed circuit.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Here are the key ideas from this lecture. First, like charges repel and opposite charges attract, a neutral object is balanced rather than empty, and a charged object can attract a neutral one by polarization. Second, Coulomb's law makes force proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the distance squared, so doubling the distance quarters the force. Third, a spark is air breaking down into a conducting channel, and E S D can destroy a chip without any sensation at all, which is why a properly connected wrist strap is used. Fourth, current is charge per unit time, one amp being one coulomb per second. Fifth, conventional current follows positive charge, so electrons in a wire drift the other way, and a negative answer just flips the arrow.
segments.expand: Pose one question from each of the five ideas and discuss the most common wrong answer for each.

lectures.title: Mechanical switches and logic inputs
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 04 - Mechanical Switches and Logic Inputs.md; Kleitz §2-5, §2-6

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Today we turn a plain mechanical switch into a proper logic input. A switch on its own only makes, breaks or selects a connection; it does not produce a 1 or a 0. To get defined logic levels we add a supply, a resistor and an output node, and then Kirchhoff's voltage law and Ohm's law prove what the output voltage is in each switch position. We will name switches by poles and throws, look at normally open and normally closed contacts and relays, work a series circuit fully, build the pull-up and pull-down, and see two wiring mistakes to avoid. We will finish with how to discover which pins of a switch are connected inside.
segments.expand: Explain why a bare switch does not by itself produce a logic level, and what the resistor adds.

segments.title: Poles and throws
segments.text: Switches are named by poles and throws. A pole is one independent electrical path the switch controls. Your instructor makes that visible by counting pivots: each moving contact turns about a pivot, and each pivot is one pole. A throw is a destination that pole can connect to. So S P S T, single pole single throw, makes or breaks one path. S P D T, single pole double throw, connects one common terminal to either of two destinations. S P 3 T selects one of three. D P D T switches two separate paths together, each between two destinations. Two traps. An S P S T switch's open position is not a second throw, because it connects to nothing. And a dashed line linking two blades means they move together mechanically; it does not join their circuits electrically. Example from class: a stereo selector must switch left and right channels together, so two poles, and choose among three inputs, so three throws. That is D P 3 T.
segments.expand: Work another pole and throw example, such as switching two channels among four inputs, and explain the dashed link.

segments.title: Normally open, normally closed, and relays
segments.text: For a momentary pushbutton, normal means released. A normally open contact, N O, is open when released and closes when pressed. A normally closed contact, N C, is closed when released and opens when pressed. A maintained toggle stays wherever you put it. Be careful with one abbreviation: N C beside a contact usually means normally closed, but N slash C beside an unused pin means no connection, so spell out the meaning when a drawing could be ambiguous. Kleitz extends this to the relay, a switch operated by an electromagnet. Current in the coil pulls the contacts over. For a relay, normal means the coil is de-energized. Energizing the coil closes normally open contacts and opens normally closed ones. A relay lets a small control current switch a separate circuit, but it is mechanical, so it is slow and its contacts can bounce.
segments.expand: Explain relay contacts in a voltage divider: what the output is with the coil off and on, for normally open contacts across the lower resistor.

segments.title: Labelling a circuit before you calculate
segments.text: Before any calculation, fully label the circuit, in this order. First the supply: its name, value, polarity and the fact that it is D C. Second an assumed current arrow with a name, such as I one. Third, each component's voltage with a clear plus and minus pair. Fourth, choose ground and label the node voltages you need. Remember the difference between the two kinds of voltage. A component voltage compares a component's two terminals: if a resistor joins nodes A and B with plus at A, then its voltage is V A minus V B. A node voltage compares one node with ground. For resistors, put the plus mark where the assumed current enters; that passive sign convention makes the resistor law simply voltage equals current times resistance. Ground here is the chosen zero-volt reference, not necessarily a physical earth, and points joined by ideal wire share one node voltage.
segments.expand: Explain the passive sign convention again with an example where the calculated current turns out negative.

segments.title: A worked series circuit
segments.text: Take a 5 volt D C supply with a 4.7 kilohm resistor and a 1 kilohm resistor in series. The same current flows through both. Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop gives 5 volts minus V R one minus V R two equals zero. Substitute Ohm's law, voltage equals current times resistance, and solve: the current equals the supply voltage divided by the total resistance, in amps, volts and ohms. That is 5 volts over 5.7 kilohms, about 0.000877 amps, or 877 microamps. Now the drops. The 4.7 kilohm resistor drops about 4.12 volts, and the 1 kilohm resistor drops about 877 millivolts. With the bottom of the 1 kilohm resistor at ground, the junction between them sits at 877 millivolts, because that node voltage equals the lower resistor's drop. Check it another way: 5 volts minus 4.12 volts is about 0.877 volts. Keep the unrounded values while working, and round once at the end.
segments.expand: Repeat the series calculation with simpler numbers, such as 10 volts across 1 kilohm and 4 kilohms, and find the junction voltage.

segments.title: The pull-up resistor
segments.text: A pull-up places a resistor between the positive supply and the output node, and the switch connects that output to ground. Use 5 volts, a 1 kilohm pull-up and a normally open pushbutton. One Kirchhoff equation covers both states: 5 volts minus the resistor voltage minus the switch voltage equals zero. What changes is the switch. Pressed, the closed switch is a short with zero volts across it, so the output is 0 volts, LOW, and the whole 5 volts sits across the resistor. The current, by Ohm's law, is 5 volts over 1 kilohm, which is 5 milliamps. Released, the open switch lets no current flow, so the resistor drops zero volts, and the output is 5 volts, HIGH. The resistor pulls the output up to the supply whenever the switch is open. So with a normally open button and a pull-up, pressing the button gives LOW: the press is active LOW.
segments.expand: Repeat the pull-up analysis with 3.3 volts and 10 kilohms, including the pressed current.

segments.title: Zero current is not zero voltage
segments.text: This is the idea that trips people most in this topic, so it gets its own moment. In the released pull-up, the open switch carries no current. It is tempting to say, no current, so no voltage. But look at what Ohm's law actually says: voltage equals current times resistance. That forces zero voltage only across something with a finite resistance, like the resistor. The resistor carries zero current, so it drops zero volts. The open switch has effectively infinite resistance, and zero times infinity tells you nothing. So instead use Kirchhoff: the supply is 5 volts, the resistor takes zero, so the remaining 5 volts must sit across the open switch. The closed switch is the mirror image: it carries 5 milliamps but has zero volts across it. Open means zero current; closed means zero voltage. The rest comes from Kirchhoff.
segments.expand: Give another example where a component carries no current but has a large voltage across it, such as a reverse-biased diode.

segments.title: The pull-down, and active HIGH
segments.text: A pull-down swaps the positions. The switch goes between the positive supply and the output, and the resistor goes from the output to ground. Released, no current flows, so the resistor drops zero volts and the output sits at ground, 0 volts, LOW. Pressed, the output connects straight to the supply, HIGH, and the resistor limits the current from supply to ground to the supply voltage divided by its resistance. So with a normally open button, a pull-down makes the press active HIGH, while a pull-up makes it active LOW. Both circuits give the output a defined level in both switch positions, which is the whole point. Which one you choose depends on whether the input you are driving should see a HIGH or a LOW when the button is pressed.
segments.expand: Compare the pull-up and pull-down side by side and discuss when each would be chosen.

segments.title: Two wiring mistakes
segments.text: The first mistake is leaving the output floating. If a switch simply connects the supply to a logic input, with nothing else attached, then opening the switch leaves the input connected to nothing. That input is floating. Floating does not mean zero volts; stored charge, leakage and interference decide its voltage, so its level is undefined. The pull-down resistor fixes that by giving a defined path to ground. The second mistake is replacing the pull-up resistor with a plain wire. Now, when the switch closes, the supply is shorted straight to ground. The current is limited only by the supply's protection and stray resistances; it is not literally infinite, but it can be large enough to heat or damage parts. So the resistor is not decorative. It sets the released level and it limits current in the pressed state.
segments.expand: Explain why a floating input can pick up noise, and what happens electrically when the pull-up is replaced with a wire.

segments.title: Finding a switch's internal connections
segments.text: Small pushbuttons often have four legs, even though a single switch needs only two electrical groups. The extra legs give mechanical strength, and some are connected together inside. You cannot tell which from the outside, so you measure. With the switch isolated and unpowered, use a meter's continuity function. Label the four terminals A, B, C and D. There are six unique pairs: A B, A C, A D, B C, B D and C D. Reversing the probes does not create a new pair, because a mechanical contact conducts the same both ways. Test each pair twice, released and pressed. A pair that beeps in both states is permanently connected. A pair that beeps only when pressed is the switched path. From that table you can map the internal circuit before wiring anything. The same method identifies the common and the two throws in each section of a multi-switch S P D T package.
segments.expand: Walk through a sample set of continuity readings for a four-pin switch and deduce the internal connections.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Four ideas to keep. First, poles count independent paths, which your instructor counts as pivots, and throws count destinations per pole; an open position is not a throw. Second, normally open and normally closed describe the released or de-energized state, and a relay's coil moves every contact away from its normal state. Third, a pull-up resistor makes an open switch read HIGH and a closed switch read LOW, while a pull-down does the reverse, and in both the resistor limits current. Fourth, zero current does not mean zero voltage: the open switch carries no current but holds the full supply, and Kirchhoff's voltage law, not Ohm's law, tells you so. Without a resistor, an input floats, and a floating input has no defined level.
segments.expand: Give a mixed question combining a normally closed button with a pull-up, and ask for the released and pressed levels.

lectures.title: Diodes, transistors and logic inputs
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 05 - Diodes, Transistors and Logic Inputs.md; Kleitz §2-7, §2-8, §2-9, §3-4

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture adds two semiconductor devices to our switching toolkit. The diode conducts in one direction only, and the N P N transistor lets a small base circuit control a separate collector to emitter path. For both we use the same method: choose a state for the device, solve the circuit, then check that the answer supports the state you chose. After that we look at how these devices sit inside logic chips, why every unused logic input needs a defined level, and how holding one input of a gate steady lets a clock through or blocks it. Throughout, we use clearly stated models, such as 0.7 volts for a conducting silicon diode, rather than exact physics.
segments.expand: Explain the assume, solve, check method and why it is needed for devices that behave differently in different states.

segments.title: Anode, cathode and bias
segments.text: A diode has two terminals, the anode and the cathode, and the straight bar in its symbol marks the cathode. On a real signal diode such as a 1 N 4148, a band on the body marks the cathode. Define the diode voltage as the anode potential minus the cathode potential. If that is positive, the diode is forward biased: the polarity favours conventional current from anode to cathode. If it is negative, the diode is reverse biased, and in our model it acts as an open circuit. Here is the trap. It is the difference that matters, not either voltage on its own. With the anode at plus 2 volts and the cathode at plus 5 volts, the diode voltage is 2 minus 5, which is minus 3 volts. It is reverse biased, even though both ends are positive compared with ground. A useful picture is a check valve in a water pipe: pressure from one side opens the flap, pressure from the other side seals it.
segments.expand: Extend the check valve analogy, including what the spring represents, and where the analogy stops working.

segments.title: The 0.7 volt model
segments.text: For calculations we use a constant forward-drop model. A conducting silicon diode has 0.7 volts across it from anode to cathode. A diode that is off carries zero current, and its voltage is set by the rest of the circuit. The 0.7 volts is an approximation, not a law of nature. A real diode's forward voltage depends on its current and temperature, and a datasheet gives it at stated test conditions. Older germanium diodes are often approximated at 0.3 volts, and L E Ds have larger drops again. There is another subtle point: forward biased does not automatically mean on in this model. A diode with only 0.3 volts forward across it is forward biased, but the silicon model still treats it as off, because it is below 0.7 volts. Finally, do not mix models. If you use an ideal diode with zero drop in one step, do not subtract 0.7 volts in the next.
segments.expand: Explain why real diode current rises gradually rather than switching at exactly 0.7 volts, and when the ideal model is good enough.

segments.title: A diode and resistor in series
segments.text: Take a 5 volt supply, a 4.7 kilohm resistor and a forward-pointing silicon diode in one loop. Try the diode off first. Then no current flows, the resistor drops nothing, and the full 5 volts appears forward across the diode. That is well above 0.7 volts, contradicting off. So the diode is on. Write Kirchhoff's voltage law: 5 volts minus the resistor voltage minus 0.7 volts equals zero. The resistor therefore has 4.3 volts across it. Ohm's law gives the current: current equals voltage divided by resistance, in amps, volts and ohms, so 4.3 volts over 4.7 kilohms is about 915 microamps. Check: the current is positive, which supports the on assumption, and 5 minus 4.3 minus 0.7 is zero. Kleitz does the same with a 1 kilohm resistor: 4.3 volts across it and 4.3 milliamps through it. Turn the diode around and it is off: zero current, zero resistor voltage, and the diode holds all 5 volts.
segments.expand: Work the reversed-diode case fully and explain why the resistor's node then sits at ground.

segments.title: Two diodes in series
segments.text: With two diodes, each could be on or off, so there are four state combinations to consider. In a single series path, though, both diodes carry the same current, so one cannot conduct while the other blocks. That rules out the mixed cases quickly. Take 5 volts, a 3.3 kilohm resistor and two forward diodes. Assume both on: the resistor gets 5 minus 0.7 minus 0.7, which is 3.6 volts, and the current is 3.6 volts over 3.3 kilohms, about 1.09 milliamps. Now lower the supply to 1.5 volts. The two diodes take 1.4 volts, leaving only 0.1 volts for the resistor, so the current falls to about 30.3 microamps. And if the supply is below 1.4 volts, the formula would give a negative current. That does not mean current flows backwards through the diodes; it means the all-on assumption failed, and the path is off, with zero current.
segments.expand: Explain how to recognise a failed assumption from a negative current, and what the correct off-state solution looks like.

segments.title: The N P N transistor
segments.text: A bipolar junction transistor has three terminals: base, collector and emitter. The N P N type has its emitter arrow pointing outward. The key idea is control. A small current in the base circuit governs a larger current in the collector to emitter path, rather like a small valve operating a bigger one. The transistor does not create that energy; the collector supply does. With conventional currents flowing into the base and the collector and out of the emitter, Kirchhoff's current law says the emitter current equals the collector current plus the base current. Watch the subscripts on voltages too. V B E means base minus emitter, and V C E means collector minus emitter. Only when the emitter is grounded does V C E equal the collector's node voltage. In the classroom model, a fully on N P N has 0.7 volts from base to emitter and zero volts from collector to emitter, assuming the base drive is sufficient.
segments.expand: Explain why emitter current equals collector plus base current, and why the classroom switching model is a simplification.

segments.title: A worked transistor switch
segments.text: The emitter is grounded. A 3.3 volt input drives the base through a 10 kilohm resistor, and a separate 5 volt supply feeds the collector through 1.5 kilohms. Solve the base loop first. The base-emitter junction takes 0.7 volts, so the base resistor has 3.3 minus 0.7, which is 2.6 volts. Base current, by Ohm's law, is 2.6 volts over 10 kilohms, which is 260 microamps. Note that the 3.3 volt input is not the base voltage; the base sits at 0.7 volts and the resistor takes the difference. Now the collector loop, with the transistor fully on and zero volts from collector to emitter. The whole 5 volts is across the collector resistor, so the collector current is 5 volts over 1.5 kilohms, about 3.33 milliamps, and the output at the collector is 0 volts. The emitter current is the sum, about 3.59 milliamps. Set the input to 0 volts and everything switches off: no current, and the collector rises to 5 volts.
segments.expand: Recompute the transistor switch with a 5 volt input and a 1 kilohm collector resistor, and check both loops.

segments.title: Why this circuit inverts
segments.text: Look at what that example did. Input 0 volts, transistor off, output 5 volts, HIGH. Input 3.3 volts, transistor on, output 0 volts, LOW. The output is the opposite of the input, so this common-emitter circuit is an inverter. The input goes to the base, the emitter is common, tied to ground, and the output is taken at the collector, which is pulled up by the collector resistor. Keep two ideas separate: the transistor's state and the output's logic level. Turning the transistor on pulls the output low. Kleitz adds one more warning in his section on T T L chips. When the transistor is off, the output is only at the full supply if nothing draws current from it. A load resistor to ground forms a divider with the collector resistor and pulls the high level down, which is why real logic chips use a stronger output stage.
segments.expand: Explain output loading on the inverter with a numeric divider example, and why a totem-pole output helps.

segments.title: From discrete parts to logic chips
segments.text: A logic chip packs many of these transistors and diodes together. T T L, transistor-transistor logic, is built from bipolar transistors like the N P N we just used. Before you wire any chip, orient the package. On a dual in-line package, find the notch or pin one marker; looking from the top, numbering runs down one side and back up the other. The exact part number and its datasheet decide which pins are power, ground, inputs and outputs, so never assume a pinout from the package shape alone. Next, give every input a defined level. An unconnected input floats, and its voltage can be pushed around by noise and coupling, so it is not a dependable HIGH or LOW. In the lab arrangement discussed, unused gate inputs are tied HIGH. Outputs are different: an unused output can be left unconnected, but a driven output must never be tied to a supply rail as if it were an input.
segments.expand: Explain why floating inputs misbehave and why inputs and outputs are treated differently when unused.

segments.title: Holding one gate input steady
segments.text: The class demonstration used a NAND gate, whose output is the inverse of the AND of its inputs. Hold one input HIGH and feed a clock to the other. One AND clock is just the clock, and the NAND inverts it, so the output is the clock turned upside down: clock LOW gives output HIGH, clock HIGH gives output LOW. This is a small case of what Kleitz calls enable and disable. With a plain AND gate, holding the control input HIGH lets the signal pass unchanged, because one and A equals A, while holding it LOW forces the output LOW, because zero and anything is zero. An OR gate works the other way: a LOW control passes the signal, and a HIGH control forces the output HIGH. The input value that takes over the output, zero for AND and one for OR, is called the controlling value.
segments.expand: Work through AND and OR enable with a clock, and explain how a run and stop control uses this idea.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: The main ideas from today. One: a diode is forward biased when anode minus cathode is positive; in our model it then holds 0.7 volts, and reverse biased it is open, so judge bias by the difference, never by one voltage alone. Two: solve device circuits by assuming a state, solving, and checking that the result supports the assumption; a negative forward current means the assumption failed. Three: an N P N transistor's base current, input minus 0.7 over the base resistor, switches its collector to emitter path, and in the common-emitter circuit that makes an inverter: transistor on, output LOW. Four: in logic chips, every input needs a defined level, and holding one gate input at a fixed value either passes a signal or blocks it.
segments.expand: Give a short diode question and a short transistor question, and discuss the typical mistake in each.

lectures.title: IC pinouts, schematics and TTL basics
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 06 - IC Pinouts, Schematics and Lab Standards.md; Kleitz §3-5, §2-9

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture moves us from discrete parts to integrated circuits. We will read a real datasheet pinout, for the 74 L S 47 decoder, a resistor array and a seven-segment display, and learn the professional conventions for putting a chip on a schematic: where pin numbers go, how to name each chip, and how active-low pins are marked. Then we look at why neat, flat wiring is an electrical issue, not only a tidy one. Finally we begin T T L itself: the transistor as a switch, the inverter, and the common gate chips such as the 7408. The theme is that a schematic is a set of instructions for someone who cannot ask you what you meant.
segments.expand: Explain why a schematic must be complete and unambiguous for someone else to build or troubleshoot from it.

segments.title: The three devices in this circuit
segments.text: The circuit discussed uses three devices. The 74 L S 47 is a B C D to seven-segment decoder and driver. It takes a four-bit binary coded decimal input and works out which of the seven segment lines to switch so that a digit appears. The seven-segment display is the digit itself: seven L E D bars, lettered a to g, plus a decimal point. The 330 ohm resistor array is a single package holding several 330 ohm resistors, one to limit the current in each segment. Using eight separate resistors would work electrically; the array is simply neater on a board. A little background explains why the resistors are there: the 47 is designed for common-anode displays, and its outputs pull low to light a segment. So current flows from the supply, through the display segment and its resistor, into the decoder's output. Without the resistor, that segment current would be far too large.
segments.expand: Explain how a B C D to seven-segment decoder decides which segments to light for a digit, using one digit as an example.

segments.title: Reading a pinout
segments.text: Doing a pinout means getting every pin's number and every pin's function onto the drawing, including the power pins, not only the ones you plan to wire. Take the datasheet from the manufacturer's own site, where the information is reliable. Pin 1 is marked on the package by a notch or a dimple, and sometimes a small dot. Hold the chip with the notch at the top: pin 1 is top left, numbering runs down that side and then back up the other. For the 74 L S 47 in its 16-pin package, the supply V C C is pin 16 and ground is pin 8. The binary inputs are capital A, B, C and D, on pins 7, 1, 2 and 6, while the lowercase letters a to g are the segment outputs. The display and the resistor array need the same care. The resistor array datasheet covers several internal arrangements, so read the one for your exact package.
segments.expand: Explain how to find pin 1 and count pins on a sixteen-pin package, and why the uppercase and lowercase letters matter.

segments.title: Overbars mean active low
segments.text: Several 74 L S 47 pins carry names with a bar over them: L T, lamp test; B I or R B O, blanking in and ripple blanking out; and R B I, ripple blanking in. Spoken aloud you might say L T bar or L T not. The bar means the function is active low: it does its job when the pin is held at logic 0, not logic 1. So to run a lamp test, which lights every segment to check the display, you pull the L T pin LOW; in normal use it sits HIGH. Active low is simply a statement about which logic level asserts the function. It does not mean a negative voltage, and it does not change what HIGH and LOW mean physically. Many control pins in digital systems are active low, so learn to spot the bar and ask, what level turns this function on?
segments.expand: Give other examples of active-low control pins, and explain how a designer decides the idle level for such a pin.

segments.title: Number outside, function inside
segments.text: One rule governs every chip you place on a schematic: the pin number goes outside the body, and the pin function goes inside. On a horizontal pin, the number sits just above the wire; on a vertical pin, it sits beside the wire. The reason is practical. Every pin's wire has to run off somewhere once the drawing is finished. If the number sat on the line the wire will follow, the wire would end up passing straight through it. Keeping the number just off the wire leaves that path clear. Many manufacturers print numbers inside the outline on their own package drawings; that is their house style, not the schematic convention used here. The resistor array is the odd one out. It is an analog part with no functions to name, so you number all its pins outside and put a small resistor symbol inside between each connected pair.
segments.expand: Explain why the resistor array is drawn with resistor symbols inside its outline when digital chips are not.

segments.title: Designators and part numbers
segments.text: Each chip on a schematic needs a designator, a unique name for that physical part. Integrated circuits use the letter U: U1, U2, U3 and so on, not I C 1. Directly below the designator goes the part number, such as 74 L S 47 or 74 L S 193. That is a part number, not a value. Pick one corner of the chip outline for this label and use the same corner on every chip, because consistency is what lets a reader find labels quickly. The reason for all of this is traceability. Someone assembling, inspecting or troubleshooting a board must be able to match every symbol on the page to one physical part, without guessing which label belongs to which chip. A designator that is missing, duplicated or placed carelessly between two chips invites exactly the kind of mix-up that costs hours on the bench.
segments.expand: Explain how designators support assembly and troubleshooting, and what goes wrong when labels are ambiguous.

segments.title: Why wiring should lie flat
segments.text: Flat wiring, with every wire lying against the breadboard and no loops jumping over other wires or over chips, has an electrical reason. A loop of wire behaves like an antenna. Put two loops side by side, and a fast clock edge in one couples a spike into the other. The digital circuit then fails now and again, with glitches on a line, even though nothing in your logic is wrong. That kind of intermittent fault is among the hardest to find. The second reason is practical: a tangle of wires cannot be traced end to end, so it cannot be troubleshot. Wire cut to length and stripped so it lies flat keeps loop area small and keeps every connection visible. Once the circuits grow to several chips, this is what makes a fault a ten-minute job instead of an impossible one.
segments.expand: Explain how loop area relates to coupling between wires, and why fast edges make it worse.

segments.title: T T L transistors as switches
segments.text: T T L stands for transistor-transistor logic: logic built from bipolar junction transistors, dating from the nineteen sixties and still in use, running from a nominal 5 volt supply. For now we model the transistor's collector to emitter path as a plain switch. With base current flowing, the switch is closed; this is saturation, fully on. With zero base current, the switch is open; this is cutoff. The base-emitter junction behaves like a diode, needing about 0.7 volts before it conducts. So a 5 volt input through a base resistor pushes current into the base and turns the transistor on, while 0 volts gives no base current and turns it off. Treat any base current means fully on as a classroom simplification: real transistors also have an active region where they amplify, and real saturation needs enough base current for the load.
segments.expand: Explain saturation, cutoff and the active region, and why switching circuits avoid the active region.

segments.title: The inverter and the gate chips
segments.text: The simplest logic function is the inverter: input LOW gives output HIGH, and input HIGH gives output LOW. It is drawn as a triangle with a small bubble on the output, and inside a real T T L inverter there are four transistors, two diodes and four resistors. The symbol is the abstraction; the transistor circuit is what is really on the chip. Kleitz's section on using logic chips introduces the common packages. The 7408 holds four two-input AND gates, the 7432 four two-input OR gates, the 7411 three three-input AND gates, and the 7421 two four-input AND gates. On these 14-pin T T L chips, pin 14 is V C C at plus 5 volts and pin 7 is ground. On the 7408, the first gate's inputs are pins 1 and 2 and its output is pin 3, and the other gates follow in the same pattern.
segments.expand: Walk through the 7408 pin arrangement for all four gates, and explain why the datasheet must be checked for other chips.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: The key ideas from today. First, a pinout means every pin's number and function, taken from the manufacturer's datasheet, with pin 1 at the notch, top left, counting down and back up. Second, on a schematic the number goes outside the body and the function inside, each chip gets a U designator with its part number below, and a bar over a pin name means active low. Third, flat wiring matters electrically, because loops act as antennas and couple glitches between signals. Fourth, T T L is built from bipolar transistors used as switches, saturated or cut off, and the common gate chips such as the 7408 put V C C on pin 14 and ground on pin 7.
segments.expand: Quiz the student on one pinout fact, one schematic convention and one T T L fact.

lectures.title: TTL inputs and Boolean gates
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 07 - TTL Inputs and Boolean Gates.md; Kleitz §3-1, §3-2, §3-3, §3-12

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Two ideas meet in this lecture. Underneath, we look inside a T T L input and see that an unusual junction, base to collector, is what actually turns the next stage on. Above that, we abstract the behaviour into gates you can describe in several equivalent ways: a symbol, a truth table and a Boolean equation. We will cover the AND and OR gates, gates with more than two inputs, how to read a timing diagram, and how an AND gate can start and stop a clock. Most of the course will live at the gate level, but it helps to see once how the transistor level supports it.
segments.expand: Explain why it is useful to understand one transistor-level circuit even though most work happens at the gate level.

segments.title: N-type, P-type and junctions
segments.text: Silicon can be treated to carry charge in two ways. In N-type silicon the majority carriers are electrons. In P-type silicon the majority carriers are holes. A hole is a missing electron that behaves like a positive mobile carrier, but a piece of P-type silicon as a whole is still electrically neutral, not positively charged. Both types also have a few minority carriers. Where P and N meet, you get a P N junction, which is the diode you already know. An N P N transistor has two such junctions sharing the thin base region: base to emitter, and base to collector. The transistor is not just two separate diodes glued together, but it helps to know that either junction can be forward biased. That fact is the key to the T T L input, because the input stage uses the base-collector junction in an unusual way.
segments.expand: Explain what a hole is, and why a P-type sample is neutral overall even though holes act as positive carriers.

segments.title: Inside a T T L input: input LOW
segments.text: Take the input transistor of Kleitz's T T L inverter. A resistor from the 5 volt rail feeds its base, the emitter connects to the input pin, and the collector drives the next transistor. Suppose the input is at 0 volts. The resistor does not hold the base at 5 volts; with the base-emitter junction conducting, the base sits at about 0.7 volts. Kirchhoff's voltage law around that path says 5 volts minus the resistor voltage minus 0.7 volts minus the input voltage equals zero, so the resistor has 4.3 volts across it. Ohm's law then gives the base current, the resistor voltage divided by its resistance. If the resistor were 4.7 kilohms, that would be about 915 microamps. The important part is where that current goes: out through the base-emitter junction into the LOW input pin. So the next stage receives nothing and stays off.
segments.expand: Work the input-LOW current with a different base resistor value and explain where the current flows.

segments.title: Inside a T T L input: input HIGH
segments.text: Now put the input at 5 volts. The base-emitter path out through the input pin can no longer take the resistor's current, because the pin is as high as the supply. So the current finds the other route: through the forward-biased base-collector junction and into the next stage, turning that stage on. This is why simply saying the input transistor is off misses the real mechanism. The base-collector junction is conducting, which is not how a transistor is normally used, and that is the unusual behaviour that makes the T T L input work. Exact voltages depend on the full chip circuit, but the direction of the current tells the story. Input LOW, current leaves through the input pin and the next stage stays off. Input HIGH, current is steered into the next stage and turns it on.
segments.expand: Compare the current paths for input LOW and input HIGH, and explain why a LOW T T L input has to sink current.

segments.title: The input clamp diode and ringing
segments.text: A protection diode sits on the T T L input pin with its anode at ground and its cathode at the pin. At 0 volts input, anode and cathode are both at zero, so it is not conducting. At 5 volts input, anode minus cathode is minus 5 volts, so it is reverse biased. So in normal use it does nothing. Its job appears on fast edges. A real voltage step can excite the small inductance and capacitance of the wiring, producing overshoot and ringing, where the voltage swings past its final value and oscillates briefly. If ringing pulls the input below ground by more than about 0.7 volts, the diode becomes forward biased and conducts, holding the pin near minus 0.7 volts instead of letting it swing further. That is an approximation at limited current; large currents can still cause damage. Short, organised wiring helps reduce the ringing in the first place.
segments.expand: Explain what causes ringing on a fast edge and how the clamp diode limits the negative swing.

segments.title: Four ways to describe a logic function
segments.text: Any logic function can be expressed four ways. One, a schematic symbol, the gate shape. Two, a truth table, listing every input combination with its output. Three, Boolean algebra, an equation. Four, a Karnaugh map, which comes in a later chapter, so we set it aside. The first three describe exactly the same thing, and moving fluently between them is most of what the Boolean part of this course asks for. A truth table is really a binary count. With n input variables, each independently 0 or 1, there are two to the n rows. Two variables give 4 rows, three give 8, and four give 16. Write the inputs out as a plain binary count, 0 0, 0 1, 1 0, 1 1, so that no row is missed and every table you make is in the same order.
segments.expand: Explain why n inputs give two to the n rows, and how counting in binary guarantees no row is missed.

segments.title: The AND gate
segments.text: For an AND gate, all inputs must be HIGH for the output to be HIGH. With two inputs, the truth table has a 1 only in the last row, where both are 1. The symbol has a flat back and a semicircular nose. The equation is C equals A B, and the AND operation is written like multiplication: A dot B, A and B in brackets side by side, or simply A B. One notation to avoid: do not write A times B with a cross, because a hand-written cross can look like a variable X and make the expression ambiguous. Kleitz also points out a switch analogy. Two switches in series with a lamp act like AND: the lamp lights only when both are closed. A pattern worth memorising: for an AND gate with any number of inputs, only one row of the truth table is 1, the row where every input is HIGH.
segments.expand: Explain the series-switch picture of AND, and give the truth table row by row for a three-input AND.

segments.title: The OR gate
segments.text: For an OR gate, any HIGH input makes the output HIGH. The output is LOW only when every input is LOW, so in the truth table only the first row, all zeros, gives 0. The symbol has a curved back and a pointed nose. The equation is C equals A plus B, and the plus sign plays the role of OR. Read it as or, not plus, because in Boolean algebra 1 or 1 is 1. There is no 2. OR is inclusive: both inputs HIGH still gives HIGH. The switch picture for OR is two switches in parallel: either one closing lights the lamp. So the two patterns to remember are mirror images. AND has a single 1, at the bottom of the table, when everything is HIGH. OR has a single 0, at the top of the table, when everything is LOW.
segments.expand: Explain why the OR plus sign should not be read as arithmetic addition, with the one or one example.

segments.title: Gates with more inputs
segments.text: Gates are not limited to two inputs. A three-input AND is written D equals A B C, a four-input AND E equals A B C D, and so on, and the rule does not change: every input HIGH for a HIGH output. The same goes for OR: any HIGH input gives HIGH. Three inputs are easy to show on a symbol, and a drafting template usually covers up to about three. Past that, a gate enlarged enough for seven or nine inputs looks ridiculous. The fix Kleitz shows is to keep the gate body its normal size and extend its input edge with a line, so all the extra input wires can land on it. The function is unchanged; it is still one AND or one OR, just with more inputs. And the truth table grows fast: an eight-input AND has two to the eight, which is 256 rows, with only the very last row giving 1.
segments.expand: Explain how the truth-table size grows with inputs, and why only one row is HIGH for any AND gate.

segments.title: Reading a timing diagram
segments.text: A logic analyzer has many leads that clip onto points around a circuit, and it displays a timing diagram: one trace per signal, all against the same time axis. The key skill is to read it vertically. Each trace, read horizontally, tells you one signal's history. To evaluate a gate, take a vertical slice at one instant, read every input's level in that column, and apply the gate's rule. Then move to the next column, placing a boundary wherever any input changes. For example, suppose A is HIGH from 0 to 4 microseconds and B is HIGH from 2 to 6. An AND output is HIGH only where both are HIGH, from 2 to 4 microseconds. An OR output is HIGH wherever either is HIGH, from 0 to 6. For a three-input OR, the output is HIGH unless all three traces are LOW in the same column.
segments.expand: Work another two-input timing example, and explain why a boundary is needed at every input change.

segments.title: The gated clock
segments.text: A state machine, a circuit that steps through a sequence of states, is usually driven by a clock that simply goes up and down, up and down. Suppose you want a run and stop control. Feed the clock and an enable line into an AND gate, so run equals enable and clock. With enable at 1, one and zero is zero and one and one is one, so the output copies the clock and the machine runs. With enable at 0, zero and anything is zero, so the output stays LOW and the machine freezes in its current state. The enable line can come from a toggle switch with a pull-up. The same idea works with an OR gate, but reversed: a LOW control passes the clock, and a HIGH control holds the output HIGH. One real world caution: if enable changes while the clock is HIGH, you can get a shortened pulse, so real clock gating needs careful timing.
segments.expand: Explain why changing the enable during a HIGH clock can produce a short pulse, and how the OR version differs.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Let us gather the main ideas. First, inside a T T L input, a LOW input draws the base current out through the input pin, while a HIGH input steers it through the base-collector junction to turn on the next stage. Second, the clamp diode on the input is idle at normal levels and conducts only when ringing drives the pin below about minus 0.7 volts. Third, a logic function can be a symbol, a truth table or an equation, and a truth table with n inputs has two to the n rows, written as a binary count. Fourth, AND is HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH, OR is LOW only when all inputs are LOW, and an enable input on an AND gate lets a clock through or blocks it. Read timing diagrams in vertical slices.
segments.expand: Give the student a quick timing-diagram question and a gate-rule question to check these ideas.

lectures.title: Schematic conventions and unused gates
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 08 - Schematic Conventions and Unused Gates.md; Kleitz §3-11, §5-2

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture is about keeping two things apart: a schematic describes function, and the package describes hardware. We will see why gates are drawn individually rather than inside a picture of the chip, how designators, gate suffixes, part numbers and pin numbers keep the link to real silicon, why power is shown once per package, and what to do with the gates and inputs you do not use. We also meet the NAND, NOR and inverter chips, and we finish with the Boolean law that lets you build a four-input AND from two-input gates. None of these conventions is decoration: each one makes a board buildable by someone else and troubleshootable by you.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between describing function and describing hardware, and why a schematic should do the first.

segments.title: Pictorial versus schematic
segments.text: The instinctive way to show a logic chip is to show the chip: a rectangle, fourteen numbered pins around its edge, and the gates placed inside. That is a pictorial, and it does not belong on a schematic. On a schematic you place one gate at a time, in the part of the circuit where that gate does its work, not grouped inside a box representing the plastic package. A pictorial answers where the chip is; a schematic answers what the circuit does. The connection to the physical part is not lost. It moves into the labels on each gate, which we cover next. These are industry practices, not a local habit. The back of the textbook shows gates labelled in exactly this way, and you will see the same conventions in published schematics for programmable logic devices.
segments.expand: Give an example of how a pictorial becomes confusing in a larger circuit, compared with a proper schematic.

segments.title: Designator, suffix, part number, pins
segments.text: Four labels attach to each gate, and each answers a different question. The designator, such as U1, says which physical chip. The gate suffix, as in U1A or U1B, says which gate inside that chip; a quad package has gates A, B, C and D. The part number, such as 74 L S 08, written below the designator, says what kind of chip it is. The pin numbers on the leads say which physical pins you used. You choose the numbering: with five chips, which one is U1 is up to you, and within a quad package you may use any gate for any job. The only requirement is that the drawing records the choice. Then a technician reading U1A, 74 L S 08, pin 1 can say: that is pin 1 of the 74 L S 08 labelled U1 on this board. The suffix and the pins are both needed, because each tells you something the other does not.
segments.expand: Explain why the gate suffix and the pin numbers are not redundant, with an example of what is lost if one is missing.

segments.title: Power once per package
segments.text: A quad gate package has one V C C pin and one ground pin, shared by all four gates. So the convention is to show the power connections on exactly one gate of each package; which gate is your choice. The other three are drawn with no power lines at all. Two reasons. First, traceability: a technician can find a package's supply connection in one place. Second, space and clarity: repeating V C C and ground on all four gates clutters the page and reads as though there were four separate supplies. Alongside the power connection goes the decoupling capacitor. Every chip gets a capacitor from V C C to ground, shown with its power connection. On the board, the class demonstration placed these capacitors across the power and ground rails beside the chips; running a supply wire over the top of the package also works but wastes a row of holes.
segments.expand: Explain what a decoupling capacitor does for a logic chip and why it sits close to the supply pins.

segments.title: Unused inputs: tie them HIGH
segments.text: Use two gates of a quad package and two are left over, still on the board and still powered. Their inputs must not be left unconnected. A floating input picks up noise, and its logic level becomes effectively random, causing failures that come and go and are very hard to find. So every input must be driven or tied. For T T L there are two choices, and both cure the noise, but they differ in current. Tied to ground, a T T L input is LOW, and a LOW input must push current out of its input stage, which is the input-LOW current path you met last lecture. Tied to plus 5 volts, the input is HIGH and draws very little. So the rule is: tie unused inputs to plus 5 volts. For a 74 L S input, a LOW can push out up to about 0.4 milliamps, so four inputs tied LOW could cost 1.6 milliamps, against about 80 microamps tied HIGH.
segments.expand: Connect the tie-high rule to the T T L input circuit from Lecture 07 and compute the current difference for several inputs.

segments.title: Unused outputs and the spare-gate column
segments.text: Outputs are different from inputs. An unused output can safely go nowhere; it causes no harm. On the schematic, mark it N C, for no connection, so the reader knows the loose end is deliberate rather than an unfinished drawing. Never tie a driven output to a supply rail as if it were an input, because the gate would be fighting the rail. A neat way to show spare gates is to stack them in a column at the edge of the sheet, out of the way of the working circuit. One plus 5 volt line can then serve every tied input in the column. The spares can come from different packages. Each still needs its designator and suffix, its pin numbers, N C on its output and its inputs tied to plus 5 volts. And a common trick: show each package's power connection on one of its unused gates, so the working circuit stays clear.
segments.expand: Describe how a column of unused gates from two different packages would be labelled completely.

segments.title: Alpha board labels and indicators
segments.text: Where your circuit meets the Alpha board, the drawing must say which board signal is used. An input that arrives from one of the board's logic outputs, the toggle switches, is labelled with that output's name, for example L O 3. Without it, a reader knows a signal arrives but not from where. An output that goes to one of the board's logic indicator lights is drawn as a rectangular indicator symbol with the indicator's name inside. That symbol has one pointed end, and the point carries information: it points in the direction of signal flow. On an output it points away from the gate. Official schematics for programmable logic devices use the same shape. Connection dots matter too: a dot marks where wires actually join, and a missing dot leaves the reader unsure whether two crossing wires connect.
segments.expand: Explain how signal-flow arrows and connection dots remove ambiguity on a schematic.

segments.title: NAND, NOR and inverter chips
segments.text: Kleitz's second section on using logic chips adds the inverting gates. The 7400 holds four two-input NAND gates, the 7402 four two-input NOR gates, and the 7404 six inverters, which is why it is called a hex inverter. The 7410 holds three three-input NAND gates. There are C M O S equivalents too, such as the 4001 NOR and the 4011 NAND. On these 14-pin T T L parts, V C C is still pin 14 and ground pin 7, but the gate pins are not all arranged the same way. On the 7408 AND, the first gate's inputs are pins 1 and 2 and its output is pin 3. On the 7402 NOR, the first gate's output is pin 1 and its inputs are pins 2 and 3. Wiring a 7402 from memory of the 7408 would connect an output to a driven input. Always use the exact part's top-view pinout.
segments.expand: Explain the danger of assuming all gate chips share one pinout, using the 7402 and 7408 as the example.

segments.title: A four-input AND from two-input gates
segments.text: The lab circuit needs a four-input AND gate, but the parts kit has none. The reasoning tool is a Boolean law. AND is associative, meaning the grouping of an all-AND expression does not change its result. So A and B and C and D equals the group A and B, and-ed with the group C and D. That identity is exact, not an approximation, and it is what makes building a wide AND from narrower gates legitimate. Its partner, the commutative law, says the order does not matter either: A and B equals B and A. Both laws hold for OR as well. These come from Kleitz's section on Boolean laws, which we will use heavily for simplification. Working out how many two-input gates you need, which package they come from, and how to label them is the design task, using everything else in this lecture.
segments.expand: Explain the associative and commutative laws with small truth-table checks, and how many two-input gates a four-input AND needs.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: The key ideas from this lecture. First, a schematic shows each gate where it works, not inside a picture of the chip; the link to hardware is carried by the designator, the gate suffix, the part number and the pin numbers. Second, power and the decoupling capacitor appear once per package, on one gate. Third, unused T T L inputs are tied to plus 5 volts, because a LOW input pushes out current and a floating one picks up noise, while unused outputs are left unconnected and marked N C. Fourth, the 7400, 7402 and 7404 give NAND, NOR and inverters, but their pinouts differ from the 7408, so always check. Fifth, the associative law lets a four-input AND be built from two-input gates.
segments.expand: Ask the student to label a spare gate fully and to explain the tie-high rule in their own words.

lectures.title: Boolean algebra and simplification
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Lectures/DIGI 210 - Lecture 09 - Boolean Algebra and Simplification to SOP.md; Kleitz §5-1, §5-2, §5-3, §5-5, §5-8

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: A schematic, a Boolean expression and a truth table are three spellings of one logic function, and the algebra is the only one of the three you can simplify. That is the theme of this lecture. We will define combinational logic, see why gate delays can cause glitches, read a circuit into algebra using intermediate variables, fill a truth table column by column, and then learn the laws that simplify expressions: the identities, absorption, and DeMorgan's theorem. We finish by cooking expressions down to a sum of products. The individual laws are easy; the skill is choosing which one to use next, and that only comes with practice.
segments.expand: Explain why algebra is the representation used for simplification, rather than the truth table or schematic.

segments.title: Combinational logic and delay
segments.text: A circuit is combinational when information flows one way, from inputs to output, and no output is fed back to an input. Its output then depends only on the present inputs, which is why a truth table describes it completely. Feed an output back and you have sequential logic, which can depend on its own history; that comes later. Real gates are fast but not instant; each has a small propagation delay. Delay alone is harmless. The trouble starts when two paths from the same input pass through different numbers of gates. A change then reaches a later gate by one route before the other, which is a race, and while it runs, the output can briefly show a wrong value called a glitch. It can be a nanosecond wide and still cause failures downstream. For now we treat gates as infinitely fast, get the logic right, and deal with races later.
segments.expand: Walk through the lecture's glitch example, holding B at 1 and C at 0 while A rises, and explain why the truth table cannot predict it.

segments.title: Intermediate variables
segments.text: To read a circuit into algebra, do not write the growing expression beside each gate on the drawing. It runs out of room and it breeds mistakes. Instead, give every internal node its own letter. In the class circuit the inputs are A, B and C, the output is Z, and the internal nodes are D, E and F. Then write one small equation per gate. D equals A and B. F equals D inverted. E equals A or C. Z equals E and F. Substitute only at the end, which gives Z equals the group A or C, and-ed with the complement of A and B. One more habit from class: read the plus sign as or and the dot as and, not as plus and times. They are written with arithmetic symbols because they distribute like arithmetic, but reading them as arithmetic tempts you into rules that do not hold.
segments.expand: Evaluate the class circuit for one input combination using the intermediate variables in order.

segments.title: Filling the truth table
segments.text: Three inputs give two to the three, which is 8 rows. List A, B and C as a plain binary count from 0 0 0 up to 1 1 1. Then fill one intermediate column at a time, in the order the signals are produced, rather than working along each row. Go down the D column looking only at A and B: D is 1 only in the two rows where A and B are both 1. Then F, which is just D flipped. Then E from A and C: it is 0 only where both are 0. Only then fill Z from E and F. Working in columns turns one hard eight-row problem into four easy ones, and a mistake stays in one place instead of spreading along a row. For this circuit, Z comes out 1 in four rows: 0 0 1, 0 1 1, 1 0 0 and 1 0 1. That list is what any simplified version of the circuit must reproduce exactly.
segments.expand: Fill the class circuit's truth table aloud column by column and confirm which rows give Z equal to 1.

segments.title: The single-variable identities
segments.text: The operators behave like arithmetic, with exceptions, and the exceptions are the point. X and 0 is 0: nothing ANDed with false is true. X and 1 is X. X and X is X, not X squared, because there are no powers here. X and X bar is 0, since one of them is always 0. For OR: X or 0 is X. X or 1 is 1: anything ORed with something always true is true. X or X is X, not 2 X. X or X bar is 1. And X double bar is X; bars cancel in pairs, so an even number of bars leaves X and an odd number leaves X bar. Watch the pair that catches everyone: X and 1 is X, but X or 1 is 1. The same 1 has opposite effects because 1 is the identity for AND, while 0 is the identity for OR. When in doubt, prove it with a truth table: one variable needs only two rows.
segments.expand: Prove X or 1 equals 1 and X and 1 equals X with two-row truth tables, and explain the identity element idea.

segments.title: Commutative, associative, distributive
segments.text: The structural laws let you rearrange. Commutative: order does not matter, X and Y equals Y and X, and the same for OR. That is a fact about these operations, not a general rule; putting on socks and then shoes does not commute. Associative: grouping does not matter, so X and the group Y and Z equals the group X and Y, and-ed with Z. Distributive: X and the group Y or Z equals X and Y, or X and Z. That is the same expansion you know from ordinary algebra, and it is the move you will use most. Even more useful is running it backwards: spotting a common factor and pulling it out. For example, A and B, or A and C, can be written as A and the group B or C. Factoring is often what makes terms collapse, as we will see in the worked example.
segments.expand: Give an example of factoring a common variable out of two product terms and explain why it helps simplification.

segments.title: Absorption, and the look-alike
segments.text: Two rules make expressions dramatically shorter. Absorption: X or the group X and Y equals X. Prove it by cases. If X is 1, the whole thing is 1. If X is 0, then X and Y is 0 too, so the whole thing is 0. Either way it equals X, whatever Y does. Its partner is X and the group X or Y, which also equals X. Now the near twin that gives a different answer: X or the group X bar and Y equals X or Y, not X. Check by cases. If X is 1, both sides are 1. If X is 0, the left side becomes X bar and Y, which is just Y, and the right side is Y. So the result is X or Y. This was the question set aside to ponder in class. If you wrote X in your notes, correct it. Changing X to X bar inside the second term changes the answer completely.
segments.expand: Prove both rules by cases again with a different letter, and give an example of each inside a larger expression.

segments.title: DeMorgan's theorem
segments.text: DeMorgan's theorem is how you get a bar off a bracket. The complement of X and Y equals X bar or Y bar. The complement of X or Y equals X bar and Y bar. The reliable way to apply it is mechanical. Write the operator explicitly, so the bar has three things to land on. When it lands on the first variable, that variable inverts. When it lands on the operator, AND becomes OR, or OR becomes AND. When it lands on the second variable, that inverts too. The common trap is inverting both variables but leaving the operator alone. One counterexample kills it. Take X equals 1 and Y equals 0. The complement of 1 and 0 is the complement of 0, which is 1. But 0 and 1 is 0. They disagree, so the operator must flip. DeMorgan matters because until the bar is off, you cannot distribute, factor or combine anything inside it.
segments.expand: Apply DeMorgan to a three-variable expression and explain the break the bar, change the operator shortcut.

segments.title: Sum of products
segments.text: A product is a set of variables ANDed together, such as A and B, or A bar and B bar and C. A single variable, such as C, counts as a product of one. A sum of products ORs such terms together and contains nothing else: no brackets, and no bar over anything larger than a single variable. Why aim for that form? Because it drops straight into a truth table. Each product term tells you exactly which rows give a 1. And a function read back out of a truth table comes out as a sum of products again, so it is the common meeting point between representations. A warning, though: sum of products is a shape, not a guarantee of being minimal. An expression can be a perfectly good sum of products and still reduce further. What you actually want is the minimum sum of products.
segments.expand: Give examples of expressions that are and are not in sum-of-products form, and explain why each fails or passes.

segments.title: Worked example from the textbook
