segments.text: Read straight off Kleitz's circuit: X equals B and the group A or C, then or C. Step one, distribute B: A and B, or B and C, or C. Step two, factor C out of the last two terms: A and B, or C and the group B or 1. Step three, B or 1 is 1. Step four, that 1 is ANDed with C, and C and 1 is C. So X equals A and B, or C. This is the step that tripped the room. Half the class said C and half said 1. The way to settle it is to ask which operator the 1 inherited. It came out of a product, C and the bracket, so it is C and 1, which is C. Had it been C or 1, the answer would have been 1. The result, A and B, or C, is a sum of products and cannot be reduced further.
segments.expand: Work Kleitz's second example, the group A or B, and-ed with B and C, then or A, step by step.

segments.title: A four-variable example and its slip
segments.text: The board example was Z equals A and B and the group C or D, or C and the complement of A or B, or A and B and C. Step one, distribute A and B: A B C, or A B D. Step two, DeMorgan on the inverted OR: the complement of A or B is A bar and B bar, so that term becomes C and A bar and B bar, one three-variable product. A classmate caught a slip here. The board split it into A bar C, or B bar C, as if distributing C across an OR, but after DeMorgan the bracket is an AND, so there is nothing to distribute. Test A equals 0, B equals 1, C equals 1: the correct term gives 0, the slip gives 1. Step three, A B C appears twice, and X or X is X. So Z equals A B C, or A B D, or A bar B bar C. No two terms differ in exactly one complemented variable, so this is a minimum sum of products.
segments.expand: Explain the rule that two product terms can merge only when they differ in exactly one variable, complemented in one and not the other.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Five ideas to carry forward. One: combinational logic has no feedback, so a truth table describes it fully, though unequal path delays can still cause brief glitches. Two: read a circuit with one intermediate variable per gate, and fill truth tables column by column. Three: the identities, especially X and 1 equals X but X or 1 equals 1, and X and X equals X, not X squared. Four: absorption gives X or X Y equals X, while X or X bar Y equals X or Y; and DeMorgan breaks the bar and flips the operator. Five: aim for a sum of products, product terms ORed with no brackets, and after DeMorgan always check whether a group is ANDed or ORed before you distribute anything into it.
segments.expand: Give the student a short simplification that uses distribution, a rule and DeMorgan, and talk through each step.

lectures.title: Number systems and codes
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Textbook/DIGI 210 - Chapter 01 - Number Systems and Codes.md; Kleitz §1-1 to §1-13; assigned problems guide (Gray code)

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture covers Kleitz Chapter 1. We start with analog versus digital, then the one idea behind every number system, place value, and use it for binary, octal and hexadecimal, including fractions and conversions both ways. Then we meet codes, where the meaning of a bit pattern depends on its encoding: B C D, A S C I I, status flags and memory addresses. We finish with Gray code from your assigned problems. The central habit is this: before converting anything, say what base and what encoding you are working in, because the same bits can mean very different things.
segments.expand: Explain why the same bit pattern can mean different things, with one pattern read as binary, B C D and A S C I I.

segments.title: Analog versus digital
segments.text: An analog quantity varies smoothly and continuously, passing through every value in between: temperature, wind speed, the pressure of a sound wave. A digital quantity takes distinct steps; in binary systems, just two states, 0 and 1. The physical signal in a digital circuit is still a voltage; the bit is the meaning we give it. To bring an analog measurement into a computer we use an analog-to-digital converter, an A D C, which samples the signal and outputs a number. A digital-to-analog converter, a D A C, does the reverse, as a music player does before the speaker. Why go digital? A receiver only has to decide whether a voltage is in the LOW range or the HIGH range, so a little noise does not change the answer. Digital is not noise-proof, though: enough noise to push a signal out of its range still causes an error, and HIGH is not always exactly 5 volts.
segments.expand: Explain why a noisy digital signal is easier to recover than a noisy analog one, and where that advantage runs out.

segments.title: Place value and binary to decimal
segments.text: Every positional number system works the same way: each digit is multiplied by a weight, and the weights are powers of the base. In decimal, base ten, the weights are 1, 10, 100. In binary, base two, they are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, doubling each place to the left. To convert binary to decimal, add the weights of the places that hold a 1. One zero one one has 1s in the 8, 2 and 1 places, so it is 11. One zero one one zero one one zero, eight bits, is 128 plus 32 plus 16 plus 4 plus 2, which is 182. The rightmost bit is the least significant bit and the leftmost the most significant. Leading zeros do not change the value, but they may be needed to show a required width. And a string like 1 0 on its own is ambiguous: it is two in binary but sixteen in hexadecimal, so label the base.
segments.expand: Convert another six-bit binary number to decimal slowly, naming each weight, and explain the M S B and L S B.

segments.title: Binary fractions
segments.text: Places to the right of the binary point keep the same rule, dividing by two each step instead of multiplying. The first place after the point is worth one half, the next one quarter, then one eighth. So one zero one point zero one one is 4 plus 1, plus a quarter plus an eighth: 5.375. Point one one binary is a half plus a quarter, three quarters. The trap is reading the digits after the point as if they were decimal. Point zero one one in binary is not eleven hundredths; it is three eighths. To go the other way, from a decimal fraction to binary, repeatedly multiply by two and collect the whole-number parts in order. Point 375 times two is 0.75, giving 0; times two is 1.5, giving 1; the remaining 0.5 times two is 1.0, giving 1. So point 375 is point zero one one in binary.
segments.expand: Convert another decimal fraction such as 0.625 to binary by repeated doubling and check it by adding the weights.

segments.title: Decimal to binary
segments.text: There are two methods. The first subtracts weights: find the largest weight that fits, mark a 1, subtract, and carry on down. For 43: 32 fits, leaving 11; 16 does not, so 0; 8 fits, leaving 3; 4 does not, 0; 2 fits, leaving 1; 1 fits. So 43 is one zero one zero one one. The second method is repeated division by two. Divide, write the remainder, divide the quotient again, and so on until you reach zero. Then read the remainders in reverse order, last one first. That reversal matters because the first remainder tells you whether the number is odd or even, which is the ones place, the least significant bit. For 93 the remainders come out one, zero, one, one, one, zero, one, and reading them backwards gives one zero one one one zero one. Always check: 64 plus 16 plus 8 plus 4 plus 1 is 93.
segments.expand: Convert a number such as 90 by both methods and compare the working.

segments.title: Octal
segments.text: Octal is base eight. Its digits run from 0 to 7, never 8, and its place weights are 1, 8 and 64. Because eight is two cubed, each octal digit stands for exactly three bits. So to convert binary to octal, split the bits into groups of three starting from the right, padding with zeros on the far left if needed, and convert each group. One one one, zero one one is 7 and 3, so octal 73. Going back, replace each octal digit with its three bits. Octal to decimal uses the weights: octal 157 is 1 times 64 plus 5 times 8 plus 7, which is 111. Decimal to octal uses repeated division by 8, reading the remainders backwards: 200 divided by 8 is 25 remainder 0, 25 divided by 8 is 3 remainder 1, and 3 divided by 8 is 0 remainder 3, so 200 is octal 310.
segments.expand: Explain why each octal digit maps to exactly three bits, and convert an octal number to binary and back.

segments.title: Hexadecimal
segments.text: Hexadecimal is base sixteen. It uses 0 to 9 and then letters: A is 10, B 11, C 12, D 13, E 14 and F 15. Each hex digit is exactly four bits, a nibble, so a byte is exactly two hex digits. That is why hex replaced octal on 8-bit and 16-bit machines. Binary to hex: group in fours from the right. Zero one one zero, one zero one one is 6 and B, so hex 6B. Hex to binary: replace each digit with four bits, keeping leading zeros, so C 5 is one one zero zero, zero one zero one. Hex to decimal: the left digit counts sixteens. Hex 86 is 8 times 16 plus 6, which is 134, and hex B 7 is 11 times 16 plus 7, which is 183. Decimal to hex: divide by 16. Twenty-nine is one sixteen with 13 left over, and 13 is D, so 29 is hex 1 D. A remainder of 10 to 15 must become a single letter.
segments.expand: Convert a three-digit hex number to decimal and a decimal number above 256 to hex, explaining the powers of sixteen.

segments.title: Binary coded decimal
segments.text: Binary coded decimal, B C D, codes each decimal digit separately in four bits. So 59 in B C D is zero one zero one for the 5, then one zero zero one for the 9. Compare pure binary, where 59 is one number: zero zero one one one zero one one, which is 32 plus 16 plus 8 plus 2 plus 1. The two patterns are different, and mixing them up is a classic error. To decode B C D, take each group of four on its own: one zero zero one, one zero zero zero is 9 and 8, so 98. Read as pure binary those same bits would be 152. Only the groups zero zero zero zero to one zero zero one, 0 to 9, are valid; the six patterns for ten to fifteen are not legal B C D digits. B C D is what displays want, one group per digit, so a three-digit voltmeter showing 120 needs twelve bits: zero zero zero one, zero zero one zero, zero zero zero zero.
segments.expand: Encode a three-digit number in B C D and in pure binary, and compare the bit counts.

segments.title: A S C I I
segments.text: A S C I I, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, is a character code. It gives each letter, digit, punctuation mark and control character a seven-bit code, 128 codes in all, usually stored in a byte with a leading zero. It exists so that text can move into and out of computers. A few anchors: capital A is hex 41, and the capitals count up from there, so E is hex 45. Lowercase a is hex 61, so upper and lower case differ. A space is hex 20. The digit characters start at hex 30, so the character 5 is hex 35. That is the key idea: the character 5 is not the number five. The text 59 stored as A S C I I is two bytes, hex 35 then hex 39, which is quite different from 59 in pure binary or in B C D. You do not need to memorise the table; you need to know the method and the distinction.
segments.expand: Decode a short hex string of A S C I I characters, and explain the difference between the character 0 and the value zero.

segments.title: Bits, states and addresses
segments.text: With n bits you get two to the n distinct patterns. As unsigned numbers they run from 0 to two to the n, minus 1. Six bits give 64 patterns, 0 to 63. Eleven bits give 2048 codes, 0 to 2047. Keep number of states and largest value apart; that off-by-one is a common slip. To encode a given number of states, choose the smallest n whose two to the n reaches it: 600 states need ten bits, since nine bits give only 512. Memory addresses use the same care. For items stored one per location, the last address equals the start address plus the item count minus one, and the number of locations is last minus first plus one. Starting at hex 120, twenty-four items occupy addresses up to hex 137, because 23 in decimal is hex 17. Counting inclusively matters: from hex 120 to hex 137 is twenty-four locations, not twenty-three.
segments.expand: Work an address range example and explain why the count is last minus first plus one.

segments.title: Status bits
segments.text: Sometimes bits are not a number at all but a set of flags. Kleitz's geothermal plant example assigns each bit to a condition. Suppose four bits, from bit 3 down to bit 0, mean over-temperature, low liquid level, door open and motor running, with 1 meaning the condition is present. A status of hex A is one zero one zero. Read it position by position: bit 3 is 1, over-temperature; bit 2 is 0, level fine; bit 1 is 1, door open; bit 0 is 0, motor stopped. So two conditions are present: over-temperature and door open. It would be wrong to say the temperature reading is ten. The pattern is a list of yes or no answers, and its meaning comes entirely from the bit map someone defined. The same bits under a different map would mean something else.
segments.expand: Decode another status value against the same bit map, and discuss how hex makes status words quicker to read.

segments.title: Gray code
segments.text: Your assigned problems add one more code, Gray code, in which neighbouring values differ in exactly one bit. In binary, going from 3 to 4, zero one one to one zero zero, flips three bits at once, and during the change a sensor could briefly read something wrong. In Gray code, 3 is zero one zero and 4 is one one zero: one bit changes. To convert binary to Gray, copy the first bit, then each next Gray bit is the exclusive OR of that binary bit and the binary bit to its left. Exclusive OR just means same gives 0, different gives 1. Binary one one zero zero becomes one zero one zero. To go back from Gray to binary, copy the first bit, then walk right: a Gray 1 flips the previous binary bit you found, a Gray 0 keeps it. Gray one zero one zero decodes to one one zero zero. Do not add place weights to a Gray word directly.
segments.expand: Convert a five-bit binary number to Gray and back, stating the rule used at each bit.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Five ideas from Chapter 1. One: analog varies continuously, digital takes distinct states, and A D C and D A C convert between them. Two: every number system is place value; binary weights double to the left and halve to the right of the point. Three: convert to decimal by adding weights, from decimal by subtracting weights or by repeated division read backwards, and between binary and octal or hex by grouping three or four bits from the point. Four: the meaning of bits depends on the encoding: pure binary is one number, B C D codes each decimal digit in four bits, A S C I I codes characters, and status words are flags. Five: n bits give two to the n states, with a largest value one less than that.
segments.expand: Give one conversion in each direction and one encoding question, then discuss the most common mistake for each.

lectures.title: Digital signals and switches
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Textbook/DIGI 210 - Chapter 02 - Digital Signals and Switches.md; Kleitz §2-1 to §2-9, §2-11, §2-12

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture covers Kleitz Chapter 2, which connects abstract bits to measurable voltages and to the physical devices that switch them. We start with waveforms: period, frequency and duty cycle. Then serial and parallel data and how long each takes. Then the switching devices in order: manual switches and relays, diodes, and the transistor, ending in the common-emitter inverter, how loading affects it, and why T T L uses a totem-pole output. We finish with T T L versus C M O S, input levels and packages. The recurring method: decide which paths conduct, replace each device with its simple model, and calculate the output node relative to ground.
segments.expand: Explain the general method of replacing each switching device with a simple model and solving the resulting circuit.

segments.title: Clock waveforms
segments.text: A digital signal plotted on an oscilloscope shows voltage on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. A clock waveform repeats. A rising edge goes from LOW to HIGH, a falling edge from HIGH to LOW. The period is the time for one complete cycle, measured between matching points on neighbouring cycles, such as rising edge to rising edge. It is not just the HIGH time. Frequency is the number of cycles per second. The two are reciprocals: frequency equals one over period, in hertz and seconds. An 8 megahertz clock has a period of one over 8 million seconds, 125 nanoseconds. A 50 nanosecond period gives 20 megahertz. A period of 400 nanoseconds gives 2.5 megahertz. The quick check: frequency in megahertz times period in microseconds equals 1. So 4 megahertz goes with a quarter of a microsecond, which is 250 nanoseconds.
segments.expand: Work more frequency and period conversions and explain the megahertz times microseconds equals one check.

segments.title: Duty cycle
segments.text: A pulse waveform spends part of each period HIGH and the rest LOW, so the period equals the HIGH time plus the LOW time. The chapter guide adds a useful measure, duty cycle: the fraction of the period spent HIGH. Duty cycle equals HIGH time divided by period, times 100 percent, with both times in the same unit. A signal HIGH for 20 microseconds in an 80 microsecond cycle has a duty cycle of 25 percent, and its frequency is one over 80 microseconds, 12.5 kilohertz. Another: HIGH for 15 and LOW for 35 microseconds gives a 50 microsecond period, so 30 percent duty and 20 kilohertz. Notice that duty cycle and frequency are separate ideas. You can change how long the pulse stays HIGH without changing how often it repeats. And real edges take time to rise and fall, but that transition time is not the period either.
segments.expand: Explain why changing duty cycle need not change frequency, with two waveforms of the same period.

segments.title: Serial and parallel data
segments.text: Serial transmission sends one bit per clock period down a single data line, one after another in time; Kleitz sends the least significant bit first. Parallel transmission gives each bit its own line and sends a whole group in one clock period. Ignoring start bits, parity and other overhead, the time for serial is the number of bits times the clock period, and for parallel it is the number of groups times the period. Three 8-bit numbers at 5 megahertz: the period is 0.2 microseconds, so serial takes 24 times 0.2, which is 4.8 microseconds, and an 8-bit parallel bus takes 3 times 0.2, 0.6 microseconds. Parallel is faster in this model but needs more conductors and circuitry. When reading a serial trace, remember the bit order: the byte one zero zero one zero one one zero sent least significant bit first appears in time as zero, one, one, zero, one, zero, zero, one.
segments.expand: Work a serial versus parallel timing example, and explain why a fast serial link can in practice beat a slow parallel bus.

segments.title: Switches: opens and shorts
segments.text: An ideal closed switch is a zero-resistance path, a short, with no voltage across it. An ideal open switch is a break, with no current through it, though it can have voltage across it. S P S T connects or disconnects one path; S P D T selects between two destinations from a common contact. Open does not mean zero volts. A pull-up resistor can hold a disconnected switch node HIGH, and closing the switch can short that node to ground. Here is Kleitz's divider idea. Put 12 volts across 3 kilohms on top and 6 kilohms at the bottom, with a switch across the bottom resistor. Open, the output across the 6 kilohms is the supply times the bottom resistance over the total, 12 times 6 over 9, which is 8 volts. Closed, the output is shorted to ground, 0 volts. Always identify the output node and its actual path to a reference.
segments.expand: Explain why an open switch can carry voltage but not current, and a closed switch the reverse, using the divider example.

segments.title: Relays
segments.text: A relay is a switch worked by a coil. Current in the coil makes an electromagnet that pulls the contacts over. Normally open and normally closed describe the contacts with the coil de-energized. Energizing the coil closes the normally open contacts and opens the normally closed ones. So if normally open contacts replace the switch across the lower resistor of that divider, coil off gives 8 volts and coil on gives 0 volts; normally closed contacts reverse the relationship. A relay's big advantage is separation: a small control current in the coil switches a completely separate contact circuit, possibly at a higher voltage. Its limits: it is mechanical, so it is slow and its contacts can bounce, so it is no substitute for a logic gate at megahertz rates.
segments.expand: Walk through a relay timing example where the coil follows a clock, and explain contact bounce.

segments.title: Diodes as switches
segments.text: A diode has an anode and a cathode; the bar in its symbol marks the cathode. When the anode is more positive than the cathode it is forward biased and conducts; reverse biased, our model treats it as open, provided we stay below breakdown. For calculations we use a constant drop of about 0.7 volts for a conducting silicon diode. With a 5 volt supply, a forward diode and a 1 kilohm resistor, the resistor gets 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts, and Ohm's law, current equals voltage over resistance, gives 4.3 milliamps. Reverse the diode and no current flows, so the resistor drops nothing. With 9 volts and 2.2 kilohms the current would be 8.3 volts over 2.2 kilohms, about 3.77 milliamps. Remember that 0.7 volts is a model: a real diode's drop varies with current and temperature, and L E Ds have larger drops.
segments.expand: Explain the constant-drop model and check a diode circuit by verifying the assumed state.

segments.title: Diode AND and OR networks
segments.text: Diodes can form simple gates. In a diode AND, a resistor pulls the output up toward 5 volts, and each input connects through a diode whose cathode is the input. With every input HIGH, no diode conducts and the output stays high. Ground any one input and its diode becomes forward biased, clamping the output at about 0.7 volts, a LOW. The other diodes turn off. One LOW input is enough to pull the output LOW, which is AND behaviour. In a diode OR, a resistor pulls the output down to ground, and each input drives a diode's anode. Put any one input at 5 volts and its diode conducts, lifting the output to 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts, a HIGH. A second HIGH input does not subtract another 0.7 volts, because the diodes are in parallel branches, not in series.
segments.expand: Explain why the diode AND output LOW is 0.7 volts rather than zero, and why the other diodes turn off.

segments.title: The transistor as a switch
segments.text: A bipolar transistor has a base, a collector and an emitter. In an N P N transistor, a positive voltage applied to the base through a resistor forward biases the base-emitter junction and turns it on. Its collector to emitter path then acts as a short; this is saturation. With no base drive, the path acts as an open; this is cutoff. In the common-emitter inverter, the input goes to the base, the emitter is common to input and output, tied to ground, and the output is taken at the collector, which is pulled up by a collector resistor. Input HIGH, transistor saturated, output pulled to about 0 volts, LOW. Input LOW, transistor cut off, no collector current, output at the supply, HIGH. So this circuit inverts. Kleitz's worked examples, such as Example 2-11, trace exactly this: the output waveform is the input clock turned upside down.
segments.expand: Explain saturation and cutoff in the inverter and trace one clock cycle through it.

segments.title: Loading the output
segments.text: When the inverter's transistor is off, the output is not automatically the full supply. Any load connected from the output to ground draws current through the collector resistor, forming a voltage divider. Output voltage equals the supply times the load resistance, divided by the collector resistance plus the load resistance, in volts and ohms. Kleitz's Example 2-13: 5 volts, a 1 kilohm collector resistor and a 10 kilohm load give about 4.55 volts. Add more loads in parallel until the load is 1 kilohm, and the output falls to 2.5 volts. Making the collector resistor small helps the HIGH level, but when the transistor turns on, the whole supply sits across that resistor. A 100 ohm collector resistor at 5 volts carries 5 volts over 100 ohms, which is 50 milliamps, and dissipates a quarter of a watt. That trade-off has no good answer with a single resistor.
segments.expand: Work the loaded-output divider with different values and explain the collector resistor trade-off.

segments.title: The totem-pole output
segments.text: T T L chips escape that trade-off with a totem-pole output. Instead of a fixed collector resistor, it uses two transistors stacked one above the other. In a settled HIGH state, the upper transistor actively drives the output up; in a settled LOW state, the lower transistor pulls it down. One is on while the other is off, so there is no steady path straight from supply to ground. That gives far better drive than a passive pull-up. T T L itself, transistor-transistor logic, is built from bipolar transistors, diodes and resistors on one chip. The 7404 hex inverter holds six such inverters. Two cautions. The output current still has datasheet limits. And two ordinary totem-pole outputs must never be wired together, because one could be driving HIGH while the other drives LOW, fighting each other.
segments.expand: Explain how the two transistors in a totem pole share the job, and why two such outputs must not be connected.

segments.title: C M O S, input levels and packages
segments.text: The other main family is C M O S, complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, built from complementary M O S transistors. Its big advantage is very low power while it is not switching, though switching still uses energy, and its speed and thresholds depend on the exact part. Whatever the family, an input reads voltage ranges, not exact values. For the 74 L S 00, an input up to 0.8 volts is guaranteed LOW and one from 2.0 volts up is guaranteed HIGH; between those, nothing is guaranteed. Those are input limits, separate from what an output guarantees. Packages matter too. A dual in-line package, D I P, has two rows of leads that go through holes in the board. Surface-mount devices sit on pads on the board's surface and are much smaller and lighter. The same logic function can come in either, with different pinouts, so check the exact package's datasheet.
segments.expand: Explain why an input voltage between the two guaranteed limits is a problem, and what floating C M O S inputs can do.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Five ideas from Chapter 2. One: frequency equals one over period, measured edge to matching edge, and duty cycle is the HIGH fraction of the period. Two: serial sends one bit per clock on one line, parallel a whole group per clock on many lines, so parallel is faster but costs wiring. Three: a closed switch has no voltage and an open one no current; a relay coil moves every contact from its normal state. Four: a conducting silicon diode drops about 0.7 volts and a reversed one is open; diodes can form simple AND and OR networks. Five: the common-emitter transistor inverts, loading pulls its HIGH level down, and T T L's totem pole fixes that with active pull-up and pull-down.
segments.expand: Ask one timing question, one switch question and one transistor question, and discuss each typical mistake.

lectures.title: Logic gates, timing and troubleshooting
lectures.source: DIGI 210/Textbook/DIGI 210 - Chapter 03 - Logic Gates and Timing.md; Kleitz §3-1 to §3-12

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture covers Kleitz Chapter 3, the basic logic gates. We cover AND, OR, the inverter, NAND and NOR, each as a rule, a truth table and an equation. Then we use gates over time with timing diagrams, see how one input can enable or disable a signal, and build waveform windows. Finally we move to the bench: gate chips and their pins, and how to troubleshoot with a logic probe and pulser. The idea running through it all is that a gate turns a rule into a circuit, and a wrong output can come from the gate, its wiring, its supply or its load.
segments.expand: Explain why each gate can be described by a rule, a truth table and an equation, and how to move between them.

segments.title: AND and OR
segments.text: An AND gate outputs HIGH only when every input is HIGH; any LOW forces a LOW. Its equation is X equals A and B, written like a product. An OR gate outputs HIGH when at least one input is HIGH; it is LOW only when every input is LOW. Its equation is X equals A or B, written with a plus sign but meaning OR, so 1 or 1 is 1. OR is inclusive: both HIGH still gives HIGH. Kleitz uses switches to picture them. Two switches in series with a lamp act as AND, since both must close. Two switches in parallel act as OR, since either one closing lights the lamp. For any number of inputs, the AND truth table has a single 1, in the all-HIGH row, and the OR table has a single 0, in the all-LOW row. With n inputs there are two to the n rows, so an eight-input AND table has 256 rows.
segments.expand: Walk through the three-input AND and OR truth tables and point out the single special row in each.

segments.title: Inverter, NAND and NOR
segments.text: The inverter complements its one input: 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1. The small circle, or bubble, on a symbol means inversion. Put a bubble on the output of an AND and you get NAND, which is AND followed by an inverter. Its output is LOW only when every input is HIGH, and HIGH otherwise. Put a bubble on an OR and you get NOR: HIGH only when every input is LOW. The equations place one bar over the whole result: NAND is A and B, all complemented, and a three-input NOR is A or B or C, all complemented. The scope of the bar matters. A and B, all complemented, is not the same as A bar and B, where only A is inverted. To evaluate a NAND or NOR, work in two steps: find the AND or OR, then flip it. A NAND with inputs 1 and 0 gives AND 0, flipped to HIGH.
segments.expand: Evaluate NAND and NOR for all four two-input rows, and explain why the bar's scope matters.

segments.title: Naming a gate from its behaviour
segments.text: Each gate can be recognised from one sentence. AND: HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH. OR: LOW only when all inputs are LOW. NAND: LOW only when all inputs are HIGH. NOR: HIGH only when all inputs are LOW. Inverter: the opposite of its single input. So when someone describes behaviour, ask two questions: which input row is the special one, all HIGH or all LOW, and is the output in that row HIGH or LOW? Kleitz also shows the rectangular I E E E and I E C symbols, where an ampersand inside the box marks AND, a greater-than-or-equal-to-one mark indicates OR, a 1 marks the inverter, and an inversion mark on the output turns AND into NAND or OR into NOR. Remember that a bubble or inversion mark means logical inversion, not a negative voltage.
segments.expand: Give three behaviour descriptions and identify the gate for each, explaining the two-question method.

segments.title: Timing analysis
segments.text: A timing diagram puts every signal on one shared time axis. To find a gate's output, mark a boundary at every point where any input changes, read the stable input combination in each interval, and apply the gate rule to find the output across that interval. Take A HIGH from 0 to 4 microseconds and B HIGH from 2 to 6. The AND output follows the overlap: HIGH from 2 to 4. The OR output is HIGH from 0 to 6, and a NOR output is HIGH only in the gaps where both are LOW. These ideal diagrams assume zero delay. Real gates have propagation delay: t P L H is the delay for the output going LOW to HIGH, and t P H L for the output going HIGH to LOW. The letters describe the output transition, even for an inverter where the input moves the other way. And a gate's delay is not the clock period.
segments.expand: Work a timing example with a NOR gate interval by interval, and explain what the two propagation delays describe.

segments.title: Enable and disable
segments.text: A second input can let a signal through, block it, or invert it. Call the data A and the control E. For AND, E at 1 passes A and E at 0 forces 0. For OR, E at 0 passes A and E at 1 forces 1. For NAND, E at 1 passes A inverted and E at 0 forces 1. For NOR, E at 0 passes A inverted and E at 1 forces 0. The value that takes over the output, 0 for AND and NAND, 1 for OR and NOR, is the controlling value. A clock enable uses exactly this: the output equals the clock ANDed with enable, passing the clock when enable is 1 and holding the output LOW when enable is 0. Two related terms. Active HIGH means a function is asserted by a HIGH; active LOW means it is asserted by a LOW, such as a reset that acts when its pin is LOW.
segments.expand: Explain the controlling-value idea for all four gates, and why changing enable during a HIGH clock can cut a pulse short.

segments.title: When an input cannot be inferred
segments.text: Sometimes you know a gate's output and one input, and must work out the other. For X equals A and B, if A is 1 and X is 0, then B must be 0. But if A is 0 and X is 0, B could be either, because A alone already forces the output LOW. In that situation B is a don't care: its value does not change the result. Kleitz marks such intervals on timing diagrams with diagonal hash marks. Be careful not to confuse this with hardware. A don't care is a statement about a truth table condition; it is never permission to leave a physical input floating. A real input must always be driven or tied to a defined level, even if its value happens not to matter for the logic at that moment.
segments.expand: Work a don't care example with an OR gate and explain the difference between a don't care and a floating input.

segments.title: Making waveform windows
segments.text: Gates can carve precise windows out of timed signals. Kleitz uses the outputs of a Johnson shift counter as a ready supply of repeating waveforms; how the counter works inside comes much later. Suppose A is HIGH from 1 to 6 microseconds and B is HIGH from 3 to 8, in a repeating frame. We want an output HIGH only from 1 to 3 microseconds. In that interval A is HIGH and B is LOW, so the output is A and B bar: invert B, then AND. If you want the same window but LOW inside and HIGH elsewhere, complement the whole result with a NAND after the inverter. To pass clock pulses only inside the window, AND the clock in too: clock and A and B bar. Without the clock, the window is a steady level, not a series of pulses.
segments.expand: Design another window from the same two waveforms, such as HIGH only from 6 to 8 microseconds.

segments.title: Gate chips and pins
segments.text: A logic diagram, an electrical family and a physical package are three separate pieces of information. A part number such as S N 74 L S 08 N names a manufacturer's low-power Schottky T T L AND chip in a plastic D I P. The common base numbers: 7400 NAND, 7402 NOR, 7404 inverter, 7408 AND, 7432 OR, 7411 three-input AND, 7421 four-input AND. On the 14-pin 74 L S 08, pin 14 is V C C and pin 7 is ground. Gate 1 takes inputs on pins 1 and 2 with output on pin 3, and the others use 4 and 5 to 6, 9 and 10 to 8, and 12 and 13 to 11. That is a top view, counting down the left and up the right. The 74 L S 02 NOR differs: its first gate outputs on pin 1 from inputs 2 and 3. So always use the exact part's pinout, and remember the output's drive comes from the chip's supply, not from its inputs.
segments.expand: Walk through the 7408 pin assignments for all four gates and explain why the 7402 must not be wired the same way.

segments.title: Troubleshooting with probe and pulser
segments.text: A logic probe touches a point and shows its state: HIGH, LOW or pulsing, depending on the instrument. A logic pulser injects a controlled test stimulus. To test one input of a gate with the pulser, hold the other input at its non-controlling value so the pulses can pass: HIGH for AND and NAND, LOW for OR and NOR. Then watch the output with the probe. An open is a broken connection, such as a lifted pin or cracked track; a short is an unintended connection, such as a solder bridge. In a larger circuit, predict each intermediate node, measure at the actual pins in signal-flow order, and find the first disagreement. Before declaring a chip faulty, check its supply at the chip, its real input levels, and whether the next stage or an indicator is loading or shorting its output. One passing test does not prove the whole truth table.
segments.expand: Walk through troubleshooting a NAND whose output reads LOW with inputs 0 and 1, including checking the load.

segments.title: Evaluating a small gate network
segments.text: When several gates connect, evaluate the intermediate nodes in order rather than jumping to the final gate. Suppose P equals A and B, Q equals C inverted, and X equals P or Q. For A equals 0, B equals 1 and C equals 0: P is 0 and 1, which is 0; Q is the inverse of 0, which is 1; and X is 0 or 1, which is 1. Writing each intermediate value stops you from applying the final gate's rule to the wrong signals. You can also translate the network into one equation, X equals A and B, or C bar. That equation is the bridge to the next topic, Boolean algebra, where the laws let you simplify such expressions so that the same function needs fewer gates.
segments.expand: Evaluate the same network for all input combinations where X equals 0, and explain why they are the only ones.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Five ideas from Chapter 3. One: AND is HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH, OR is LOW only when all inputs are LOW, and NAND and NOR are those with the output inverted. Two: in a timing diagram, divide at every input change and apply the rule in each interval; ideal diagrams ignore delay, and t P L H and t P H L describe the output's transitions. Three: a control input with the non-controlling value passes a signal, and with the controlling value forces the output. Four: gate chips such as the 7408 put V C C on pin 14 and ground on pin 7, but check each pinout, since the 7402 differs. Five: troubleshoot by predicting, measuring in signal-flow order and finding the first disagreement.
segments.expand: Ask one gate identification question, one enable question and one troubleshooting question.

lectures.title: Component models and measurement
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Lectures/ELTR 238 - Lecture 01 - Component Models and Measurement.md; Boylestad §1.5, §1.7, §2.2, §2.4, §4.2, §4.3, §4.7, §6.8; §10.3, §10.10, §11.3, §11.4 at model level only

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This first lecture builds the habit that runs through the whole course: connect a physical component, the relationship between its voltage and current, a labelled diagram, and a calculation you can check. We will meet three ideal element models, the resistor, the capacitor and the inductor. We will look at Ohm's law as an equation and as a graph, and at what a rate of change means without any heavy calculus. Then we turn to charge and the direction of conventional current, the difference between an open path and a closed one, and finally what makes a measured number trustworthy: precision, accuracy, resolution and significant figures. If you keep one sentence from today, keep this one: every quantity needs a unit, and every voltage and current needs a clear reference, or the number means nothing.
segments.expand: Explain why pairing a component, its voltage-current relationship, a diagram and a calculation catches mistakes that any one of them alone would miss.

segments.title: Three ideal element models
segments.text: An element model is an idealized description of how a component behaves. The resistor has resistance, R, measured in ohms. The capacitor has capacitance, C, measured in farads. The inductor has inductance, L, measured in henries. Each model links the voltage across the element to the current through it. For the resistor, voltage equals current times resistance. For the capacitor, current equals capacitance times the rate of change of its voltage. For the inductor, voltage equals inductance times the rate of change of its current. The subscripts in names like v sub R tell you which element a quantity belongs to, and a lowercase v or i reminds you the quantity might change with time. Real parts are never perfectly ideal; a real resistor has a little inductance, and a real coil has resistance in its wire. The model is a useful description, not the whole truth.
segments.expand: Compare the three relationships side by side, and explain what an unwanted, or parasitic, resistance or capacitance means in a real part.

segments.title: Ohm's law in three forms
segments.text: For an ideal resistor carrying steady current, Ohm's law says the voltage across the resistor equals the current through it times its resistance: volts equal amps times ohms. Rearranged, current equals voltage divided by resistance, and resistance equals voltage divided by current. The critical detail is that the voltage and the current belong to the same resistor: the voltage across it and the current through it. Here is the class example. A 2 kilohm resistor has 6 volts across it. Current equals 6 volts over 2 kilohms. Notice a handy pairing: volts divided by kilohms gives milliamps, so the answer is simply 6 over 2, which is 3 milliamps. If your calculator shows 0.003 amps, that is the same current, written in engineering form as 3.00 milliamps. And remember that dividing needs a nonzero denominator: the point of zero volts and zero current alone cannot tell you a resistance.
segments.expand: Work a second example that uses a different prefix pair, such as volts over megohms giving microamps.

segments.title: The graph is the same law
segments.text: Plot a fixed resistor with current along the horizontal axis and voltage up the vertical axis, and you get a straight line through the origin. The slope of that line, the change in voltage divided by the change in current, is the resistance. So a larger resistance gives a steeper line on these axes. For the 2 kilohm resistor, 1 milliamp goes with 2 volts, 2 milliamps with 4 volts, 3 milliamps with 6 volts; the slope is 2 volts per milliamp, which is 2 kilohms, not 2 ohms, because of the milli on the axis. Swap the axes, putting current up the side, and the slope becomes current over voltage, which is the conductance, one over the resistance. Then the larger resistance is the flatter line. A curved characteristic, like a diode's, cannot be described by one fixed resistance across its whole range.
segments.expand: Explain how to read the prefixes on a graph's axes before computing a slope, with an example of the factor-of-a-thousand error.

segments.title: Rate of change, without heavy calculus
segments.text: A rate of change is a slope: how much a quantity changes divided by the time the change took. For a straight segment of a graph, that is just the change over the elapsed time. The capacitor model says its current equals its capacitance times the rate of change of its voltage. The class example: a 1 microfarad capacitor whose voltage rises steadily from 0 to 2 volts in 2 milliseconds. The rate of change is 2 volts over 2 milliseconds, 1 volt per millisecond. Multiply by 1 microfarad and you get 1 milliamp while the voltage is rising. Once the voltage stops changing, the rate of change is zero, so the ideal capacitor current is zero, even though the voltage is still 2 volts. That is the key idea: a nonzero level can have zero slope. A capacitor holding a steady voltage carries no ideal current.
segments.expand: Walk through how the capacitor current would look while the voltage rises, holds, then falls, and why it goes negative when the voltage falls.

segments.title: The inductor is the mirror image
segments.text: The inductor swaps the roles. Its voltage equals its inductance times the rate of change of its current: volts equal henries times amps per second. The class example: a 2 millihenry inductor whose current rises steadily from 0 to 3 milliamps in 3 milliseconds. The rate of change is 3 milliamps over 3 milliseconds, 1 amp per second. Multiply by 2 millihenries and the voltage is 2 millivolts while the current is rising. Once the current holds steady, its rate of change is zero and the ideal inductor voltage is zero, even though a current is still flowing. A real coil also has resistance in its winding, so a real steady current would still show a small resistive drop. For now, what you need is the pattern: capacitor current follows changing voltage, inductor voltage follows changing current.
segments.expand: Explain why an ideal inductor with steady current behaves like a plain wire, and what the winding resistance adds in a real one.

segments.title: Charge and conventional current
segments.text: Electric charge comes in two signs. Like signs repel and opposite signs attract. Current is the flow of charge, and by convention its direction is the way positive charge would move. That is conventional current, and it is what every arrow in this course means. In a metal wire, though, the charges that actually move are electrons, which are negative, so they drift the opposite way to the conventional current arrow. Both descriptions are correct; just pick the conventional one and use it consistently. One more point that saves a lot of confusion: electrons are already present throughout the wire, and a load does not use them up. In a steady single loop, the same current enters and leaves every part. What a resistor converts is energy, into heat, not charge.
segments.expand: Give an everyday picture of why the same current enters and leaves a resistor, and what actually is being used up.

segments.title: Open paths and closed paths
segments.text: Closed means the conducting path is complete; open means it is broken somewhere. A closed ideal switch has zero volts across it, because it is just a piece of ideal wire. An open switch carries zero current, because there is no path. But an open switch can still have a voltage across it. The class example: a 6 volt supply, a 2 kilohm resistor and a switch in one loop. Closed, the current is 6 volts over 2 kilohms, 3 milliamps, and the switch drops nothing. Open, the current is zero, so the resistor drops current times resistance, which is zero, and the whole 6 volts appears across the switch gap. No current and no voltage are different statements. A fuse fits the same picture: intact, it is a closed low-resistance path; blown, it is an open, deliberately broken path.
segments.expand: Explain why you cannot find the open-circuit voltage by multiplying zero current by infinite resistance, and what to reason with instead.

segments.title: Precision, accuracy and resolution
segments.text: A meter display is a measurement result, not a guarantee. Three words describe how good it is. Precision is how closely repeated readings agree with one another. Accuracy is how close a reading is to the accepted true value. Resolution is the smallest change the instrument can display. These are independent. Picture a meter that reads a known 5.000 volt reference as 5.199, 5.200 and 5.201 volts. Those readings are tightly clustered, so the meter is precise, but every one sits about 0.2 volts high, so it is not accurate. That pattern points to a systematic offset. More digits on the display improve resolution, which lets you see smaller changes, but they do not remove a bias. When the last digits flicker, the stable digits, the meter's specification and the conditions decide what you can honestly report.
segments.expand: Describe how you would test whether a meter has a systematic offset, and why averaging more readings does not fix one.

segments.title: Comparing sizes and counting figures
segments.text: Before judging whether a difference matters, put both quantities in the same unit. One millivolt compared with one kilovolt: a millivolt is ten to the minus three volts and a kilovolt is ten to the three volts, so the ratio is ten to the minus six, one millionth. Small, perhaps negligible for some jobs, but not zero. Significant figures tell the reader how precisely a number is known. Leading zeros only locate the decimal point, so 0.00420 volts has three significant figures: four, two and the final zero. Zeros between nonzero digits count, so 2.005 kilohms has four. A whole number like 1000 ohms is ambiguous; writing 1.00 kilohms says three figures clearly. Engineering notation uses powers of ten in steps of three to match the prefixes: 0.00420 volts is 4.20 times ten to the minus three volts, which is 4.20 millivolts.
segments.expand: Give more examples of zeros that do and do not count, and explain why a prefix change never changes the number of significant figures.

segments.title: Recap of lecture one
segments.text: Here are the ideas to carry forward. First, three ideal elements: a resistor, where voltage equals current times resistance; a capacitor, whose current follows the rate of change of its voltage; and an inductor, whose voltage follows the rate of change of its current. Steady voltage means zero ideal capacitor current; steady current means zero ideal inductor voltage. Second, Ohm's law in any of its three forms, always with the voltage across and the current through the same resistor, and its graph, where the slope of voltage against current is the resistance. Third, conventional current follows positive charge, electrons drift the other way, and resistors convert energy, not current. Fourth, open means zero current but not necessarily zero voltage. Fifth, precision, accuracy and resolution are different questions, and extra digits are not extra truth.
segments.expand: Quiz me quickly on one example from each of the five recap points.

lectures.title: Measurement, charge, current and voltage
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Lectures/ELTR 238 - Lecture 02 - Measurement, Charge, Current and Voltage.md; Boylestad §1.5 to §1.8, §2.2 to §2.4, §2.8, §2.10, §5.7, §6.5, §10.2

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Lecture two ties four ideas together. Charge is conserved. Current describes how quickly charge moves. Voltage describes energy per charge. And measurement lets us test those ideas, provided we report numbers honestly. We start with Kirchhoff's current law, which is charge conservation at a junction. Then we tighten up significant figures, engineering notation and the SI prefixes. After that we look inside the atom, see why copper conducts, and meet the electric field and Coulomb's law. Finally we define current as charge per time and voltage as energy per charge, and end with a uniform resistor whose midpoint sits at half the voltage. Keep an ear out for units throughout: coulombs, amps, volts, joules and newtons each measure something different.
segments.expand: Explain how charge, current and voltage relate, using a single simple circuit as the example.

segments.title: Kirchhoff's current law
segments.text: Kirchhoff's current law comes straight from conservation of charge. In a steady circuit, charge cannot keep piling up at a junction, so the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it. You can state it two ways. Count entering currents as positive and leaving currents as negative, and the signed sum is zero. Or put the entering currents on one side and the leaving currents on the other, as plain sizes. Just do not mix the two descriptions in one equation. The class example: 5 amps enters a node, and 4 amps and 1 amp leave. Five minus four minus one is zero, so the node balances. If two currents enter, 3 amps and 2 amps, and one of two leaving currents is 4 amps, the other must be 1 amp.
segments.expand: Work a node with four branches, choosing a sign convention first, and show how an unknown current's sign reveals its true direction.

segments.title: When measured currents do not balance
segments.text: Now the same node with real meter readings: 5.01 amps entering, and 4.01 amps and 1.01 amps leaving. The signed sum is 5.01 minus 4.01 minus 1.01, which is minus 0.01 amps, minus 10 milliamps. Has charge conservation failed? No. The negative sign simply says the displayed outgoing total is 10 milliamps more than the displayed incoming total. That is the size of ordinary meter uncertainty, contact effects, or readings taken at slightly different moments, or perhaps a branch you did not account for. The right response is to investigate, not to discard the law, and certainly not to round the readings selectively until they balance. Keep the measured values as they were recorded and explain the residual. The zero-sum node equation assumes charge is not accumulating at the node, which holds for the steady circuits in this course.
segments.expand: List the checks you would make, in order, when measured currents at a node leave a residual.

segments.title: Significant figures are not decimal places
segments.text: Significant figures are the meaningful digits in a reported value. Nonzero digits count. Zeros between them count. Leading zeros never count, because they only place the decimal point. A trailing zero after the decimal point does count, because someone deliberately recorded it. So 0.004070 has four significant figures, 4, 0, 7 and the final 0, and 1.000 has four. A whole number like 1400 is ambiguous. Scientific notation removes the doubt: 1.40 times ten to the three has three figures, and 1.400 times ten to the three has four. Carry extra digits while you calculate and round once, at the end. The course reports calculated final answers to three significant figures in engineering notation, but that formatting rule does not make a measurement more accurate than it really is.
segments.expand: Explain why rounding intermediate results causes errors, using a two-step calculation as the example.

segments.title: Engineering notation and SI prefixes
segments.text: Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient from 1 up to 10 times a power of ten. Engineering notation allows a coefficient from 1 up to 1000 but restricts the power to multiples of three, so that it lines up with an SI prefix. Climbing the ladder: tera, ten to the twelve; giga, nine; mega, six; kilo, three. Going down: milli, ten to the minus three; micro, minus six; nano, minus nine; pico, minus twelve; femto, minus fifteen. The symbols are case-sensitive: capital M is mega and lowercase m is milli, a factor of a billion apart. The class example: 0.000047026 amps. One microamp is ten to the minus six amps, so this is 47.026 microamps, which rounds to 47.0 microamps at three figures. The zero after the 47 is what keeps the third figure.
segments.expand: Practise converting a few awkward values into engineering notation, including one that rounds across a prefix boundary.

segments.title: Compare in the same unit
segments.text: Prefixes make comparison easy, but only after both values use the same unit. The class example compares 2.40 milliamps with 8.00 microamps. Comparing the bare numbers, 2.40 against 8.00, would suggest the second is larger. Convert first: 2.40 milliamps is 2400 microamps, and 2400 over 8 is 300. So the milliamp current is three hundred times larger. The same discipline applies to powers of ten. When you multiply, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents: eight times ten to the minus three times four times ten to the five is 32 times ten to the two, which is 3.2 times ten to the three in engineering form. When you add, first match the exponents. Changing a prefix changes the number you write, never the physical quantity it describes.
segments.expand: Explain the exponent rules for multiplying, dividing and raising a power of ten to a power, with a quick example of each.

segments.title: Atoms, charge and why copper conducts
segments.text: In the simple atomic model, protons in the nucleus carry positive charge, neutrons carry none, and electrons outside the nucleus carry negative charge. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. Remove electrons and it becomes a positive ion; add electrons and it becomes negative. The size of one electron's charge is about 1.602 times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs, so one coulomb is about 6.24 times ten to the eighteen electrons' worth of charge. Copper has 29 electrons, arranged in the shell model as 2, 8, 18 and 1. That single outer electron is loosely held, and in the metal it becomes delocalized, free to drift when a field is applied. Silver conducts a little better than copper, while gold is valued for resisting corrosion, not for conducting better.
segments.expand: Explain what a delocalized electron is and why a metal stays neutral overall while carrying current.

segments.title: Electric fields and Coulomb's law
segments.text: Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges: force equals a constant times the product of the charges, divided by the distance between them squared. Force is in newtons, charge in coulombs, distance in metres, and the constant is about 8.99 times ten to the nine. Like signs repel; opposite signs attract. Double either charge and the force doubles. Double the distance and the force falls to one quarter, because distance is squared. The electric field describes the force a small positive test charge would feel, per unit of its charge: field equals force over charge, in newtons per coulomb, which is the same as volts per metre. The field points away from positive charges and toward negative ones. A positive charge is pushed along the field; a negative charge, such as an electron, is pushed the opposite way.
segments.expand: Explain why we divide by the test charge to define a field, and why the test charge must be small.

segments.title: Current is charge per time
segments.text: Average current is the charge that crosses a chosen surface divided by the time it took: current in amps, charge in coulombs, time in seconds. One amp is one coulomb per second, so amps already mean per second; amps per second would be a rate of change of current, a different quantity. In a metal external circuit, conventional current leaves the battery's positive terminal and electrons drift from its negative terminal. Why does a lamp light the instant you close a switch, when electron drift is slow? Because charges are already present everywhere in the wire, and the electrical disturbance travels through the circuit far faster than any electron drifts, like a wave passing along water that only moves locally. Three instruments came up: the multimeter measures voltage, current and resistance; the oscilloscope shows voltage against time; the function generator supplies a test signal.
segments.expand: Explain drift velocity versus signal speed with a second analogy, and why a resistor does not use up current.

segments.title: Voltage is energy per charge
segments.text: Voltage is a difference in electric potential between two points. The voltage from A to B equals the potential at A minus the potential at B, and one volt is one joule per coulomb. So a voltage is neither a force nor an energy by itself: it is energy per unit charge, and the energy transferred depends on how much charge moves. Now a useful example. Take a uniform resistor with constant material and cross-section, so its resistance is proportional to length. Put 6 volts across a 2 kilohm uniform resistor, with the lower end as the zero volt reference. Treat it as two equal 1 kilohm halves. The current is 6 volts over 2 kilohms, 3 milliamps. The lower half drops 3 milliamps times 1 kilohm, 3 volts, so the midpoint sits at 3 volts, provided nothing is connected there.
segments.expand: Explain why the midpoint rule fails if the resistor is not uniform or if a load is connected at the midpoint.

segments.title: Meters connect differently
segments.text: Voltage is a difference between two points, so a voltmeter connects across the element, in parallel with it, reading the red probe's potential minus the black probe's. Current passes through a path, so an ammeter must be inserted in series: open the path and let the current flow through the meter. The ideal voltmeter draws no current, which means infinite resistance; the ideal ammeter has zero resistance and drops no voltage. Those are the instruments' ideal limits, and real meters come close enough for most work. One safety point follows directly: an ammeter's low resistance must never be placed straight across a supply, where it acts almost like a short circuit.
segments.expand: Explain what happens, step by step, if an ammeter is mistakenly connected across a supply.

segments.title: Recap of lecture two
segments.text: Five ideas from lecture two. One: Kirchhoff's current law, current in equals current out at a node, because charge is conserved; a small residual in measured data is a measurement question. Two: significant figures count meaningful digits, leading zeros never count, and you round once at the end. Three: engineering notation uses powers of ten in steps of three to match the prefixes, and capital M and lowercase m are a billion apart. Four: charge is measured in coulombs; like charges repel, and Coulomb force falls with distance squared; a field is force per charge. Five: current is charge per time, one amp being one coulomb per second, and voltage is energy per charge, one volt being one joule per coulomb, always between two points.
segments.expand: Quiz me on the units: which quantity is measured in coulombs, amps, volts, joules and newtons per coulomb?

lectures.title: Components, measurements and circuit nodes
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Labs/ELTR 238 - Lab 01 - Components, Measurements and Circuit Nodes.md; Boylestad §1.7, §3.5, §3.6, §3.8, §5.9, §5.13; §10.4 markings only

segments.title: What this lab session covers
segments.text: This lab connects four things: a part in your hand, its schematic symbol, its measured value, and its place in a circuit. We will recognise the three basic passive elements, read prefixes and capacitor markings, understand the three terminals of a potentiometer, decode the resistor colour code and its tolerance, measure resistance properly with a bench multimeter, compare measured and nominal values, and finally read node voltages and carry a schematic onto a connection board by its nodes. Only the technical skills are covered here; your own readings are what belong in your own records.
segments.expand: Explain why translating between a physical part, its symbol and its measured value is the core skill of bench work.

segments.title: Three basic passive elements
segments.text: The resistor, capacitor and inductor are the three basic passive elements. A resistor relates voltage and current and dissipates energy as heat. A capacitor stores energy in an electric field associated with separated charge; an inductor, usually a coil, stores energy in a magnetic field associated with its current. Ideal capacitors and inductors give stored energy back; none of the three generates energy. A fixed resistor has no polarity, so reversing it changes nothing. For a fixed voltage across a resistor, current equals voltage over resistance, so doubling the resistance halves the current: 10 volts across 10 kilohms gives 1 milliamp, and across 20 kilohms gives 500 microamps. That is why resistors are used to limit current, though a resistor alone does not fix one current regardless of the circuit.
segments.expand: Explain what passive means, and why it does not mean a component only works in unpowered circuits.

segments.title: Prefixes and capacitor markings
segments.text: Read the prefix as part of the unit. Capital M is mega; lowercase m is milli; lowercase k is kilo. A label may print u F when the micro symbol is unavailable. In engineering notation, 0.000047 farads is 47 microfarads, and 0.0033 henries is 3.3 millihenries. The class capacitor was marked 47 microfarads and 50 volts. The 47 microfarads is its nominal capacitance. The 50 volts is its voltage rating, the most it should ever have across it, not the voltage it holds and not a voltage it produces. Its actual voltage depends on the circuit. It was a polarized electrolytic, so orientation matters: in the course symbol the curved plate is negative, and on the body a stripe marks the negative lead. Reverse voltage or overvoltage can damage it.
segments.expand: Explain how to identify an electrolytic capacitor's negative lead, and why a longer lead is an unreliable clue once leads are trimmed.

segments.title: The potentiometer's three terminals
segments.text: A potentiometer has a resistive track with two fixed ends and a movable wiper. In the lab the ends were called A and B and the wiper C. The end-to-end resistance stays about constant; for a 10 kilohm pot it is 10 kilohms. Moving the wiper splits the track into two segments that always add up to that total, so as one grows, the other shrinks. At the midpoint, each is 5 kilohms. Over the full travel, each segment can range from about zero to the full 10 kilohms, not just half of it. If the track measures 10.0 kilohms and one segment reads 3.20 kilohms, the other segment should be about 6.8 kilohms. Always identify the wiper from the part's pinout rather than guessing from which pin is in the middle.
segments.expand: Explain how to find which pin is the wiper using only an ohmmeter.

segments.title: Decoding a four-band resistor
segments.text: On a four-band resistor, bands one and two are digits, band three is the multiplier, and band four is tolerance. The digit colours run black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9. The nominal value is the two-digit number times ten to the multiplier's power. Brown, black, red is 10 times a hundred, 1 kilohm. Brown, black, orange is 10 times a thousand, 10 kilohms. Brown, black, yellow is 100 kilohms. Only the third band changed, and each step is a factor of ten, which is why similar-looking parts must be kept sorted. A gold fourth band means plus or minus 5 percent, silver 10 percent, and no band 20 percent. As multipliers, gold means times one tenth and silver times one hundredth.
segments.expand: Walk through reading a five-band precision resistor and how it differs from a four-band one.

segments.title: Measuring resistance with the bench meter
segments.text: Resistance is measured on an unpowered, isolated part. The meter supplies its own small test current, so outside voltage ruins the reading. Use the two-wire resistance function, with the red lead in the volts-and-ohms input and the black lead in its low terminal, not the sense pair or the current jack. Choose autorange or a suitable manual range. Clip onto metal, not insulation, wait for a steady display, and read the prefix as carefully as the digits: ohms, kilohms and megohms are different scales. An overload message such as OVLD is a prompt, not a value. A 3.3 kilohm resistor on a 1 kilohm range overloads; so can an open connection. Holding both metal ends with your fingers puts your body in parallel and makes the reading low.
segments.expand: Explain why touching both leads lowers a resistance reading, using the idea of two paths in parallel.

segments.title: Nominal, tolerance and measured value
segments.text: Keep three ideas apart. The nominal value is what the marking says. The tolerance is the permitted manufacturing spread. The measured value is what the instrument reports. The allowed spread is the tolerance times the nominal value. For 3.3 kilohms at 5 percent, the spread is 165 ohms, so the part may be anywhere from 3.135 to 3.465 kilohms. Percent deviation equals the difference between measured and nominal, divided by nominal, times 100. The class reading of 3.286 kilohms differs from 3.3 by 14 ohms, which is about 0.424 percent, low but inside a 5 percent band. A 98 kilohm reading on a 100 kilohm part is 2 percent low; it is not a 10 kilohm resistor, so check the multiplier band before assuming a wrong part.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between a component's tolerance and the meter's own measurement uncertainty.

segments.title: Drawing symbols in the course's language
segments.text: The course resistor symbol is the zigzag with three peaks and three troughs. A voltage source is a circle with plus and minus marks. A cell is a long and a short plate, with the long plate positive; several pairs make a battery. A current source is a circle with an arrow. A circle marked V or A is a voltmeter or ammeter. A triangle at a node marks the local zero volt reference, while three decreasing bars mean an actual earth connection, which is a different thing. Label each resistor with its name and value, each voltage with a polarity, and each current with a named arrow. The plus and minus beside a resistor are your chosen voltage reference, not a property of the part; with current entering the plus terminal, the resistor's voltage equals current times resistance.
segments.expand: Explain why a circuit can work without any earth connection, and what the reference triangle is really for.

segments.title: Node voltages and differences
segments.text: A node is every point joined by ideal wire, with no component in between; bends in a wire do not create new nodes. Name nodes with lowercase letters. A single subscript, V sub A, means the voltage at node A with respect to the marked reference. A double subscript, V sub A B, means the voltage at A with respect to B, which equals V sub A minus V sub B; the first letter is the red probe and the second the black. The class example had node A at 10 volts, node B at 5 volts, and node C as the zero volt reference. So the voltage across R one, V sub A B, is 5 volts; across R two, V sub B C, is 5 volts; and V sub A C is 10 volts. Swap the probes and V sub B A reads minus 5 volts. The circuit did not change.
segments.expand: Work the same three-node circuit with the reference moved to node A, and show which numbers change.

segments.title: Building the circuit by its nodes
segments.text: The last task put two resistors in series between the supply's positive and negative connections. The skill is to preserve the nodes, whatever the physical layout looks like. Node A joins the supply's positive terminal and one lead of R one. Node B joins R one's other lead and one lead of R two. Node C joins R two's other lead and the supply's negative terminal, the local zero volt reference. First learn which holes on the board share a metal connection; physical closeness means nothing. Give each node its own group, place each resistor so its two leads land in two different groups, and check every connection against the node list. If both leads of a resistor share one group, that resistor is bypassed. Red conventionally goes to the positive supply and black to the return.
segments.expand: Explain a systematic way to check a finished board against a schematic, node by node.

segments.title: Recap of lab one
segments.text: Five points from lab one. One: the resistor dissipates energy, while ideal capacitors and inductors store it; a capacitor's voltage marking is a maximum rating, and an electrolytic's curved plate is negative. Two: a potentiometer's two segments always add up to the end-to-end resistance, and each can span nearly the whole range. Three: four-band resistors read digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance, and the allowed spread is tolerance times nominal. Four: measure resistance unpowered and isolated, read the prefix, and treat an overload message as a prompt to check range and contacts. Five: nodes are defined by connections, V sub A B means A minus B, and a board is built node by node, never by appearance.
segments.expand: Give me a quick colour-code drill: say three bands and I will name the value.

lectures.title: Fields, resistance and meters
lectures.source: ELTR 238/Lectures/ELTR 238 - Lecture 03 - Fields, Resistance and Meters.md; Boylestad §2.2, §2.5, §2.10, §3.2 to §3.5, §3.8, §3.13, §4.2, §4.4, §5.3, §6.8, §7.8, §10.2

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: Lecture three shifts from single points to relationships across a whole circuit. A field relates a charge to the force it would feel. A voltage relates two points. A current describes charge passing through a path. A resistance links the voltage across an element to the current through it. We start with field versus force, then diodes, light and solar cells. Next comes resistance as a quantity versus the resistor as a component, and how to place meters correctly. Then we think in complete circuits, look at real wire, gauge and temperature, resistor construction and power ratings, and finish with the potentiometer as an adjustable voltage divider. Three distinctions run through it all: field versus force, across versus through, and property versus component.
segments.expand: Explain the three distinctions, field versus force, across versus through, property versus component, with one example each.

segments.title: Field versus force
segments.text: Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges: a constant times the product of the charges, over the distance squared. Mass does not appear; electric force depends on charge. Now divide that force by the test charge it acts on, and you get the field produced by the source charge at that spot, in newtons per coulomb. The field describes the electrical environment; the force is what a particular charge experiences in it: force equals charge times field. The class example: a plus 20 nanocoulomb source, and a point 300 millimetres away. The field there is about 2 kilonewtons per coulomb, pointing away from the positive source. Place a minus 3 nanocoulomb charge there and the force is 3 nanocoulombs times 2000, 6 micronewtons, pointing toward the source, opposite the field, because the charge is negative.
segments.expand: Explain why a field still exists at a point after the test charge is removed, and why field strength falls with distance squared.

segments.title: Diodes, and arrows that mean light
segments.text: Conventional current is a sign convention: it points the way positive charge would move. An ordinary diode strongly favours one direction. Its forward conventional current flows from the anode to the cathode, and the cathode is the bar on the symbol. Treating a diode as a perfect one-way switch is only an approximation; real diodes leak a little and can break down in reverse. Watch the extra arrows on diode symbols. Arrows pointing in, on a photodiode, mean incident light, not current. Arrows pointing out, on a light-emitting diode, mean emitted light. Light itself is electrically neutral; photons bring energy that can free carriers in the junction, and those carriers make a measurable current. The light must reach the device's sensitive region, and the response depends on wavelength.
segments.expand: Explain the difference between a photodiode used as a sensor and a photovoltaic cell used as a source.

segments.title: The solar cell's internal resistances
segments.text: A photovoltaic cell delivers electrical energy from light. With nothing connected it can show an open-circuit voltage; connect a load and it delivers current, with the light supplying the energy. A useful model draws the light-generated current dividing three ways: some through the junction diode, some leaking through an internal shunt resistance, and the rest out to the load. The output current also passes through an internal series resistance, which drops voltage equal to current times resistance. So the design goal is a large internal shunt resistance, so little current leaks away inside, and a small internal series resistance, so little voltage is lost. Do not confuse a small internal series resistance with making the external load as small as possible; those are different resistors doing different jobs.
segments.expand: Explain what happens to a solar cell's output if its shunt resistance becomes small, say through damage.

segments.title: The load chooses the operating point
segments.text: A solar cell is neither an ideal voltage source nor an ideal current source across all loads. Its output depends on the illumination, the temperature and the load. Delivered power equals the load voltage times the current. At open circuit, the current is zero, so delivered power is zero, even though a voltage is present. At a short circuit, the voltage is zero, so delivered power is again zero, even though current flows. Useful maximum power lies at an operating point somewhere between those two extremes. That is why a panel's rated output only makes sense with its stated test conditions, and why a voltmeter reading on an unloaded panel tells you nothing about its maximum power. The same idea, power equals voltage times current, will follow us through every circuit.
segments.expand: Explain why the maximum power point lies between open circuit and short circuit, using power equals voltage times current.

segments.title: Resistance, resistors, and labels
segments.text: Resistance is a physical quantity, R, in ohms. A resistor is a manufactured component made to provide a chosen resistance. Wires, contacts and semiconductors have resistance too, without being resistors. For a resistor under steady conditions, voltage equals current times resistance; current equals voltage over resistance; and resistance equals voltage over current, as long as the current is not zero. The voltage is across that resistor, and the current is through that same resistor. A diode is not a fixed resistor: its voltage-to-current ratio changes with operating conditions. Fully label every resistor: its name and value, its voltage with a plus and minus reference, and its current with a named arrow. When the current arrow enters the plus terminal, voltage equals current times resistance and positive power means the resistor absorbs energy.
segments.expand: Explain why careful subscripts on voltage and current prevent the most common Ohm's law mistake.

segments.title: Meters: through and across
segments.text: To measure current, the current must pass through the ammeter, so power off, open the path, and insert the meter in series, with conventional current entering the red current input and leaving the common terminal for a positive reading. Choose the right jack and range. To measure voltage, connect the voltmeter across the two terminals you care about; it reads the red probe's potential minus the common's. The ideal ammeter has zero resistance; the ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance. Never put a current input across a supply. The worked example: an ideal 6 volt supply across a 1 ohm resistor. Current equals 6 volts over 1 ohm, 6 amps, and the resistor would dissipate 6 volts times 6 amps, 36 watts. Check: 6 amps times 1 ohm returns 6 volts. The answer is a current in amps, not a resistance in ohms.
segments.expand: Explain what a burden voltage is and why a real ammeter always has some.

segments.title: Thinking in complete circuits
segments.text: In a single loop, moving an ideal ammeter from before a resistor to after it changes nothing: it still reads the same current.
