segments.text: An identity is true for every angle in its domain, and proving one means transforming one side until it matches the other. A trigonometric equation is the opposite kind of object: it is true only for particular angles, and solving it means finding those angles. That difference in purpose changes the permissions. In a proof you may not multiply both sides or move a term across, because that assumes the very thing being proved. In an equation you may; the usual algebra is back, the same operation on both sides, exactly as in the algebra lectures. The finishing condition differs too. A proof is finished when the two sides read the same. An equation is finished when the angles are listed, together with their families, which is the next point and the one that costs the most.
segments.expand: Give one example of a legal move in an equation that would be illegal in an identity proof, and say why.

segments.title: Every answer is a family
segments.text: The unit circle closes on itself. An angle that satisfies the equation still satisfies it after one more full turn, after a hundred more, and after any number of turns backwards. So a trigonometric equation with any solution at all has infinitely many, and the answer must be written in a form that says so: x equals theta nought plus 2 n pi, with n an integer. The symbol for the integers is a capital Z, and n in Z reads n is an element of the integers, so n may be 0, or 1, or 15, or negative 3; each choice adds or removes that many complete circles. Here is the most expensive habit in the topic. Writing x equals 5 pi over 6 and x equals 7 pi over 6 and stopping is not a slightly incomplete answer. It is two answers out of an infinite number, and the class put it plainly: two over infinity is essentially nothing. The general term is not decoration; it is most of the answer. Only when a question restricts x to one interval, such as 0 to 2 pi, are the bare angles enough.
segments.expand: Write the general solution for an equation whose solutions in one turn are pi over 4 and 3 pi over 4, and list the n equals negative 1, 0 and 1 members.

segments.title: Four ways to make it familiar
segments.text: The method the whole lesson runs on was given a name in class: lazy mathematics. Not laziness about the work, but refusing to invent a new technique when an old one can be made to fit. Four tactics, chosen by the shape of the equation. One trig function to the first power only: do the algebra until the function stands alone. A squared trig function sitting alone: take both square roots, plus and minus. Every term sharing a common factor: factor, and use the zero-product rule to split into two simpler equations. A squared function and a first power of the same function: substitute a letter, factor as a quadratic, then undo the substitution. Factor first if you can; it was called out as the move that always makes things simpler, because it splits one hard equation into two easy ones. The zero-product rule only works against zero, so getting everything onto one side is a precondition, not tidiness. A fifth move sits behind all of these: when sine squared and cosine squared are mixed, convert with the Pythagorean identity to reach one function.
segments.expand: For each of the four tactics, give a short example equation that calls for it and nothing else.

segments.title: Worked example: isolate, then read the circle
segments.text: Solve 2 cosine x plus root 3 equals 0. Step one, algebra until the function stands alone: 2 cosine x equals negative root 3, so cosine x equals negative root 3 over 2. Step two, the reference angle, the acute angle between the terminal arm and the horizontal axis, comes from the size of the number with the sign set aside. From the special triangles, cosine of pi over 6 is root 3 over 2, so the reference angle is pi over 6. Step three, choose the quadrants from the sign. Cosine is the x coordinate, so a negative cosine means the left of the vertical axis, quadrants two and three. Step four, build each angle from the reference: in quadrant two, pi minus pi over 6, which is 5 pi over 6; in quadrant three, pi plus pi over 6, which is 7 pi over 6. Step five, extend to every turn: x equals 5 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi, or 7 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi, n an integer. The commonest wrong answer is pi over 6 and 11 pi over 6, the reference angle used as if the number were positive; those solve cosine x equals positive root 3 over 2. Check the sign before the size.
segments.expand: Solve 2 sine x minus 1 equals 0 with the same five steps, naming the reference angle and the quadrants.

segments.title: Why 2 n pi and not n pi
segments.text: The step size of the family is a property of the particular equation, not a rule to memorise. For cosine x equals negative root 3 over 2, a half turn from 5 pi over 6 lands at 11 pi over 6, where cosine is positive root 3 over 2, the wrong sign. The two solutions in one revolution are not half a circle apart, so nothing smaller than a full circle maps one onto the other, and each family needs the full 2 n pi. The test is always the same: add pi to a solution and check whether the original equation is still satisfied. If it is, half turns stay inside the solution set and n pi covers everything with fewer families. If it is not, use 2 n pi. The next example is the case where half a turn does work, and the reason is that the equation is blind to the sign of the function.
segments.expand: Test whether n pi works for tangent x equals 1 by adding pi to pi over 4 and checking.

segments.title: Worked example: a squared function and both roots
segments.text: Solve 4 sine squared theta equals 3. Isolate the squared function: sine squared theta equals three quarters. Take the square root of both sides, keeping both signs, because squaring destroyed the sign information and undoing it must restore both possibilities: sine theta equals plus or minus root 3 over 2. The denominator simplifies exactly because 4 is a perfect square; the numerator does not, so root 3 stays. Dropping the negative root loses half the solutions, and no later step can recover them. Sine is the y coordinate, so plus or minus root 3 over 2 describes two heights, each reached twice: four points, one in every quadrant, all with reference angle pi over 3. In one revolution they are pi over 3, 2 pi over 3, 4 pi over 3 and 5 pi over 3. Now the shortcut: pi over 3 plus pi is 4 pi over 3, and 2 pi over 3 plus pi is 5 pi over 3. Each solution's diametrically opposite point is also a solution, so two families cover all four: theta equals pi over 3 plus n pi, or 2 pi over 3 plus n pi. Listing four families with 2 n pi describes the same set; the two-family form is just shorter.
segments.expand: Solve 2 cosine squared theta equals 1, keeping both roots and writing the shortest general solution.

segments.title: Worked example: factor out the common factor
segments.text: Solve 2 cosine theta sine theta minus cosine theta equals 0. Everything is already on one side, so factor. Both terms carry cosine theta: cosine theta times the bracket 2 sine theta minus 1 equals 0. The zero-product rule splits it: cosine theta equals 0, or 2 sine theta minus 1 equals 0. The cosine branch: cosine is the x coordinate, zero where the terminal arm lies along the vertical axis, at pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2. Those are half a circle apart, so one family covers both: theta equals pi over 2 plus n pi. The sine branch: sine theta equals one half, positive y, quadrants one and two, reference angle pi over 6, so theta equals pi over 6 plus 2 n pi or 5 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi; here the full 2 n pi is needed, since half a turn from pi over 6 reaches 7 pi over 6 where sine is negative one half. Never divide the common factor away. Cancelling cosine theta from both sides to leave 2 sine theta minus 1 equals 0 silently deletes the entire cosine branch, because you divided by something that is zero at exactly the angles you were about to lose.
segments.expand: Solve sine theta tangent theta equals sine theta by factoring, and say what dividing by sine theta would have lost.

segments.title: A correction from class
segments.text: The transcript records the cosine branch of that example as cosine theta equals 0 giving theta equals n pi, listed as 0, pi, 2 pi, 3 pi. That cannot be right, and it is worth being certain rather than taking a guide's word for it. Substitute theta equals pi into the original equation: 2 cosine pi sine pi minus cosine pi is 2 times negative 1 times 0, minus negative 1, which is 0 plus 1, which is 1, not 0. So pi is not a solution. The angles where cosine vanishes are pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2, not 0 and pi. Theta equals n pi is the answer to sine theta equals 0, the neighbouring fact and easy to reach for. Checking theta equals pi over 2 the same way gives 2 times 0 times 1, minus 0, which is 0. Whether the slip was on the board or in the recording cannot be told, so check this line against your own notes. The four solutions of the equation in one turn are pi over 6, pi over 2, 5 pi over 6 and 3 pi over 2.
segments.expand: Verify each of the four solutions in the original equation by substitution, using exact values.

segments.title: Worked example: substitute to expose a quadratic
segments.text: Solve 2 sine squared x minus 3 sine x plus 1 equals 0. Recognise the shape: a squared term, a first-power term of the same function, and a constant. That is a quadratic wearing a disguise. Let y equal sine x, and the equation becomes 2 y squared minus 3 y plus 1 equals 0. Factor: looking for numbers with product 2 and sum negative 3 gives negative 1 and negative 2, so it is 2 y minus 1 times y minus 1 equals 0, and y is one half or 1. Expand to check. Now undo the substitution; the question was never about y. Sine x equals one half, or sine x equals 1. The first is the branch from the previous example: pi over 6 plus 2 n pi or 5 pi over 6 plus 2 n pi. The second is the maximum sine ever reaches, attained at the single point at the top of the circle: pi over 2 plus 2 n pi. Three families, not four, and the asymmetry is the useful part. A value strictly between negative 1 and 1 is hit twice per revolution; the extremes plus and minus 1 once; a value outside that range never, so an equation reducing to sine x equals 2 has no solution rather than a hard one.
segments.expand: Solve 2 cosine squared x plus sine x minus 1 equals 0 by converting cosine squared first, then substituting.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: An equation is true for particular angles, and you may do the same thing to both sides; an identity is true for all angles and you may not. Every solution is a family: base angle plus 2 n pi, or plus n pi when a solution plus pi is still a solution, and two bare angles are two answers out of infinity. Four tactics, chosen by shape: isolate a first-power function; take both square roots of a squared function; factor out a common factor and use the zero-product rule, never dividing it away; substitute a letter for a squared-and-first-power function, factor, and undo the substitution before touching the circle. Convert mixed sine and cosine squares with the Pythagorean identity. Read the circle by reference angle for size and quadrant for sign, remembering cosine is zero at pi over 2 plus n pi and sine is zero at n pi, and count the expected solutions per turn before you finish.
segments.expand: Restate the four tactics and give the shape of equation each one is for, in one line each.

lectures.title: Soldering fundamentals and bench setup
lectures.source: EFAB 202/Lab/EFAB 202 - Lab 01 - Soldering Fundamentals and Bench Setup.md

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture walks through the first soldering lab: what the wire and the solder are made of, how the station and the tip behave, how heat actually gets into a joint, what a finished joint should look like, and how the bench and the hand tools fit around all of that. If you keep one sentence, keep this one: you do not make the solder joint, you make the conditions, and the joint forms itself. Clean metal, both parts hot, and surface tension does the rest. Almost every fault you will see on this bench traces back to heat that never arrived. So as we go, keep asking: where is the heat going, and is it reaching both pieces of metal?
segments.expand: Give a short overview of why heat arriving in both parts is the theme, with a one-sentence preview of the thermal bridge.

segments.title: Tinned copper wire
segments.text: Start with the wire in the parts kit. It looks silver, but it is copper. A thin layer of tin has been plated over it. Copper oxidises in air, and oxide is exactly what stops solder from bonding. So the tin takes the oxidation instead, and the copper surface underneath stays clean and easy to wet. That is the whole purpose of the coating: protect the copper and keep it solderable. Two cautions follow. First, a silver surface does not certify a current rating. How much current a wire can carry depends on the size of the conductor, the insulation, the temperature and how it is installed, not on the plating. Second, the coating is thin. Grip tinned wire hard with sharp serrated plier jaws and the teeth bite through the tin into the copper, opening the very path the coating exists to close. Use smooth or fine jaws on tinned wire, and keep the aggressive serrated jaws for work where the surface does not matter.
segments.expand: Explain why oxide blocks wetting and why a thin sacrificial tin layer helps, and give the plier-jaw example again.

segments.title: Solder and what flux does
segments.text: The solder is a lead and tin alloy with flux in its core. Flux has one job, and it is worth saying precisely: flux removes oxide so the solder can wet the metal. Wetting means the molten solder bonds to the surface and spreads across it instead of sitting on top as a ball. Now the distinction that matters at the bench. On fresh, clean, tinned wire, the flux in the core may be all you need for the joint we practise, and the proof is that the solder wets properly as it heats. On a surface that is already oxidised, the core flux may not be enough. There is more oxide than that small amount of flux can clear, and the solder will sit on top instead of bonding. Then you clean the surface and use approved extra flux. Notice what flux does not do. It adds no strength and it is no substitute for heat. It only clears the way.
segments.expand: Describe what wetting looks like versus solder balling up, and why more flux cannot fix a joint that is not hot enough.

segments.title: The station and its sleep mode
segments.text: The soldering stations are temperature controlled, with a stand and a heat resistant pad for the iron. The stands are sensing stands: park the iron and after a while the station drops into a sleep mode, shown on the display. Lift the iron and it is back at working temperature in about five seconds. Sleep exists to extend tip life, so let it work; leaving the iron out of the stand to keep it hot just wears the tip for nothing. On temperature, the instruction is simple: use the approved bench setting and do not raise it on your own. Here is the reasoning. A hotter tip can move heat faster, but it also raises the risk of damaging the component, and it does not guarantee less total heat in the part. What controls the heat is good contact and short dwell time. If a joint is slow to heat, suspect contact first: a dirty tip, the wrong face, or the wrong tip size.
segments.expand: Go deeper on why dwell time and contact quality, not the number on the display, decide how much heat the component absorbs.

segments.title: Tip care: brass wool, never a file
segments.text: Oxide on the tip is a thermal barrier. Watch a freshly cleaned and tinned tip and you can see it go from bright to dark in a few seconds; that is the oxide re-forming. So the tip is cleaned immediately before every joint, not at the start of the hour. The cleaning motion matters. Wipe and roll the tip through the brass wool as you pull it out. That shears the oxide off. Stabbing the tip into the wool does not clean it and shortens its life. Never file a tip. A tip is plated, and a file goes straight through the plating. A tip that is dull, dark and will not take solder after proper cleaning is replaced, not resurfaced. And before you switch the station off, leave fresh solder on the tip; that coating protects it in storage. Bright tip, every joint.
segments.expand: Explain what the plating on a tip is for and why filing destroys it, and describe the wipe-and-roll motion in more detail.

segments.title: Contact area moves heat
segments.text: Here is a principle you will use on every joint: heat moves through contact area. A wedge tip has a flat face and a rounded edge. Put the flat face against the work and it touches over an area, and heat flows in. Touch the work with the rounded edge and it meets at essentially one point, and almost nothing transfers, even though the tip is exactly as hot. This is also why tip size and shape are chosen to fit the joint. A tip too small for the joint gives a poor contact area no matter how precise it looks. And it is why a clean tip matters: oxide between the tip and the work is a layer that heat has to fight through. Temperature is only one part of heat transfer. Area of clean contact is the part you control with your hands.
segments.expand: Give an everyday analogy for contact area and heat flow, and connect it to why oxide on the tip slows a joint.

segments.title: Two round wires and the thermal bridge
segments.text: Now the central problem of the lab. Cross two round wires so they touch, and the contact between them is essentially a single point. Almost no heat crosses from one to the other. Heat the top wire and the bottom wire stays cold. Solder then wets the hot wire and lies against the cold one without bonding. That is a cold joint, and the dangerous thing about it is that it looks finished. The fix is a deliberate technique called a thermal bridge. Clean and tin the tip, place the iron so it touches the joint, and add a small amount of solder right at the point where the iron meets the work. That molten solder spreads the contact and conducts heat into both wires at once. Then leave the iron there and let the heat go in. Location is everything: solder somewhere nearby, or solder kept only on the tip, bridges nothing. Do not confuse this with an electrical bridge, which is unwanted solder shorting two separate pads.
segments.expand: Explain step by step why a point contact conducts so little heat and how the bead of molten solder changes the geometry.

segments.title: Feed from the far side
segments.text: With the bridge in place and the iron resting on the joint, feed the solder from the side of the joint opposite the iron. This is a test as much as a technique. If solder melts when it touches the far side, the joint itself is hot enough, not just the iron. If it does not melt, the joint is not ready, so keep the iron there and wait. The work tells you when it is time; you do not count seconds. The shortcut to avoid is melting solder on the iron and wiping it across the metal. That produces a blob that looks finished and has never bonded, because the metal under it never reached temperature. When the solder has flowed around the joint, take the solder away first, then the iron. The order of the whole thing, then: clean and tin the tip, place the iron, build the bridge, leave the iron, feed from the far side, let it flow, remove solder, remove iron.
segments.expand: Walk through the full joint sequence again slowly and explain what a wipe-on blob looks like compared with a wetted joint.

segments.title: The fillet and how much solder
segments.text: What does a finished joint look like? The solder pulls itself into a concave, feathered curve where it meets each wire. That curve is the fillet, and it is made by surface tension, the same property that shapes a water droplet. On a joint this small, surface tension dominates and gravity matters very little. You do not shape the fillet; you create the conditions and it forms itself. How much solder? Roughly an eighth of an inch of solder wire was the cue for the demonstrated joint, but that is a cue for that solder diameter and that joint, not a specification. On stranded wire there is a clear test: you should still be able to see the individual strands through the solder. The layer is thin and has wetted into the strands. If you cannot see the strands, there is too much solder, and a smooth blob hides exactly the evidence an inspector wants.
segments.expand: Describe a convex ball versus a concave fillet and what each says about wetting, and why extra solder is not extra strength.

segments.title: Set the bench up for your hand
segments.text: The benches are shared between classes, and the layout you sit down to was set up by someone with the other dominant hand. Resetting it is part of starting work. The iron stand goes on your dominant side and close to the work, because a long reach is a long time holding a hot iron over the joint you just made. Bring the cleaning pad forward, near the front edge; if it sits behind the work, every trip to clean the tip drags the iron across what you built. Uncoil and separate the cords. Coiling a cable twists it along its own axis, and that stored twist is what leaves cords permanently kinked; keep the power leads apart from each other and clear of the hot tip. Solder also needs the work to be stable, which is what the vise and holding fixtures are for: find an arrangement that keeps it steady and leaves both hands free.
segments.expand: Describe the right-handed and mirrored left-handed layouts in words, and why a stable workpiece matters for wetting.

segments.title: Fumes, lead and burns
segments.text: Three physical facts about the bench. First, smoke. As flux burns and solder melts it gives off fumes, and the extraction filters pull that smoke away from your face. The switches are ganged: turning one on turns them all on, so it affects everyone in the room. If extraction seems ineffective, stop and report it rather than assuming the filter is the fault. Second, lead. The solder is a lead and tin alloy, and residue on your hands travels to your face, your food and your belongings later. Use the hand wash station after soldering. Third, heat. At working temperature the tip burns on contact, and when you do eventually touch a hot iron, it is most likely to be further down the barrel rather than the tip itself. So the iron lives in its stand whenever it is not in your hand, and you know where that stand is without needing to check.
segments.expand: Explain the exposure route for lead residue and why hand washing matters even though nobody eats in the lab.

segments.title: Hand tools and the combination tool
segments.text: Three tools carry most of the work: small needle-nose pliers, small wire cutters, and a combination crimping tool. The combination tool packs several features. Serrated jaws at the tip grab and hold, but remember what they do to tinned wire. Stripping holes are sized by wire gauge; match the hole to the gauge in your hand. A shaping hole lets you form a loop by moving the wire around it progressively. Threaded screw holes restore a damaged thread: run the screw in, cut the excess, and back it out. The crimp dies are colour coded red, yellow and blue to match the insulated terminal's colour, and each die has a flat side and a round side, so the terminal goes in the correct way round. One rule to carry: a crimp is a complete connection on its own. Crimp or solder, never both. Seat the terminal properly and squeeze fully.
segments.expand: Explain why a crimp is not soldered afterwards and what seating the terminal fully means for a hand crimper.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Five ideas from this lab. One: the wire is tinned copper and the solder carries flux, and both exist to fight oxide, because solder only wets clean metal. Two: heat moves through clean contact area, so wipe and roll the tip bright before every joint and put the flat face on the work. Three: two crossed round wires touch at a point, so you build a thermal bridge, a little solder at the iron contact, and leave the iron there. Four: feed from the far side; when the work melts the solder the joint is ready, and a wipe-on blob has never bonded. Five: the fillet is concave and made by surface tension, strands stay visible through the solder, and more solder is not more strength. Around all of it: stand on your side, pad forward, extraction on, hands washed.
segments.expand: Quiz the student with one mixed question that combines the thermal bridge, far-side feeding and reading the fillet.

lectures.title: Soldering techniques and tool selection
lectures.source: EFAB 202/Lab/EFAB 202 - Lab 02 - Soldering Techniques and Tool Selection.md

segments.title: What this lecture covers
segments.text: This lecture covers the second soldering lab: the two hand tools and what makes a good pair, how to read a fillet and diagnose a joint from it, the mechanical joints that come before any solder, the hook joint and its rules, the layers of a printed circuit board and what a plated hole changes, the three ways to form a component lead, and the tip routine you run every single time. The idea that connects all of it is that the joint is decided before the iron ever touches it. Forming, cleanliness and a tight mechanical wrap are what make solder work; the solder only fills what the forming already holds. Keep that in mind and the rest follows.
segments.expand: Preview why mechanical forming comes before solder, with the hook-joint wrap as the example.

segments.title: Needle-nose pliers: the jaw surface
segments.text: The first tool is a pair of needle-nose pliers, and the jaw surface is the whole point. The jaws must be flat and smooth, never serrated. Serrated jaws cut through the coating on the wire. On tinned copper that coating is what keeps the copper from oxidising, so every serration mark is a corrosion site you built yourself. When you buy them, check the jaws by eye before you pay. After you form a hook, inspect the gripped section for nicks or exposed copper before you solder it; a good bend can still hide a broken coating. Bargain sets were described from direct experience as unusable; one good pair you can actually form wire with is worth more than two bad ones.
segments.expand: Explain why a tiny break in the tin coating matters over the life of a joint, and what to inspect after forming.

segments.title: Cutters: flush or side, and lending
segments.text: The second tool is a cutter, and there are two designs. Flush cutters are spring loaded; the blades cross over and cut cleanly. Side cutters are the long-standing squeeze and release design, and they tend to fold the wire as they cut. Either is acceptable for this work. You do not need both; what matters is a cutter of the right size, the size that was passed around in class. Now a warning about lending. A borrowed pair of cutters came back with a perfect semicircular notch bitten out of the blades, because someone used them on tungsten, which is roughly ten times harder than the wire they are designed for. A notched blade cannot be repaired. Cutters are rated for soft wire; whether a wire fits between the jaws says nothing about whether the blade can take it. If someone genuinely needs a cut made, make the cut for them and keep the tool in your own hand.
segments.expand: Describe the difference in the cut face between flush and side cutters, and why hardness matters more than thickness for blade damage.

segments.title: Reading the concave fillet
segments.text: A sound joint shows a concave fillet. The solder curves inward, meeting both the wire and the pad at a shallow angle, pulled into that shape by surface tension as it bonds to the copper. You do not make the fillet; you let the heat and the surface tension make it. So you should not have to shape it, and you should not have to add extra solder to get it. That gives you a diagnostic you can apply to your own work. If you had to keep adding solder to make the joint look right, the joint is wrong. Reheat and redo the whole thing, both parts. Never paint solder over a bad joint; you are relying on a bond that is not there. A joint that is convex, rounded or balled has not wetted. And one that looks fine on one side but rolls under itself on the other has a rolled region where nothing is stuck at all.
segments.expand: Describe the three cross sections, sound concave fillet, convex ball, and rolled-under edge, and what each says about wetting.

segments.title: Hot and clean: which one fails
segments.text: Two conditions must both hold: both parts hot, and both parts clean, free of plastic, oxide and old solder. Hot is not sufficient. The rolled-under failure is the instructive one, because it can happen on a joint that was hot enough. If the metal was not clean, the solder will not stick no matter how much heat arrives. Heat is the condition people check; cleanliness is the one that quietly fails. When heat was adequate and the solder still lifted, clean and reflux the surface, then rework. Heat also does not arrive evenly. On a joint between two different wires, one heats quickly and the other does not. Put the iron where the slow one is and let the fast one come along with it. Then read the joint: watching which side the solder flows toward tells you which side actually got hot. A fixed count of seconds tells you nothing; the solder does.
segments.expand: Explain why cleanliness is easy to overlook, and how to tell from solder flow which part of a joint reached temperature.

segments.title: The pad and the butt joint
segments.text: For a wire soldered onto a board pad, the rules are short. The wire sits on the pad; nothing overhangs past it. Cut the wire a little shorter rather than letting it run past. Solder going over the pad edge does not matter. Fully covering the pad is not required. What does matter is the concave fillet where the wire meets the pad. Now the butt joint, where two wire ends meet end to end. It is tested by pulling hard on it, not lightly. But even a well-made butt joint is held only at the end of the metallic layer: the contact area is the cut face of the wire and nothing more. There is no overlap and no wrap. That is why it is discouraged for anything structural. It can pass a visual inspection and still be the weakest thing on the board, because the weakness is in the geometry, not in anything you can see.
segments.expand: Contrast the butt joint's end-face contact with a hook joint's wrap, in terms of what actually resists a pull.

segments.title: The hook joint
segments.text: The hook joint is where mechanical forming does the work. Bring the wire in and hook it round the terminal. Put your finger inside the loop and wrap it tight, pushing each turn in hard against the last. Continue for a minimum of six turns. Then clip the ends so nothing pokes out, and bend the remainder in tight. The finger inside the loop is not a detail. Wrapping without it leaves the wire standing off the post, and you finish with visible gaps between the turns. Solder does not close a gap that the forming left behind. It fills a tight wrap; it does not replace one. The wrap is the mechanical hold, and the solder bonds a wrap that is already tight. If you can see daylight anywhere in the wrap, undo it and do it again before any solder goes near it. The forming takes practice, and that is where the effort belongs.
segments.expand: Explain why a gap in the wrap cannot be fixed with solder, in terms of what holds the joint mechanically.

segments.title: Insulation gap, bus wire, strands, turrets
segments.text: A few more forming rules. On a hook terminal there is a deliberate gap between where the insulation ends and where the joint begins, and its length equals the diameter of the insulation on that same wire. Measure it against the wire in your hand; that is what the specification is referenced to, not a fixed number. On a bus wire, hook around as normal, but the hook must not extend past the boundary of the bus wire. Stranded wire is prepared in a fixed order: twist, then tin, then form the loop. Tinning binds the strands so they bend as one wire, and the loop then holds its shape well; formed before tinning, loose strands keep the shape poorly. For a turret, tin the wire to the turret first, then attach it to the board, wrapping about three-quarters of the way around and cutting. Turrets cause trouble because heat travels through the post: sit on one joint too long and you reflow the joint on the other side. Get in and out quickly, and support the work with a third hand or a vise.
segments.expand: Go through the stranded-wire order again and explain why tinning before forming makes the loop hold, then the turret reflow problem.

segments.title: The board: FR4, finish, mask, silkscreen
segments.text: The board in your hand is a printed circuit board, though a limited one, because it carries only pads and not the printed wiring that gives the board its name. The common material is FR4, a fibreglass substrate with copper bonded to it; the fibreglass is the structure and the copper is the conductor. Over the pads sits a tin based finish. Copper oxidises, so the tin is allowed to oxidise instead, protecting the copper without thinning it; that is why you see no bare copper on a new board, and it is the same logic as the tinned practice wire. The green layer is solder mask. It masks off everything not meant to be soldered. That is what makes machine soldering possible, and it prevents a great many bridges and shorts in hand soldering too. The white printing is silkscreen, the legend; any shape can go on it. Green and white are common here, not a universal rule.
segments.expand: Explain how solder mask prevents bridges between neighbouring pads, and why the finish over the pads is like tinned wire.

segments.title: Holes: unplated, plated, multilayer
segments.text: How many sides you solder is decided by the hole. A single-sided board has copper on one face only. A double-sided board with unplated holes has copper on both faces but nothing inside the hole, just bare fibreglass. A lead pushed through has to be soldered on each side separately, because nothing carries between the two faces. A plated through hole is different: copper is deposited on the hole wall as well, forming a barrel that connects the layers. For the demonstrated process you heat and feed from the specified side, and wetting and capillary action carry the solder up through the barrel. Gravity is barely involved; the fill would happen much the same upside down. You still check the result: the required fill and fillet have to be there, and sometimes the solder only reaches partway up the hole. Beyond that are multilayer boards, with conducting layers buried between sheets of FR4; boards with eighteen layers exist, and space hardware goes further.
segments.expand: Describe capillary action drawing solder into a wetted copper barrel and why an unplated hole has no such path.

segments.title: Lead forming and clipping
segments.text: A component lead can sit in its hole three ways. Straight through gives the least support; it is simple, but the part can fall out while you work. Fully clinched, bent flat along the pad, gives the most support and also lowers the part's height, but it is the hardest to remove later. Set over to one side gives enough support to hold the part and is quick to undo, and that is the everyday choice. Whichever form you use, mind the clipped end. If you cut the lead after soldering, you can be left with a bare copper end sticking out of the solder. If the lead was tinned before it went in, you are fine. If bare wire runs through, the cut end must finish covered. Check every clipped end; clipping can create a defect as easily as finish a joint.
segments.expand: Compare the three lead forms on support, height and ease of removal, and explain the bare-copper-end problem.

segments.title: Tip discipline, every single time
segments.text: Before you start, reset the bench: no tangled wires, nothing lying near the iron tip. Check the tip every time it leaves the holder, not once at the start of the session. A clean tip is bright and shiny. Oxidation impairs wetting and the heat transfer at the contact, so the routine is fixed. Lift the iron and check the tip. Wipe it, every time, without exception. If a wipe does not clean it, add a little fresh solder to the tip and wipe again. Then go to the joint with a clean, hot iron. The diagnostic for a dead tip: put solder on it and watch. If the solder pulls away into a ball instead of spreading, surface tension is not working for you; there is an oxide coating on the tip. Clean it properly with tip cleaner. If that does not recover it, the tip is replaced, never filed. And you cannot wait for a convenient moment. A tip sitting in your hand goes dark while you are deciding.
segments.expand: Explain why solder balling on the tip proves an oxide layer, and walk through the check, wipe, re-tin, wipe routine.

segments.title: Recap
segments.text: Five ideas from this lab. One: smooth flat plier jaws and one good cutter of the right size; serrations cut the coating, and a cutter lent out on hard wire comes back notched. Two: a sound joint has a concave fillet you did not shape; if you had to add solder to make it look right, redo it, and never paint over a bad joint. Both parts hot, both parts clean, and cleanliness is the one that quietly fails. Three: forming comes first. Finger in the loop, six tight turns minimum, no daylight, because solder fills a tight wrap but cannot close a gap. Four: the hole decides the soldering. Unplated means each side separately; plated means capillary action carries the solder through, and you still check the fill. Five: set the lead over for everyday work, cover every clipped end, and check and wipe the tip every time it leaves the holder.
segments.expand: Quiz the student with one mixed question that combines the hook wrap, the insulation gap and reading the fillet.
